member.name: F:Il2CppPuppetMasta.SubBehaviourHandPose.HandPose.Custom
member.summary: Uses the five curl amounts passed to SetHandPose instead of replacing them with a named gesture.

remarks.para: Each amount blends that finger between the configured OpenHand pose at 0 and Fist pose at 1. The arguments are thumb, index, middle, ring, and pinky, in that order; they are unitless blend amounts, not angles. For example, Custom with thumb=0, index=0, and the other three at 1 produces the same finger targets as FingerGun.

Values outside 0 to 1 are limited to the endpoint poses during interpolation. The optional curl arguments default to 1, so choosing Custom without supplying them requests all fingers closed. To supply an entirely different HandPoseData asset, use SetTargetPose instead.

member.name: F:Il2CppPuppetMasta.SubBehaviourHandPose.HandPose.IndexPoint
member.summary: Requests an open index finger while curling the thumb and the other fingers toward a fist.

remarks.para: The preset curl amounts are thumb 0.9, index 0, middle 0.95, ring 0.95, and pinky 0.95. Here 0 is the configured OpenHand finger pose and 1 is the configured Fist finger pose. These are blend amounts, not degrees. The thumb and remaining fingers are nearly closed rather than all being fully closed.

member.name: F:Il2CppPuppetMasta.SubBehaviourHandPose.HandPose.LooseFist
member.summary: Requests a partially closed fist, with every finger blended 70% from OpenHand toward Fist.

remarks.para: The 0.7 value is a blend amount between this behavior’s two configured pose assets, not a 70-degree bend. The exact finger shape therefore depends on those assets. SetHandPose replaces any caller-supplied curl amounts with this preset.

member.name: F:Il2CppPuppetMasta.SubBehaviourHandPose.HandPose.MiddleFinger
member.summary: Requests an almost open middle finger while leaving the other fingers mostly curled.

remarks.para: The preset curl amounts are thumb 0.85, index 0.96, middle 0.05, ring 0.95, and pinky 0.95. A value of 0 uses the configured OpenHand finger pose and 1 uses Fist. The middle finger is therefore near its open pose, rather than exactly at it; these values are blends, not angles.

member.name: F:Il2CppPuppetMasta.SubBehaviourHandPose.HandPose.RelaxedOpen
member.summary: Requests a mostly open hand, with every finger blended 20% from OpenHand toward Fist.

remarks.para: A curl of 0.2 leaves the fingers near the configured open pose with some closure. It is a unitless blend between the two pose assets, not a fixed angle; their data controls the final shape. SetHandPose uses these preset amounts instead of any supplied curl arguments.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArenaLootItem.LootType.HEAVYGUN

remarks.para: CopyWaveProfile with randLoot enabled selects a random entry from StaticProfiles.shotgunLootList. It does not inspect a weapon’s mass or switch the configured object to heavy ammunition.

The random list selectors choose by list index and ignore each candidate’s percentage setting. Ordinary arena spawning uses the entry’s spawnable directly, so this category does not transform that object when randomization is disabled.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Arena_GameController.ArenaStartMode.CUSTOM
member.summary: Omits the automatic session-begin and entry/bell countdown choices so another caller can arrange the start.

remarks.para: OnArenaSessionBegin only schedules its opening sequence for ON_START. ARENA_PlayerEnter only schedules its entry countdown for ON_TRIGGER or prepares the bell stage for ON_TRIGGER_BELL, and ARENA_RingTheBell only acts in that bell mode. Selecting CUSTOM skips those automatic choices.

Arrange a caller to perform ready/entry setup and explicitly start a countdown or call StartNextWave. assignedRoundProfile is the selected collection of rounds and enemy waves. isPlayerReady permits player entry; ARENA_StartMatch sets it true before its ready actions. ACTIVE is the arena state that permits StartNextWave. The current round and wave numbers must select existing entries: the routine subtracts one from each number for its list lookup, so 1 selects the first round or wave. For example, a custom scene interaction can do its own countdown before invoking StartNextWave; the enum alone neither runs the interaction nor advances a wave.

This is a start strategy, separate from RoundProfileGroup.ArenaGameMode.CUSTOM, which describes the selected gameplay mode and its friendly-NPC setup; an NPC is a character controlled by the game. Other explicit controller paths, such as objective-start methods or testing helpers, can still start timed work regardless of this omitted automatic entry choice.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Arena_GameController.ArenaStartMode.ON_START
member.summary: Schedules the opening countdown when the arena’s base session begins and an assigned profile group exists.

remarks.para: Start is Unity’s startup callback, a routine Unity calls when the component first starts. The controller’s Start begins the base session, and its enabled session listener, a routine called when the session-begin notification fires, handles this start mode. The assigned profile group is the selected collection of rounds and enemy waves. OnArenaSessionBegin marks isPlayerReady true before calling ARENA_PlayerEnter; entry then invokes playerEnter before its sound, ammunition snapshot and profile setup. The session handler schedules the opening countdown afterward. The described playerEnter and playerReady event calls supply no arguments.

Because readiness is normally already true, its later ready-up block skips playerReady and geometry/weapon ready setup. That block can run if entry actions cleared the flag: it sets readiness true before playerReady and its setup. ON_START does not itself set arenaState to ACTIVE, so prepare the selected group and state before expecting the countdown to start enemies.

The opening countdown uses arenaStartDelay, the requested starting duration in seconds of scaled game time. Its coroutine, a sequence that continues over frames, uses arenaTimerValue, the controller’s shared remaining-time value in seconds. For a positive duration it subtracts the frame’s scaled game-time duration, yields to a later frame, then checks whether that shared value is zero or below before calling StartNextWave. Crossing zero does not guarantee the call occurs in that same frame. For example, 3 requests about 3 game-time seconds, which can take longer in real time during slow motion. Zero reaches the start call immediately; a negative duration is replaced with 10 seconds by this countdown. StartNextWave still requires arenaState to be ACTIVE.
Selecting this enum later does not itself call Start or begin a new session. It is the session-begin notification that runs this checked producer.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Arena_GameController.ArenaStartMode.ON_TRIGGER
member.summary: Schedules the opening countdown when ARENA_PlayerEnter is called for a ready player.

remarks.para: isPlayerReady permits player entry, and ARENA_StartMatch sets it true before its ready actions. The assigned profile group is the selected collection of rounds and enemy waves. Entry rejects the call while isPlayerReady is false. An eligible call invokes playerEnter with no arguments first, requests playerEnterClip, then starts the countdown before taking the ammunition snapshot and refreshing the current profile caches. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action; entry listeners therefore run before that countdown starts.

Arrange the scene trigger or another caller to invoke ARENA_PlayerEnter. This enum chooses the entry behavior; the inspected Start, OnEnable and OnDisable routines do not connect arenaStartTrigger to ARENA_PlayerEnter, so configure the scene action or call it explicitly. Calling the method directly also takes this path, so a physical trigger crossing is not required by the method itself.

The opening countdown uses arenaStartDelay, the requested starting duration in seconds of scaled game time. Its coroutine, a sequence that continues over frames, uses arenaTimerValue, the controller’s shared remaining-time value in seconds. For a positive duration it subtracts the frame’s scaled game-time duration, yields to a later frame, then checks whether that shared value is zero or below before calling StartNextWave. Crossing zero does not guarantee the call occurs in that same frame. For example, 3 requests about 3 game-time seconds, which can take longer in real time during slow motion. Zero reaches the start call immediately; a negative duration is replaced with 10 seconds by this countdown. StartNextWave still requires arenaState to be ACTIVE, the state that permits a wave to start.

There is no entry-only-once latch in this path. Repeated eligible entry calls can start additional countdowns while replacing the saved handle, without first stopping the prior countdown. These countdowns share arenaTimerValue. Starting another one resets that value to the requested starting duration (or the negative-duration fallback); while several run, each can subtract frame time from the same value, so the countdown can progress faster than one sequence. This does not guarantee a fixed speedup or number of wave starts. Choose one scene entry action rather than relying on the enum to suppress repeated calls.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Arena_GameController.ArenaStartMode.ON_TRIGGER_BELL

remarks.para: isPlayerReady permits player entry, and ARENA_StartMatch sets it true before its ready actions. The assigned profile group is the selected collection of rounds and enemy waves. PROTECT is the gameplay mode whose entry sets up the king character, separately from this start-strategy choice. ARENA_PlayerEnter requires isPlayerReady true, invokes playerEnter, requests the entry sound and then invokes readyUpBell for an assigned group other than PROTECT. The described playerEnter, readyUpBell and ringBell calls supply no arguments. readyUpBell is a configurable action list for preparing the bell stage. ARENA_PlayerEnter itself does not set isRung or start the countdown in this branch; the configured actions can change the latch or call other methods.

ARENA_RingTheBell acts only in this start mode while isRung is false. It sets isRung true before invoking ringBell, then starts the countdown. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action; ringBell listeners therefore see the latch already true before the new countdown starts. ARENA_ResetTheBell clears the latch for another accepted action.

PROTECT entry skips readyUpBell, clears isRung and starts a coroutine, a sequence continuing over frames, with a 5-real-time-second wait target, then continues on a frame to request the king; this wait is unaffected by slow-motion game-time scaling; SpawnKing then calls ARENA_RingTheBell without waiting for the king’s spawn request to finish. The bell method’s QUIT check skips its later loot request, but happens after its event and countdown.

The opening countdown uses arenaStartDelay, the requested starting duration in seconds of scaled game time. Its coroutine, a sequence that continues over frames, uses arenaTimerValue, the controller’s shared remaining-time value in seconds. For a positive duration it subtracts the frame’s scaled game-time duration, yields to a later frame, then checks whether that shared value is zero or below before calling StartNextWave. Crossing zero does not guarantee the call occurs in that same frame. For example, 3 requests about 3 game-time seconds, which can take longer in real time during slow motion. Zero reaches the start call immediately; a negative duration is replaced with 10 seconds by this countdown. StartNextWave still requires arenaState to be ACTIVE, the state that permits a wave to start.

Configure the actual trigger/bell actions to call the entry and bell methods. The bell method itself does not require isPlayerReady or ACTIVE, so a direct call can ring before entry; the eventual StartNextWave still requires ACTIVE. Assigning this enum or invoking the event list directly does not itself perform either method’s readiness/latch/countdown work.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Arena_GameController.ArenaState.ACTIVE
member.summary: Allows StartNextWave and the ordinary enemy producer to run their combat paths.

remarks.para: Challenge selection and resume set this value. StartNextWave checks it before resolving the selected profiles and starting its timer/enemy work. The ordinary enemy-spawning routine also needs isSpawning to permit spawning, fewer currently alive enemies than currentWave.maxConcurrent (the wave’s maximum simultaneous enemy count), and an unused enemy profile (settings for an enemy request). For example, 2 alive with a maximum of 3 permits another request subject to the other conditions; ACTIVE alone does not make an enemy appear.

Setting ACTIVE does not ready the player, ring the bell or start a countdown. ARENA_QuitChallenge accepts a quit only from this state. At the end of wave-reset cleanup, ACTIVE returns without calling EndOfMode; the other four named states call EndOfMode. CoEndOfWave can separately request the next wave’s loot after starting the reset, while that reset is still running.

There is no universal ACTIVE check on every notification or counter: enabled headshot/projectile callbacks can count outside combat, and the wave-end kill-count check excludes FAILED specifically. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. Use the actual operation’s gates when arranging a custom start.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Arena_GameController.ArenaState.FAILED
member.summary: Ending state that suppresses the checked wave-completion test and EndOfMode’s success score/completion handling.

remarks.para: FailProtectMode, unless the arena is already WIN, sets FAILED first, requests failModeClip and starts wave-reset cleanup. The reset fires waveEnd before clearing its spawning and ongoing-wave flags; a callback is a routine called to perform or report an action, so listeners can still see the prior flags while arenaState already says FAILED.

EndOfMode skips its CalculatePlayerScore, UpdateChallengeCompletion and modeWin branch for FAILED, then continues its general cleanup and selects WAITING. If the configured challenges form a stacked sequence (several challenges played in order) and another challenge remains, EndOfMode then calls ProgressToNextProfile: it selects the next challenge as ACTIVE and separately sets isPlayerReady true. This progression is outside the success-only branch, so FAILED does not prevent it. This is not a global ban on every separate score call: other callbacks can calculate or submit score through their own paths.

A method named for failure need not assign this enum. The checked FailObjectiveMode stops its coroutines, plays the failure sound, fires ObjectiveFailed and ends the base session without writing arenaState to FAILED. Read or set the actual arena state when that distinction matters.

Assigning arenaState changes this stored control value only. SetArenaState also requests the corresponding fail/win sound for those values, but does not run the full reset. It does not by itself cancel enemySpawnCTS, stop saved coroutines or despawn NPCs. enemySpawnCTS is the cancellation source used to ask the enemy-spawning routine to stop. NPCs are computer-controlled characters; despawning removes them from active play. The async spawning routine can pause until a spawn request or a frame wait finishes, then continue; it is separate from the saved coroutines. A coroutine is a sequence that continues over frames. The ordinary async enemy loop requires ACTIVE and can repeatedly log without pausing for another frame if moved into another state without cancelling it.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Arena_GameController.ArenaState.WIN
member.summary: Success state selected by limited-profile completion and explicit objective/cure victory paths.

remarks.para: Limited-profile completion means finishing the finite configured rounds and waves. CheckProfileForNextWave selects WIN when the configured rounds and waves are exhausted and the first configured round’s roundMode is LIMITED; ARENA_ObjectiveProfileCompleted and StopSpawningAndCureAll are the explicit objective/cure victory methods. Those paths set WIN before requesting winModeClip and starting their appropriate reset or cure sequence. SetArenaState(WIN) likewise sets the stored state before requesting the sound, but does not itself complete a profile or start reset cleanup.

NPCs are computer-controlled characters. The registered NPC-death handler returns early in WIN, and FailProtectMode leaves an existing WIN untouched. StartNextWave requires ACTIVE, so it does not start another combat wave from this state. A wave reset in WIN eventually calls EndOfMode, whose normal success handling calculates score, updates completion and invokes modeWin before its later cleanup selects WAITING. If the configured challenges form a stacked sequence (several challenges played in order) and another challenge remains, EndOfMode then calls ProgressToNextProfile: it selects the next challenge as ACTIVE and separately sets isPlayerReady true.

modeWin is not exclusively tied to this value: EndOfMode’s success condition also covers other non-FAILED, non-QUIT states and a SURVIVAL quit. WinStateFX only plays the success clip without setting WIN. Neither hearing the sound nor receiving that event alone proves the current state is WIN.

Assigning arenaState changes this stored control value only. SetArenaState also requests the corresponding fail/win sound for those values, but does not run the full reset. It does not by itself cancel enemySpawnCTS, stop saved coroutines or despawn NPCs. enemySpawnCTS is the cancellation source used to ask the enemy-spawning routine to stop. NPCs are computer-controlled characters; despawning removes them from active play. The async spawning routine can pause until a spawn request or a frame wait finishes, then continue; it is separate from the saved coroutines. A coroutine is a sequence that continues over frames. The ordinary async enemy loop requires ACTIVE and can repeatedly log without pausing for another frame if moved into another state without cancelling it.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArmFinale.ArmStage.Ascent
member.summary: Tracks the player’s reported grip during ascent and switches to Dropped after the release timeout.

remarks.para: Update is Unity’s routine called once per rendered frame while the component is active. A joint is a physics connection between objects. Target angular velocity is the requested turning speed; the angular-X drive is the spring/damping control that tries to turn around the joint’s X direction. The normal entry is an Update in Hold with _attachedHandCount greater than zero. It sets Ascent before stopping decent, playing ascent and setting windmillJoint’s target angular velocity and angular-X drive. A PlayableDirector plays a prepared timeline of animation and other scene actions; the assigned ascent timeline supplies that presentation.

On subsequent Ascent Updates, a positive hand count refreshes _timer with Time.time, Unity’s scaled game-time clock in seconds, following changes to game speed. If the count becomes zero or negative and Time.time − _timer is greater than 0.5 seconds, the stage becomes Dropped. This uses the last positive-count Ascent Update, not the detach callback itself; a callback is a routine called to report an action.

Directly assigning Ascent skips the Hold-to-Ascent director and drive changes. Entry through Hold also does not initialize _timer until a later positive-count Ascent Update, so an immediate release before that update can use an older timestamp. This stage does not itself test a fall, move the player or cancel windmill-adjustment sequences.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArmFinale.ArmStage.Decent
member.summary: Stage recorded by GongHit before it plays the arm’s descent timeline.

remarks.para: GongHit first enables offscreen updates on an assigned armMesh, keeping the animated mesh updating outside the camera’s view, then sets Decent and calls Play on decent. A PlayableDirector plays a prepared timeline of animation and other scene actions. The spelling "Decent" follows the upstream enum and director name even though the action is descent.

Update is Unity’s routine called once per rendered frame while the component is active. ArmFinale’s Update does no stage-specific work while Decent is selected. ReadyForAscent changes the stage to Hold; only an Update with a positive reported hand count then stops the descent director and plays the ascent director. Selecting Decent by assigning _armStage does not itself call GongHit, start playback or reset _timer.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArmFinale.ArmStage.Dropped
member.summary: Repeatedly offers the most recently detached player rig to the arm’s palm seat after the ascent release timeout.

remarks.para: Ascent changes to Dropped when the reported hand count is nonpositive and more than 0.5 scaled game-time seconds have passed since the stored _timer timestamp. Ascent refreshes that timestamp on positive-count Updates, but entry from Hold does not initialize it; a release before the first such Update can therefore use older data. Scaled game time follows changes to game speed. This is a grip-report timeout, not a collision or measured-fall test.

Update is Unity’s routine called once per rendered frame while the component is active. Every Dropped Update sets palmSeat’s ingressSmoothTime, its entry-position smoothing time, to 0.75 seconds and calls IngressRig with _lastRmToDetatch, the RigManager cached by the most recent hand-detach callback, a routine called to report a hand letting go. Each detach updates that cache; it does not wait for the final hand. RigManager groups the objects representing the player’s tracked controls and in-game body. The smoothing time controls how gradually the player moves toward the seat, not an exact duration until seating completes.

Seat ignores an entry request if it already has a registered rig. An empty seat requires a valid supplied rig. Dropped does not advance to another stage after one request, so later frames keep applying the smoothing setting and requesting entry. Assigning this stage alone uses whatever detached-rig cache already exists; it does not populate the cache or physically prove that someone fell.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArmFinale.ArmStage.Hold
member.summary: Waits for a positive reported hand count before starting the ascent timeline and windmill drive.

remarks.para: Update is Unity’s routine called once per rendered frame while the component is active. A joint is a physics connection between objects; its angular-X drive uses spring and damping to request turning around the joint’s X direction, rather than directly prescribing the achieved rotation. ReadyForAscent selects Hold without stopping the descent timeline, playing the ascent timeline or resetting _timer. On an Update with _attachedHandCount greater than zero, it changes the stage to Ascent before stopping decent, playing ascent and setting the windmill joint’s angular drive.

An already-reported grip satisfies this test; a new hand-attach report after entry is not required. With a zero or negative count, the checked Hold branch makes no changes. Selecting Hold does not by itself freeze the arm’s physics or any timeline already playing, so "waiting" is the controller’s rule rather than a guarantee that the arm is stationary.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArmFinale.ArmStage.Preshow
member.summary: Initial stage whose Update branch performs none of the arm’s later grip, seat or release actions.

remarks.para: Awake is Unity’s initialization callback, a routine Unity calls to set up the component, and sets Preshow. Update is Unity’s routine called each frame while the component is active. The checked ArmFinale Update only handles Decent, Hold, Ascent, Dropped and Void specially, so Preshow waits for a caller such as GongHit or ReadyForAscent to select another stage.

This value does not freeze physics, stop an existing timeline, clear the hand count or reset _timer. Setting it later is not a full finale reset. WindmillProjectRotation has no stage guard and can still start its coroutine, a sequence that continues over frames, while Preshow is selected.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArmFinale.ArmStage.Void
member.summary: Runs the finale’s offscreen-renderer restriction and delayed grip/seat release checks.

remarks.para: ReadyForVoid sets Void, activates holeStopper and then saves Time.time into _timer. Time.time is the scaled game-time clock in seconds, following changes to game speed; it supplies the reference timestamp for the later delays. Activating the stopper can run enable callbacks, routines Unity calls to respond to becoming active, before that new timestamp is saved.

Update is Unity’s routine called each frame while the component is active. Every Void Update disables offscreen updates on an assigned armMesh, stopping animated-mesh updates outside the camera’s view. After elapsed game time is greater than one second, a positive reported hand count makes hostManager.ForceDetachAll request release from each configured host, one of the managed grabbable objects. After greater than 0.75 seconds, a valid palmSeat seat Rigidbody, Unity’s component for physics motion, allows an EgressRig(true) request. That routine itself exits only if a player rig is registered; the Rigidbody test is not an occupancy test.

If both thresholds pass on the same Update, the force-detach call happens before the seat-exit request. The checks repeat while their conditions remain true. Selecting Void by assigning _armStage skips holeStopper activation and the new timestamp, so existing _timer data controls the delays. ReadyForVoid can be called again to record a new time after activation.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.DebugMode.MINIMAL
member.summary: Writes short session messages and selected messages about computer-controlled characters to Unity’s Console log.

remarks.para: The Console log is a list of messages for developers to read. Beginning or ending a session writes a short message without the game-clock time that VERBOSE adds. Some character messages, such as choosing a friendly target or reporting a friendly character’s death, still appear. The extra registration and despawn messages that require VERBOSE are skipped. Despawning means removing a character from active play.

For example, choose MINIMAL when you want confirmation that a session started without the extra character-registration details. This setting does not hide the timer or character-count text on screen, and some error messages are written regardless of the selected debug mode.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.DebugMode.NONE
member.summary: Skips the session and character log messages that check the controller’s debug setting.

remarks.para: This is the controller’s initial debug setting. Beginning or ending a session skips the normal session message, and character registration, death, and despawn skip their optional diagnostic messages. Despawning means removing a character from active play.

NONE does not silence every message. For example, reporting the death of a character that was never registered still writes an error to Unity’s Console log, the message list for developers. A mismatch between the friendly-character count and its list also still writes an error.

The timer and character-count text can still update on screen. For example, choose NONE to reduce optional log messages while keeping the session’s normal time and count displays; hide those display objects separately if you want them invisible.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.DebugMode.VERBOSE
member.summary: Adds game-clock times and extra character-registration and removal details to Unity’s Console log.

remarks.para: The Console log is a list of messages for developers to read. Beginning and ending a session include Unity’s current game-clock time in seconds. This is the game’s running clock, which is affected by the game’s time scale; it is not the session timer value or a real-world date and time. Time scale is the game’s speed setting: lower values make the game clock advance more slowly; for example, 0.5 makes it advance at half speed.

Registering a computer-controlled character adds its name, the game-clock time, and the current active-enemy count before registration changes that count. Extra messages also report a character being added to the controller’s data and being despawned, meaning removed from active play. VERBOSE includes the selected character messages that MINIMAL also allows.

For example, use VERBOSE to compare when a session began with when characters were registered or removed. It does not turn on a separate on-screen diagnostics display: the normal timer and character-count text updates do not check this setting.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.EndMode.EXPLICIT
member.summary: Requests the level chosen in explicitSceneCrate after the session’s end countdown and transition effect.

remarks.para: Value 3. explicitSceneCrate is a reference to the packaged level to open. When the base controller’s end countdown finishes in this mode, a missing reference causes no load request. With a reference, the controller requests a transition-effect object. If that object is created with the required FadeVolume component, the later spawn callback installs a function to run when the fade finishes. A callback is a function called later when an event occurs; FadeVolume is the component that runs the fade effect. The fade-finished function asks the scene streamer, the game’s level-loading system, to load the chosen level with the configured loading level.

The end countdown uses delayedEndMaxTime in game-time seconds. A positive value starts that countdown; a negative value replaces it with defaultEndDelayedMaxTime. Exactly 0 makes the routine return without requesting a transition. Each frame subtracts Time.deltaTime, the game-time seconds since the previous frame, so slow motion stretches the wait in real time. The action is checked on a later frame after the countdown reaches 0 or below; the configured time is not an exact wall-clock deadline.

For example, choose a destination level in explicitSceneCrate and set delayedEndMaxTime to 5 for a five-game-second end countdown followed by the transition effect. The request starts loading work that can finish later; EndSession returning does not mean the destination is already loaded. The mode and destination are read when the countdown finishes, so changing them during the wait changes the selected action.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.EndMode.LOAD_NEXT
member.summary: Selects the base controller’s next-level end mode, which performs no level load in this build.

remarks.para: Value 0. EndSession starts the same end-countdown routine as the loading modes, but its LOAD_NEXT branch simply finishes. The separate LOADNEXTLEVEL method also has an empty body. This setting therefore does not automatically choose or open the next story level through the base controller.

The end countdown uses delayedEndMaxTime in game-time seconds. A positive value starts that countdown; a negative value replaces it with defaultEndDelayedMaxTime. Exactly 0 makes the routine return without requesting a transition. Each frame subtracts Time.deltaTime, the game-time seconds since the previous frame, so slow motion stretches the wait in real time. The action is checked on a later frame after the countdown reaches 0 or below; the configured time is not an exact wall-clock deadline.

For example, selecting LOAD_NEXT does not provide automatic story progression when the countdown ends. A level-specific controller or event must supply its own transition if that is needed. This description covers the base controller’s inspected methods; other level scripts may have separate behavior.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.EndMode.NONE
member.summary: Ends the base controller’s session without starting its automatic end-countdown transition.

remarks.para: Value 2. EndSession still fires sessionEnd, marks the session as no longer ongoing, stops its stored timer coroutine, and updates the displayed time. A coroutine is a routine that can pause and continue on later frames. NONE skips starting the separate routine that would wait and select a level action.

For example, use NONE when the session should end while the player stays in the level to view results or use another exit. sessionEnd listeners, functions called by that event, may still request their own loads. The event runs before the session flag is cleared and before endMode is checked, so a listener can change the mode chosen by this call.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.EndMode.RELOAD_CURRENT
member.summary: Requests a reload of the current level after the session’s end countdown.

remarks.para: Value 1. When the base controller’s end countdown finishes in this mode, it calls RELOADCURRENTLEVEL, which asks the scene streamer to reload. This starts loading work that can finish later; it does not guarantee that the reload has completed before EndSession returns. The scene streamer ignores the request if it is already loading.

The end countdown uses delayedEndMaxTime in game-time seconds. A positive value starts that countdown; a negative value replaces it with defaultEndDelayedMaxTime. Exactly 0 makes the routine return without requesting a transition. Each frame subtracts Time.deltaTime, the game-time seconds since the previous frame, so slow motion stretches the wait in real time. The action is checked on a later frame after the countdown reaches 0 or below; the configured time is not an exact wall-clock deadline.

For example, set delayedEndMaxTime to 3 to wait about three game-time seconds before requesting the reload. Setting it to 0 does not produce an immediate reload through EndSession. The mode is read again when the countdown finishes, so changing endMode during the wait can select a different action.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.GameMode.ARENA
member.summary: Selects the arena-combat category and enables the base controller's arena-specific enemy targeting and death records.

remarks.para: This value is 1. When gameMode is ARENA, RegisterNPCBase assigns a registered enemy a target through the friendly-target list, provided that list is not empty. The list can include the player and friendly characters. An NPC is a character controlled by the game. Friendly NPCs do not receive this enemy-target assignment.

When a registered NPC dies in this mode, OnNPC_DeathBase also records its death time from the game clock, in seconds, and adds its data to the controller's extra dead-NPC data list. This applies to registered friendly characters as well as enemies. Changing gameMode affects these checks on later registration and death calls; it does not retarget every existing enemy immediately.

For a level with combat waves, select ARENA and configure that level's wave rules, timerMode and leaderboard scoreType too. The enum choice alone does not start a wave, choose a timer direction or decide how a score is submitted.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.GameMode.LINEAR
member.summary: Selects normal level-play mode, which skips the base controller's arena-specific target assignment and extra death records.

remarks.para: This value is 0 and represents the category used for a level with structured progression or objectives. In RegisterNPCBase and OnNPC_DeathBase, only ARENA enables the extra targeting and death-time bookkeeping. Normal enemy registration, living/dead lists and kill counts still follow those routines' other rules.

For example, a campaign-style level can use LINEAR while its level controller and triggers handle objectives and the next-level transition. Setting this value does not itself complete an objective or load the next level. BeginSession selects its timer from timerMode, and SubmitScoreByType selects the score format from the leaderboard's scoreType, independently of this enum.
NPC means a non-player character controlled by the game.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.GameMode.TIME_TRIAL
member.summary: Selects the time-trial challenge category, which skips the base controller's arena-specific enemy targeting and extra death records.

remarks.para: This value is 2. Use it to identify a challenge where completion speed matters. In RegisterNPCBase and OnNPC_DeathBase, it follows the non-ARENA path: it does not add the arena-only target assignment or extra death-time record. Other enemy registration and kill-count rules can still run.

Configure timerMode separately to choose how the session clock runs. BeginSession reads that timer setting rather than gameMode. Leaderboard submission also reads the leaderboard data's scoreType: a time score can use whole seconds or milliseconds, while a points score uses score, the controller's stored point total. For example, a timed course can select TIME_TRIAL to identify its category, choose timerMode for its clock, and configure a time-based leaderboard. Choosing this enum alone does not start a timer or measure a completed run.
NPC means a non-player character controlled by the game.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.TimerMode.COUNT_DOWN
member.summary: Counts remaining game-time seconds down to zero, then ends the session.

remarks.para: The timer starts from maxTime, the requested session duration in seconds. If maxTime is zero or negative, it copies defaultMaxTime, the fallback duration in seconds, into both maxTime and the timer value. This mode therefore replaces the previous timer value when its sequence begins.

Each frame subtracts Unity's scaled frame duration. Time.timeScale is the unitless game-speed factor: 1 means normal speed, 0.5 means half speed, and 0 means game-time pause. For example, a 60-second countdown takes about 120 real seconds at a steady timeScale of 0.5, and stops decreasing at 0.

The frame subtraction can leave a small negative remainder. On the next timer step, a value at or below zero causes EndSession to run; this is not a clamp that stores exactly zero. EndSession sends sessionEnd, its session-end notification with no arguments, before setting isSessionOngoing to false and stopping the timer.

BeginSession reads timerMode when it starts the timer coroutine, a sequence that continues over several frames. A frame is one game update step. Choose this value before starting the session; changing timerMode afterward does not replace the timer sequence already running.
isSessionOngoing is the controller’s flag meaning the session is active.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.TimerMode.COUNT_UP
member.summary: Adds elapsed game-time seconds to the controller's timer while the session is running.

remarks.para: Each frame adds Unity's scaled frame duration to the existing timer value. Time.timeScale is the unitless game-speed factor: 1 means normal speed, 0.5 means half speed, and 0 means game-time pause. At a steady value of 0.5, two real seconds add about one timer second; at 0, the timer stops increasing.

The count-up sequence and BeginSession do not reset the timer to zero. A start path must initialize its value if you need a fresh measurement. The delayed-start sequence clears it after finishing a start countdown, but its immediate-start branch can begin without that reset.

This timer keeps increasing while isSessionOngoing is true and does not end the session merely because maxTime, the requested session-duration limit in seconds, has been reached. Another action must end the session.

BeginSession reads timerMode when it starts the timer coroutine, a sequence that continues over several frames. A frame is one game update step. Choose this value before starting the session; changing timerMode afterward does not replace the timer sequence already running.
isSessionOngoing is the controller’s flag meaning the session is active.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.TimerMode.COUNT_UP_REALTIME
member.summary: Adds real-time-speed seconds to the controller's timer, but stops increasing during a game-time pause.

remarks.para: Each frame adds the unscaled frame duration, the number of real seconds between frames. Time.timeScale is the unitless game-speed factor: 1 means normal speed, 0.5 means half speed, and 0 means game-time pause. At 0.5 this timer still gains about one second per real second, unlike COUNT_UP.

The compiled sequence explicitly checks for timeScale equal to zero and skips the addition in that case. Consequently, slow motion does not slow this timer, but a pause implemented by setting timeScale to 0 does stop it.

The count-up sequence adds to the existing timer value; neither that sequence nor BeginSession resets it to zero. A start path must initialize the value for a fresh measurement. The delayed-start sequence clears it after finishing a start countdown, but its immediate-start branch can begin without that reset.
It runs while isSessionOngoing is true and has no automatic end at maxTime, the requested session-duration limit in seconds. Another action must end the session.

BeginSession reads timerMode when it starts the timer coroutine, a sequence that continues over several frames. A frame is one game update step. Choose this value before starting the session; changing timerMode afterward does not replace the timer sequence already running.
isSessionOngoing is the controller’s flag meaning the session is active.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BaseGameController.TimerMode.REALTIME
member.summary: Shows real seconds since the application started, rather than time elapsed in the current session.

remarks.para: Every timer frame replaces the controller's timer value with Unity's realtimeSinceStartup clock. For example, if the application has already been running for five minutes when the session begins, the value is about 300 seconds, not zero. This clock is not the time of day or the time since loading the current level.

Time.timeScale is the unitless game-speed factor: 1 means normal speed, 0.5 means half speed, and 0 means game-time pause. This mode does not test that factor: it continues reading the real-time clock in slow motion and at 0, provided the timer sequence is still running and Unity continues processing frames.

The sequence runs while isSessionOngoing is true. It does not end the session at maxTime, the requested session-duration limit in seconds, and it overwrites a manually changed timer value on the next timer frame.

BeginSession reads timerMode when it starts the timer coroutine, a sequence that continues over several frames. A frame is one game update step. Choose this value before starting the session; changing timerMode afterward does not replace the timer sequence already running.
isSessionOngoing is the controller’s flag meaning the session is active.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BehaviourCrablet.JumpType.Attack
member.summary: Launches toward the sensed target's head, then checks for a close-range attack during the jump.

remarks.para: The jump calculation starts at the Crablet's first physical body and aims at the targetHead body stored by its sensors. A physical body, called a Rigidbody in Unity, stores an object's motion. The calculation predicts target movement using world-space head velocity, measured along the level's shared coordinate axes rather than axes that turn with the target, and limited to between -3 and 3 Unity units per second on world X and Z and between -0.8 and 0.8 Unity units per second on world Y (these speeds correspond to meters per second only if the scene uses 1 Unity unit = 1 meter). The random speed choice multiplied by jumpCharge, the accumulated amount of jump preparation with no distance or time units, supplies a speed input to the aiming calculation. After aiming, the shared jump code multiplies each physical body's calculated velocity by two unitless movement factors for that body: one from its clamped reported health, and one from its stun state. Its written velocity can therefore differ from the speed input. The enum value 1 is only a mode label.

Launching clears the previous attack flags. During the jump, a separate approach check starts the attack animation. The subsequent hit check sends an attack to receivers on the target head's object only when that head is less than 0.15 Unity units from a point 0.25 Unity units forward of the Crablet's eye transform. The eye transform is the scene marker storing the eye's position and facing direction. Those forward Unity units follow the eye's facing direction; they correspond to meters only if the scene uses 1 Unity unit = 1 meter. Choosing Attack selects the attack-mode jump. Separate timing and approach checks must pass before animation and hit dispatch, so selecting it alone does not ensure an attack is sent or damage is dealt. Selecting it also does not attach the Crablet to the face.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BehaviourCrablet.JumpType.Dash
member.summary: Launches toward the navigation agent's current steering point without the attack or face-mount checks.

remarks.para: The navigation agent is Unity's path-following helper; its steering point is the next point it is trying to reach. This mode calculates a launch from the Crablet's parent object position to that world-space point, treats the point as stationary, and accounts for world Y gravity. World space uses the level's shared coordinate axes rather than axes that turn with the Crablet.

The speed supplied to the launch calculation is 12 times jumpCharge Unity units per second. Here jumpCharge is the accumulated charge amount with no distance or time units; for example, a charge of 0.5 supplies 6 Unity units per second to that calculation as a speed input. These values correspond to meters per second only if the scene uses 1 Unity unit = 1 meter. After the aiming calculation, the shared jump code multiplies each physical body's calculated world velocity by its health and stun movement factors. These are unitless numbers describing how able that body is to move, so the velocity written to the body can differ from the speed supplied to the calculation. The number 0 identifying Dash is not a speed. In the inspected jumping update, this mode skips the extra attack and face-engagement checks.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BehaviourCrablet.JumpType.FaceMount
member.summary: Launches toward a point above the sensed target's head and prepares a joint for a possible face attachment.

remarks.para: The aim point is the targetHead body's current position plus 0.14 Unity units along that body's own up direction. For example, a tilted head makes this offset tilt with it rather than always pointing straight up in the world. The offset is 14 centimeters only if the scene uses 1 Unity unit = 1 meter. The launch calculation uses the target's world-space velocity, limited to between -3 and 3 Unity units per second on X and Z and between -0.8 and 0.8 Unity units per second on Y, and a speed input of 12 times jumpCharge Unity units per second. jumpCharge is the accumulated unitless charge amount. World space uses the level's shared coordinate axes rather than axes that turn with the head.

Before applying the launch velocities, this mode tries to create a ConfigurableJoint connecting to the target head. A physics joint is a connection that can restrict how two physical bodies move relative to each other. At this preparation stage its movement limits are free; this is not proof that the Crablet is already mounted. After the aiming calculation, the shared jump code multiplies each physical body's calculated world velocity by its health and stun movement factors. These are unitless numbers describing how able that body is to move, so the velocity written to the body can differ from the speed supplied to the calculation.

Later jumping updates compare the Crablet's mouth position with the head position and check their facing alignment. Only after those checks pass and an existing joint can be tightened does the behavior change to its engaged state, the face-attached behavior state used once the joint has been tightened for face attachment. The number 2 identifies this attempt mode; it does not report a completed mount.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BehaviourCrablet.JumpType.OffmeshLink
member.summary: Launches toward the world-space destination saved by LinkJump to cross a gap in a navigation path.

remarks.para: A navigation mesh marks where an enemy can normally walk. A link connects two separated parts of that walkable area, such as opposite sides of a gap. The supplied target transform records the destination scene object's position and orientation. World space uses the level's shared coordinate axes rather than axes that turn with that object. LinkJump accepts this request while the Crablet is standing or walking, copies the supplied target transform's current world position into linkTarget, saves the supplied speed in linkJumpForce, and selects this mode.

The launch calculation starts at the Crablet's parent object position, treats the saved destination as stationary, and accounts for world Y gravity. Despite its name, linkJumpForce is passed as a launch-speed input in Unity units per second, not a force in newtons. For example, LinkJump with its default value 7 supplies 7 Unity units per second to the aiming calculation as a speed input. After the aiming calculation, the shared jump code multiplies each physical body's calculated world velocity by its health and stun movement factors. These are unitless numbers describing how able that body is to move, so the velocity written to the body can differ from the speed supplied to the calculation. These speeds correspond to meters per second only if the scene uses 1 Unity unit = 1 meter. This does not guarantee a final velocity of 7 Unity units per second or a successful landing.

Moving the target transform after LinkJump has copied its position does not move this saved aim point. The number 3 is a mode label with no physical units. This mode does not use the separate attack or face-engagement branch in the inspected jumping update.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BodyVitals.MeasurementState.CUSTOM
member.summary: Marks measurements as manually adjusted instead of identifying one of the seven named sizes.

remarks.para: This value is 0. The body-measurement menu selects CUSTOM when a manual measurement button is used, then adjusts the requested saved length by 0.01 meters, or 1 centimeter, when its limit allows. It saves the values, sends them to BodyVitals and runs calibration. For example, manually increasing chest circumference changes the stored chest measurement and marks the set CUSTOM.

CUSTOM is a label for the measurements, not a separate set of lengths. CalibratePlayerBodyScale still uses the numerical height, chest, underbust, waist, hips, wingspan and inseam fields. Changing the enum choice alone does not replace those numbers or apply a new body shape.

The shirt-size arrows cycle through the seven named sizes and skip CUSTOM when wrapping. If CalculateMeasurements is explicitly called with CUSTOM selected, it still uses row 0 of the configured shirt-size multiplier list for the four torso circumferences; CUSTOM does not make that routine preserve every manual value.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BodyVitals.MeasurementState.LARGE
member.summary: Chooses the large size row used by the measurement menu to estimate the four torso circumferences.

remarks.para: This value is 4. The body-measurement menu uses it to choose row 4 of shirtSizeModifier, its configured list of unitless size multipliers. CalculateMeasurements multiplies the menu's medium chest, underbust, waist and hip measurements by that row's multiplier and stores the results in meters. Underbust means the distance around the torso just below the chest; the other three values are also distances around the body.

The exact measurements depend on the configured multiplier and medium measurements, rather than the name LARGE. For example, with a medium chest circumference of 1.054 meters and a multiplier of 1.1 in row 4, the calculated chest circumference is 1.1594 meters, about 116 centimeters. This row does not choose height, wingspan or inseam; that same calculation estimates wingspan and inseam separately from the saved height.

Choosing a size through the menu recalculates and saves the measurements, then sends them to BodyVitals and runs body calibration. Assigning measurementPresets on BodyVitals alone only changes its stored choice: CalibratePlayerBodyScale reads the numerical measurement fields rather than selecting a size row itself.

This row does not choose height, wingspan or inseam; that same calculation estimates wingspan and inseam separately from the saved height.

Choosing a size through the menu recalculates and saves the measurements, then sends them to BodyVitals and runs body calibration. Assigning measurementPresets on BodyVitals alone only changes its stored choice: CalibratePlayerBodyScale reads the numerical measurement fields rather than selecting a size row itself.

BodyVitals starts with the MEDIUM choice in its constructor. The menu's medium measurement values and the multiplier at row 3 are separate settings, so the enum value 3 does not itself mean 3 meters or a multiplier of 3.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BonelabProgressionHelper.Level.Ascent
member.summary: Chooses Ascent as the level whose partial saved progress is kept during the four-level cleanup.

remarks.para: Passing this value to DeletePartialProgressForLevelsExcept skips cleanup for Ascent and clears partial progress for Descent, LongRun and Outro. The cleanup removes saved in-progress items and ammunition, the saved progress record named SLZ.Marrow.progress, and saved level-object records whose names do not start with SLZ. Other names beginning with SLZ. are kept.

Choosing this value does not load Ascent, mark it completed, or create a checkpoint by itself. It identifies the exception to cleanup; the helper performs the changes and then requests a save of the active save data.

remarks.para: Passing this value to DeletePartialProgressForLevelsExcept skips cleanup for Descent and clears partial progress for LongRun, Ascent and Outro. The current EnemyDamageReceiver.ReceiveAttack and Enemy_Health.OnReceivedDamage routines do not use this region label to choose a damage multiplier.
