member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Activate.order
member.summary: Advances the activation-clip counter, with the first clip selected twice at each wrap.

remarks.para: For a nonempty clips_Activate array, each AUDIOACTIVATE call increments _last_activate, the stored selection counter, before choosing a clip. The method ignores its supplied clip argument in this mode.

When the counter reaches the number of clips, it chooses position zero, the first clip. On the next call it resets the counter to zero and chooses that first clip again. For example, with three clips and a counter starting at zero, the selected positions are 1, 2, 0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 0. Positions 0, 1 and 2 mean the first, second and third clips.
An empty array returns without advancing the counter. Switching into this mode uses the stored counter rather than restarting the list.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Activate.random
member.summary: Chooses an activation clip afresh at random for each AUDIOACTIVATE request.

remarks.para: The choice comes from clips_Activate, the configured array of activation sound recordings. The supplied clip argument is ignored; the same entry can be chosen again on consecutive requests.
This mode does not advance the stored ordered-selection counter. An empty array makes the method return without a playback request.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Activate.single
member.summary: Uses the clip position supplied to AUDIOACTIVATE instead of choosing randomly or advancing the sequence.

remarks.para: The clip argument is a zero-based position in clips_Activate: zero selects its first sound recording, one its second, and so on. The default argument is zero. For example, clip 2 selects the third recording whenever that same argument is used.

Use a position that exists in the configured array; the method does not clamp an invalid position to a valid one. Different arguments can select different clips while this mode stays selected. An empty array returns without requesting playback, and this mode does not advance the ordered-selection counter.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Click.order
member.summary: Advances the stored click counter and uses it to choose an entry from clips_Click.

remarks.para: Each AUDIOCLICK call with a nonempty clip list increases its stored counter by 1, resets it to 0 only if it is greater than the number of clips, and selects the counter's remainder after division by that number. Clip indices start at 0. This replaces the caller's clip index.

For example, with three clips and the counter initially 0, calls choose indices 1, 2, 0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 0 and so on. The repeated index 0 is part of this implementation; the counter resets only after it has passed 3.

A supplied clipOverride replaces the selected clip after the array entry has been read, but the counter still advances. The clip array must be assigned and nonempty for this path to run; an empty array produces no request, even with an override. Choosing the mode alone does not play a sound.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Click.random
member.summary: Chooses a random entry from clips_Click whenever AUDIOCLICK requests a click sound.

remarks.para: For a nonempty list, the chosen index ranges from 0 through one less than the number of clips. This replaces the caller's clip index. The selection code does not reject the previous choice, so consecutive calls can choose the same clip.

A supplied clipOverride replaces the selected clip after the array entry has been read. The array must still be assigned and nonempty; an empty list produces no sound request even with an override. Selecting this mode only changes later AUDIOCLICK calls.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Click.single
member.summary: Uses the clip index supplied to AUDIOCLICK instead of choosing it randomly or advancing the click counter.

remarks.para: The clip argument is a zero-based position in clips_Click, so clip = 0 selects the first entry and clip = 2 selects the third. The default argument is 0. The mode does not require the array to contain exactly one clip.

For a nonempty array the supplied index must be valid. A clipOverride replaces the chosen clip only after that array entry is read, so an override does not bypass an invalid index. The array must be assigned; an empty array returns without requesting audio.
The mode value 2 is an identifier with no physical units. Writing clickMode alone does not play a clip; selection happens when AUDIOCLICK is called.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Confirm.order
member.summary: Selects a confirmation clip using an advancing counter stored on this Feedback_Audio component, including a repeated first clip at the wrap.

remarks.para: Each AUDIOCONFIRM call advances _last_confirm before selecting an entry from clips_Confirm. An index is a position in the array: 0 is the first clip, 1 the second, and so on. The caller's clip index is ignored in this mode.

The counter resets to 0 only when it is greater than the number of clips. At exactly that number, remainder arithmetic also selects index 0. With three clips and the untouched starting counter of 0, successive calls therefore select 1, 2, 0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 0. It does not begin with clip 0 or loop evenly through every clip.

Each call requests one sound, not automatic playback of the entire array. A valid clipOverride replaces the selected sound after the index has already advanced. The array must exist; an empty array requests no sound and does not advance this counter.

_last_confirm is the whole-number counter stored on this Feedback_Audio component, recording how far this selection has advanced. The divisor is the number of clips in clips_Confirm. The selected index is the remainder, what is left after dividing the counter by that clip count: 3 divided by 3 leaves 0, so counter 3 selects the first clip. At counter 4 with three clips, the strict greater-than reset first changes the counter to 0, selecting that first clip again.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Confirm.random
member.summary: Selects one random entry from clips_Confirm each time confirmation audio is requested.

remarks.para: AUDIOCONFIRM chooses an array index from 0 through the number of clips minus 1, ignoring the caller's clip index. Index 0 means the first clip. With four entries, any of indices 0, 1, 2 or 3 can be selected.

There is no repeat-avoidance check, so two calls can choose the same sound. A valid clipOverride replaces the chosen sound after selection. The clips_Confirm array must exist and contain at least one entry even when supplying an override; an empty array requests no sound.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Confirm.single
member.summary: Selects the clips_Confirm entry at the clip index supplied to AUDIOCONFIRM.

remarks.para: An index is a position in the array: 0 means the first clip, 1 the second, and so on. In this mode the method uses its clip argument directly, rather than choosing randomly or advancing _last_confirm. Calling with clip equal to 2 selects the third array entry.

The index must be at least 0 and less than the number of entries. A valid clipOverride replaces that selected sound, but the array lookup happens first, so an override does not rescue an invalid index. An empty array requests no sound, including an override. This mode does not mean the array may only contain one clip.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Deactivate.order
member.summary: Advances a saved counter to select deactivation clips on successive calls.

remarks.para: This mode has numeric value 1 and ignores the call's clip argument. For a nonempty clips_Deactivate array, the component increases its saved deactivation counter by 1 first. It resets the counter to 0 only when the increased value is greater than the number of clips, then selects the counter's remainder after division by that number. The counter and array position are whole-number counts with no physical units.

With three clips and the fresh counter value of 0, successive selections are positions 1, 2, 0, 0, then 1, 2, 0, 0 again. The first selection is therefore the second clip, and the first clip is selected twice at each wrap. This describes the implemented order rather than a simple 0, 1, 2 loop.

The constructor and Start routine do not change this counter from its fresh zero value. Switching to random or single mode does not advance or reset it, so returning to order mode continues from the saved value. Each call requests one selected clip; it does not wait for the previous sound to finish before choosing the next one.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Deactivate.random
member.summary: Requests a randomly selected deactivation clip on each call.

remarks.para: This mode has numeric value 0. With a nonempty clips_Deactivate array, the component chooses an array position from 0 through the clip count minus 1 and ignores the call's clip argument. The same clip can be selected on consecutive calls; there is no check here to prevent repeats.
For three clips, a call can select position 0, 1, or 2. Positions are zero-based: 0 means the first recording, 1 the second, and 2 the third. This mode does not advance the saved order-mode counter.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Deactivate.single
member.summary: Requests the deactivation clip at the index passed to .

remarks.para: This mode has numeric value 2. The clip argument is a zero-based position in clips_Deactivate: 0 selects the first clip and is the default, while 2 selects the third clip. It is an array position, not a volume or a time in seconds.

For a nonempty array, supply an index from 0 through the clip count minus 1. The method does not clamp or wrap an invalid index; an index outside that range fails the array access. An empty array returns before selecting a clip. This mode leaves the saved order-mode counter unchanged.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Hover.order
member.summary: Chooses a hover clip using the saved hover counter, advancing it before each request.

remarks.para: AUDIOHOVER ignores its clip index argument in this mode. It increases the saved hover counter by one, resets the counter to zero only if it is greater than the number of clips, then selects the counter's remainder after division by that number. Clip positions start at 0.

With a fresh counter of 0 and clips [A, B, C], successive requests select B, C, A, A, B, C, A, A. The first request starts at array position 1, and position 0 repeats at each wrap because a counter exactly equal to the clip count also selects position 0 before the next call resets it.

A provided clipOverride whose clip still exists replaces the selected clip after this counter update; a missing or destroyed override leaves the selected clip in place. The array must still be nonnull and nonempty. Start, a method Unity calls before the first frame update, does not reset the hover counter; changing modes also leaves its saved value in place. These are successive playback requests, not an automatic playlist that waits for each sound to finish.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Hover.random
member.summary: Chooses a random entry from the hover clip array for each AUDIOHOVER call.

remarks.para: It picks a zero-based position from 0 through the last entry in clips_Hover, ignoring the clip index argument. For three entries, any of positions 0, 1 and 2 can be chosen. There is no check to prevent the same clip being selected twice in a row.

A provided clipOverride whose clip still exists replaces the selected clip afterward; a missing or destroyed override leaves the selected clip in place. The array must still exist and contain at least one entry; an empty array returns without playing even an override. This mode does not advance the saved order counter. Choosing the mode alone does not start a sound; AUDIOHOVER must be called.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Hover.single
member.summary: Uses the clip index supplied to AUDIOHOVER instead of choosing a random or ordered entry.

remarks.para: The default index is 0, the first entry of clips_Hover. For clips [A, B, C], passing index 2 chooses C. Use an index from 0 through the array length minus 1; a negative or too-large index reaches an array error.

A provided clipOverride whose clip still exists replaces that entry only after the array lookup; a missing or destroyed override leaves the selected clip in place. The override does not make an invalid index safe. A nonnull empty array returns without playing even the override. This mode does not advance the saved order counter and does not require that the array contain exactly one clip.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GeoManager.GeoState.CLEARED
member.summary: Named cleared-state marker, with numeric value 0.

remarks.para: This is the manager field’s normal initial value before another state is assigned. The complete GeoManager routines and its delayed-start routine inspected here, plus GeoMover’s main movement routine, do not assign CLEARED when geometry is hidden or a lowering movement finishes.
It therefore does not by itself prove that every object is below the floor or that clearing has completed. ClearCurrentGeo can hide ordinary geometry directly without updating this marker.

A newly created manager normally begins with value 0, CLEARED, before another state is assigned. For example, hiding an arena object can leave an earlier UP value stored; hiding does not automatically change this field to CLEARED.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GeoManager.GeoState.MOVING
member.summary: Marker set when a selected geometry object is activated and its move-up sequence is started; numeric value 1.

remarks.para: ToggleGeo, or its delayed continuation, resets the selected mover to its configured startPos relative to its parent and activates the object. It then sets this state before starting MoveGeo(true). A coroutine is an animation routine that continues across frames; it moves toward the configured endPos.

The marker records the start path rather than measuring current height or velocity. If the death-pit branch is waiting through its configured delay, the state is not changed to MOVING until that wait finishes and the selected object is activated.

Geometry means the movable arena objects, such as the floor or obstacles. startPos and endPos are the configured starting and target positions, in Unity distance units relative to the parent object that contains this mover. A frame is one game update. When the previous active object is the death-pit geometry, the delayed path waits the floor’s configured move-up duration plus 0.1 seconds. This is a timed wait; it does not check that the floor has arrived.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GeoManager.GeoState.MOVING_TO_CLEAR
member.summary: Named clearing-movement marker, with numeric value 3.

remarks.para: The complete GeoManager routines and delayed-start routine inspected here, plus GeoMover’s main movement routine, do not set this value when clearing or lowering begins. In those paths, clearing can directly hide ordinary geometry and lowering can run without this state change.
Treat this as a stored enum choice, not proof that a lowering animation is currently active. This finding is limited to those inspected routines; external callers or mods may assign it.

An enum is a fixed set of named choices. Geometry means the movable arena objects, such as the floor or obstacles. This field can store the MOVING_TO_CLEAR choice even when none of those objects is running a lowering animation.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GeoManager.GeoState.UP
member.summary: Completed move-up marker set before the manager’s move-up completion notification; numeric value 2.

remarks.para: MoveUpComplete stores the reporting mover as activeGeoMover, stops the movement sound, sets this state, then invokes OnMoveUpComplete if assigned. A callback is a routine called to report an event; this manager notification sends no arguments.

The main mover coroutine follows the same completion order after reaching its configured endPos, a position relative to the mover’s parent. For a death-pit mover, it can start lowering the separate floor after the manager notification. UP therefore does not mean every related object has stopped moving or every piece is at a universal arena height.

A coroutine is a routine that continues over several game updates. endPos is the configured target position in Unity distance units relative to the parent object that contains the mover. Calling the public MoveUpComplete directly reports completion and sets UP; that method does not check whether the mover has actually reached endPos.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LData.iVel
member.summary: Stores the calculated starting velocity for a launch, as a direction and speed in the scene.

remarks.para: This Vector3 has X, Y and Z components in meters per second along the world axes, rather than the launch object's own rotated axes. Positive Y is upward. For example, (4, 8, 0) describes a proposed starting speed of 4 meters per second along world X and 8 meters per second upward, with no world Z speed.

CalculateLaunchData and CalcInitialVelocity calculate this vector from the launch object's world position, the target position, the chosen peak height and gravity. Peak height is the intended rise above the starting position in meters; gravity is acceleration in meters per second squared. CalcInitialVelocity can then multiply the vertical and horizontal components by separate unitless drag-compensation settings, so the returned vector may include extra speed intended to counter slowing during flight.

This is stored launch data, not the body's measured current velocity. A Rigidbody is Unity's component for a physical body. Launch code uses the vector to build the push applied to the player or another character's bodies, and may first adjust it or subtract their current velocity. Assigning iVel alone does not move a body. The paired ttTarg stores the calculation's estimated flight duration in seconds.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LData.ttTarg
member.summary: Stores the calculated flight duration, in seconds, for the launch described by this data.

remarks.para: This is the estimated time from launch until reaching the target along the calculated path. It is a duration, not an absolute clock time or a countdown that decreases each frame. For example, 1.5 describes an estimated flight lasting 1.5 seconds; it does not mean the target is reached at game-clock time 1.5.

CalculateLaunchData and CalcInitialVelocity estimate it by adding the time spent rising to the chosen peak and the time spent falling from that peak to the target's height. The calculation uses the starting and target world Y positions in meters, the peak rise above the start in meters, and vertical gravity in meters per second squared. CalcInitialVelocity can multiply the returned starting velocity by drag-compensation settings without recalculating this duration.

The path-drawing code uses this duration to spread its predicted positions across the flight. Player launch code can also use it to time its movement-error checks, while character launch code adds it to the current game time, plus a 0.5-second margin, when setting a flight-related deadline. It is an estimate: collisions, drag and later adjustments to the applied launch push can change the real arrival time. Changing this field alone does not launch or move a body.

These deadlines use game-clock seconds: one second passes as the game's clock advances by one. Slowing or pausing game time stretches or pauses the corresponding real-world wait. The 0.5-second margin uses this same clock.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LinkType.CLIMB
member.summary: Chooses a block climb that pulls a humanoid non-player character (NPC) through hand and chest targets.

remarks.para: A LinkData link is a special connection between places an NPC can walk, such as the ground and the top of a block. For this choice, CreateEdgeObjectsByType prepares target objects: small markers whose positions say where body parts should move. The top height, edgeHeight, is measured along the link object's local positive Y axis, its own up direction, above its local origin, its own zero point. It uses local Unity units, normally metres when the link and its parents have scale 1; changing scale changes the distance in the scene. The hand and chest targets are arranged around that edge before traversal starts.

The humanoid routine first holds the chest near the edge, then adds arm joints on the elbow bodies to guide the hands toward the first pair of hand markers. It pulls the chest forward and upward, changes the arm joints' attachment points to the second pair of hand markers, and finally releases the temporary physics joints. A physics joint is a connection that constrains or pulls a simulated body part. An obstruction can delay the arm attachment, and a failed entry-height check can cancel the attempt.

For example, use this choice for a humanoid NPC climbing over a box, with the link endpoints on the reachable ground and the target markers placed around the box edge. The inspected humanoid routine follows the hand and chest targets; it does not follow the knee targets created during setup. Crablets are routed to a separate jump-attempt routine instead of this humanoid climb.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LinkType.CLIMB_BARS
member.summary: Moves a humanoid non-player character (NPC) hand over hand between targets made from the configured bars.

remarks.para: Supply the physical bar objects in barObjs, an array or numbered list, before creating the link targets. Setup builds grabObjs, the corresponding numbered list of hand-target markers, from those bars in list order. It needs at least two hand targets because traversal starts with one arm joint guiding a hand toward the first marker and the other arm joint guiding the other hand toward the second. This setup creates target markers; the level supplies the physical bars.

The humanoid routine alternates arm joints on the elbow bodies to guide the hands toward the next target markers. It also pulls the chest along the route with a physics joint, a connection that guides a simulated body part. It pauses between stages and releases the joints when it finishes. A failed entry-height check can cancel the attempt.

For example, arrange three overhead bars in the order the NPC should cross them, create the targets, and connect the walking route to the bar section. Reordering the supplied bars changes the order of the hand targets. Crablets select a separate jump-attempt routine for this value.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LinkType.CLIMB_LEDGE
member.summary: Pulls a humanoid non-player character (NPC) up over a ledge using staged hand, arm, chest and head attachments.

remarks.para: Create the link targets around the ledge before traversal. The top height, edgeHeight, is measured above the link object's local origin, its own zero point, along its local positive Y axis, its own up direction. It uses local Unity units, normally metres when the link and its parents have scale 1; changing scale changes the distance in the scene. The generated markers describe desired body-part positions around that top edge; the level still needs a ledge and reachable walking endpoints.

The humanoid routine holds the chest near the edge, attaches the hands to the first hand markers, then adds arm joints on the elbow bodies and changes the chest joint's anchor toward the first chest marker. An anchor is a joint's attachment point; a physics joint is a connection that constrains or pulls a simulated body part. Later stages release the initial hand joints, change the arm anchors toward the later hand markers, and change the chest anchor toward the later chest marker. Finally a head joint guides the head before the remaining attachments are released and the routine finishes. The markers supply configured positions; this routine changes the joint attachment points toward them rather than moving the marker objects. The complete humanoid ledge routine creates no knee joints. This attempt can fail its entry-height or movement-state checks, so selecting this value does not guarantee a completed climb.
For example, use it for an NPC pulling itself onto a raised platform rather than walking up a ramp. Crablets are routed to a separate jump-attempt routine for the same enum value.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LinkType.ESCALATOR
member.summary: Selects the escalator placeholder, which marks a humanoid NPC's navigation connection finished and then waits briefly.

remarks.para: An NPC is a non-player character. Its navigation map, called a NavMesh, tells it where it can walk. When the NPC is on that map, the selected escalator routine immediately marks the special connection between walking areas complete. It then requests a wait of 0.5 game-time seconds and ends. Game time follows game speed, so slow motion makes this wait take longer in real time; it can resume on a later frame, so this is a requested wait rather than a promise of an exact frame count.

The inspected escalator routine supplies no movement or attachment to moving stairs. The link-target setup also has no escalator-specific target-building branch. For example, choosing this value on a connection across moving stairs does not itself make a humanoid NPC ride those stairs. Any physical ride must be provided by other level behavior.
Crablets do not start an escalator traversal routine in the inspected dispatcher.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LinkType.JUMP
member.summary: Chooses a jump or drop that aligns a humanoid non-player character (NPC), releases its chest and lets physics carry it onward.

remarks.para: Prepare the link endpoints and chest target before the NPC reaches this special connection in its walking route. The humanoid routine briefly pulls the chest to its starting target with a physics joint, a connection that guides a simulated body part, then removes that joint. If addFallForce is enabled, it also gives the chest an extra push along the link object's forward direction, its local positive Z axis.

The configured launchTime is the finish-wait duration in game-time seconds after the chest is released. Game time follows game speed, so slow motion makes the wait take longer in real time. The routine marks its link attempt complete after that wait; it does not first prove that the NPC has landed at the other endpoint. Waiting can end on a later frame, so launchTime is not an exact elapsed frame count or a measured flight time.

For example, use it for a humanoid NPC leaving an upper platform for a lower one. Crablets use their separate jump-attempt routine; omniwheel NPCs use a separate jump-down routine. This choice does not apply the humanoid launch velocity used by LAUNCH.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LinkType.LAUNCH
member.summary: Requests a launch push for an NPC's simulated body parts, using the configured target or opposite endpoint according to the drag setting.

remarks.para: An NPC is a non-player character. Velocity gives speed and direction, measured in metres per second. With applyDragForce enabled, the launch calculation targets the opposite endpoint according to which side the NPC enters from; drag means slowing caused by resistance. With this drag correction disabled, it aims at launchTarget, the configured target marker, then adds or subtracts a correction along the link object's forward direction, its local positive Z axis, according to the entry side. The routine sends physics requests to the NPC's Rigidbody components, the Unity components that simulate moving body parts, so physics can carry the NPC through the air. Those requests are applied during a later physics simulation step, when Unity calculates body movement.

In the branch with drag correction disabled, launchForceMult has no physical units and multiplies the requested added velocity change. For example, 2 doubles that change; it does not replace each body's existing velocity. With drag correction enabled, the routine instead calculates the change from the desired velocity minus the current chest velocity and requests a push adjusted for each body part's mass. Set up the launch endpoints, target and height before traversal. edgeHeight is the link's top height above its local origin, its own zero point, along local positive Y, its own up direction; launchHeight adds extra height in that same frame. These are local Unity units, normally metres when the link and its parents have scale 1; changing scale changes the distance in the scene. The endpoint positions are positions in the whole scene. For example, a launch link can send an NPC from a pad on one side of a gap toward the endpoint on the other side with drag correction enabled, or toward its configured target with that correction disabled.

launchTime is the configured wait in game-time seconds before this traversal routine calls its completion logic. Game time follows game speed, so slow motion makes this wait take longer in real time. It pauses and resumes across frames, so the configured wait does not specify an exact frame count. The routine also calculates a flight-time value separately. These values need not match, and completing the routine does not prove that the NPC has landed. The inspected dispatcher chooses this launch routine for humanoid and omniwheel NPCs; crablets select their separate jump-attempt routine.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LinkType.SLIDE
member.summary: Chooses a low sliding traversal that pulls a humanoid non-player character (NPC) through hand and chest targets.

remarks.para: Create the targets before traversal and place the link so those markers fit the passage or chute. The generated target parent is the object containing the markers in Unity's object hierarchy, the list of objects inside other objects. Setup places both chest targets 0.5 local Unity units above that parent's local origin, its own zero point, along its positive Y axis, its own up direction. This is normally 0.5 metres when the parent and its parents have scale 1; changing scale changes the distance in the scene. The hand targets have an initial pair and a later pair farther along the route.

The humanoid routine changes the NPC's movement state, adds arm joints on the elbow bodies to guide the hands toward the first hand markers, pulls the chest toward the first chest target, changes the arm-joint attachment points toward the later hand markers, and changes the chest target before releasing the temporary joints. A physics joint is a connection that guides a simulated body part. The sequence pauses between stages; it is not completed in the frame when traversal is requested.

For example, use this choice for a low passage or a sloped chute whose geometry matches the targets. The enum value does not create that geometry or require the route to point downhill. Crablets select a separate jump-attempt routine for this value.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LinkType.ZIPLINE_DOWN
member.summary: Starts a downward zipline attempt for an NPC, requesting a handle before attaching its body.

remarks.para: An NPC is a non-player character. For humanoid NPCs, the routine first aligns the chest and requests a zipline-stick object at LinkData.zipSpawn, the configured marker supplying its position and orientation in the whole scene. AgentLinkControl.zipStickSpawn supplies the asset to spawn and its pool settings, which control creating or reusing that object. The request returns before the new object has necessarily appeared. A callback, a function called when the spawn result is returned, then connects the NPC's body parts to the returned stick using physics joints. A physics joint is a connection between simulated body parts or objects. A request alone does not establish a successful spawn or ride.

Prepare the zipline route, stick asset, manager and end trigger before using this choice. The manager coordinates the links, and the end trigger is an invisible area that detects this NPC arriving. zipTime is the configured ride timeout in game-time seconds, counted down after the initial attachment stages. Each resumed frame subtracts the game-time seconds since the previous frame. Game time follows game speed, so slow motion makes the timeout take longer in real time; frame timing also affects when expiration is checked. Entering the matching end trigger or stretching the attachment too far can detach the NPC earlier; checks happen across frames.
For example, connect the upper end of a configured zipline to the walking route and place its end trigger where the rider should let go. Crablets select a separate zipline routine for this value.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LinkData.LinkType.ZIPLINE_UP
member.summary: Attaches a humanoid non-player character (NPC) to the configured zipline mover and starts it carrying the NPC along the link.

remarks.para: Prepare zipJointMover, the moving handle and its body setup, along with the link manager and end trigger before traversal. The manager coordinates the links, and the end trigger is an invisible area that detects arrival. The humanoid routine aligns the chest. With physics joints, connections between simulated bodies, it attaches the chest to the mover body and one elbow and hand to the grip body, the simulated part of the handle. It chooses the side whose elbow is nearer the grip body. It then starts the mover's routine, which changes its joint target position over successive frames.

zipTime is the configured ride timeout in game-time seconds, counted down once the mover has started. Each resumed frame subtracts the game-time seconds since the previous frame. Game time follows game speed, so slow motion makes the timeout take longer in real time. The matching end trigger or an attachment stretched too far can cause an earlier release. The timeout is checked once per resumed frame, so it does not guarantee an exact ride duration or successful arrival at the endpoint.

For example, use it for a powered handle that carries a humanoid NPC from the lower end of an already configured zipline to the upper end. Crablets do not start an upward zipline routine in the inspected dispatcher.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.MineCartControl.RideSpeed.Boost
member.summary: Selects the configurable boost preset for the cart’s spline drive.

remarks.para: Numeric value 5. UpdateSpeed with this value copies velocity_boost, damper_boost, and force_boost into the current settings and passes them to splineBody. Assigning rideSpeed alone only stores the choice; call UpdateSpeed to perform those setting changes.

The target velocity is in meters per second along the spline joint’s movement direction, not a world X-axis speed. Damping is in newton-seconds per meter, describing how strongly the drive resists a speed difference; maximum force is in newtons. A physics joint is a connection that restricts movement and can apply drive forces. The spline body marks its settings changed and wakes its Rigidbody, the component that lets physics move the cart, for the track’s later physics update.
This replaces the requested drive settings with the boost values rather than adding a one-time velocity impulse. The preset is not required by code to be faster or stronger than the other presets.

A spline is the curved path used as the track. A drive acts like a motor, applying force toward the requested travel speed. The speed difference is the requested target minus the cart’s actual speed along that joint’s movement direction. Waking the Rigidbody lets physics calculate its movement again if it was sleeping. Maximum force caps each configured contact joint’s drive; it is not a promise of the cart’s total force across all contacts.

For example, a configured target of 5 meters per second requests that travel speed. If the actual travel speed along the joint’s direction is 3 meters per second, the speed difference is 5 - 3 = 2 meters per second. The drive responds to that difference using its damping and force cap; selecting the preset does not instantly set the cart to 5 meters per second.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.NooseBonelabIntro.NooseStage.Cut
member.summary: Handles recovery from a pending hanging-death sequence and the delayed hiding of the dagger and gallows.

remarks.para: NooseCut normally requests removal of the chest connection, disables noose grabs and collisions, schedules cleanup five game seconds ahead, and enters Cut before calling the dagger’s cut helper. It later sends nooseCutEvent as a notification to configured listeners with no arguments. On an eligible scene/player-ready Update, if _skipUpdate is true, the code stops this component’s pending death sequence and restores full health before testing the cleanup deadline. That sequence is the component’s delayed steps that notify death and request a later transition; stopping its coroutine does not cancel an asynchronous callback already issued.

Game seconds use the clock affected by game speed and pause settings. Cleanup requires current game time strictly greater than the saved deadline and _nooseBool false, meaning cleanup has not already run. For example, cutting at time 10 saves deadline 15: exactly 15 does not qualify, and cleanup can run on the first later eligible Update. It stops and disables the cutscene, clears the hanging flag and marks cleanup as done, then requests the dagger and gallows hides. The cutscene is the configured Timeline sequence that plays the reveal; a hide request is not proof of completed visibility changes.

Selecting this enum value alone does not cut any connection or schedule that five-second deadline. It selects Update’s cleanup branch. The stage is not proof that a blade collision occurred or that the player has reached a particular chute.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.NooseBonelabIntro.NooseStage.Hanging
member.summary: Runs the ordered platform-release sequence, then permits choking damage once the hanging flag is set.

remarks.para: LockedNeck normally enters this stage before starting the reveal cutscene, with the first release deadline set from sceneRevealToPlankDrop seconds. Game seconds use the clock affected by game speed and pause settings. The platform joints, connections between objects in the physics simulation, release their configured X-axis rotation limits one at a time in array order 0 through 6; this is the joint’s own configured axis, not a guaranteed scene axis.

After each release, the next deadline is set to the current game time plus plankDropTimer, the configured interval in game seconds. A later eligible Update releases at most one joint when that deadline is reached, including equality. Slow frames can stretch the gaps; the method does not release several overdue joints to catch up. For example, interval 0.5 second and a release at time 10.1 schedule 10.6. If the next eligible Update is 10.7, it releases then and schedules 11.2.

On the later call with step 7, no new deadline wait is required: _isHanging becomes true before daggerSpawnEvent notifies its configured listeners with no arguments. The notification is a cue, not proof that a dagger spawned. That Update can then test damage. Being in this stage alone does not prove the player is physically suspended, that the platform has already dropped, or that a damage tick has occurred.

Damage requires the chest connection’s upward force along world Y, the whole scene’s up axis, to be strictly greater than 0.5 × mass × 9.81. Force is in newtons, mass is the avatar’s stored mass in kilograms, 9.81 is gravitational acceleration in metres per second squared, and 0.5 selects half its weight. Accumulated game seconds must also be strictly greater than damageTickRate, the configured interval in seconds. damagePerTick is the requested health-point amount per hit. At most one damage request occurs per checked Update; the counter resets after it and also when a fresh upward-force reading is 500 newtons or less. This 500-newton rule is separate from the half-weight comparison. For a 100-kilogram avatar half weight is 490.5 newtons, so 600 newtons passes that force check; the time interval must still pass. A requested damage call does not guarantee that this exact health amount was lost.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.NooseBonelabIntro.NooseStage.Initial
member.summary: Checks the noose’s position and tilt on eligible scene/player-ready frames and attaches it to the player’s chest when those checks pass.

remarks.para: When the scene and player are ready, the eligible Update path performs the geometric check using anchor points: marked positions fixed relative to the knot and the two side pieces. The side bodies are the noose pieces moved by physics. The physical chest is the chest object moved by the game’s physics simulation.

The check compares those positions with the physical chest in the head’s orientation: directions measured along the head’s own left/right, up/down and forward/back axes, rather than the whole scene’s axes. Passing it creates the chest-to-knot physics connection and enters Reeling. It does not require a hand-grab notification or prove that the rope mesh truly wraps around the head.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.NooseBonelabIntro.NooseStage.Locked
member.summary: Keeps the knot’s left/right chest target current while waiting to reveal the scene and enter Hanging.

remarks.para: ReelingNeck normally enters this stage after clearing both the chest connection’s limit spring strength and its damping, making the knot’s mass 30 kilograms, and scheduling nooseOnToSceneReveal game seconds from the current time. The limit spring is the setting that pushes connected objects back toward their allowed separation; damping is resistance that slows that movement. Both settings become zero. It writes Locked and the deadline before nooseOnEvent notifies its configured listeners with no arguments.

Game seconds use the clock affected by game speed and pause settings. The saved deadline is checked on eligible later frames, meaning Update passes when the scene and player are ready. For a 4-game-second delay beginning at time 10, the deadline is 14; exactly 14 does not pass, and the first eligible Update after 14 transitions.

Once a later frame is strictly past the saved deadline, the code sets Hanging, resets the platform step to 0, schedules its first release from sceneRevealToPlankDrop, and invokes nooseOnAndHeldEvent before starting the cutscene. This is a no-argument notification to configured listeners and does not check for a held hand. The cutscene is the configured Timeline reveal sequence. Merely selecting Locked does not install the connection or calculate the deadline.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.NooseBonelabIntro.NooseStage.Reeling
member.summary: Tightens the player’s chest-to-knot connection while keeping its target on the appropriate side of the chest.

remarks.para: A physics joint connects the chest and knot and pulls toward its target. AttachNeck normally starts this stage with a deadline one game second ahead. Game seconds use the clock affected by game speed and pause settings. Each eligible Update, when the scene and player are ready, strengthens the joint’s limit spring until the measured separation is strictly below 10 centimetres or game time is strictly past that saved deadline. The limit spring pushes the connected objects back toward their allowed separation, while its damping resists and slows that movement.

The separation is the three-dimensional distance from the physical chest, the chest object moved by physics, to the midpoint, halfway between fixed anchor points on the two noose side pieces. It is not pulling force or hand speed. At exactly 10 centimetres and exactly the saved deadline, reeling continues; at 9 centimetres or on an eligible Update strictly after the deadline, it finishes.

Completion clears both the spring strength and damping, enters Locked, sets the knot mass and the next deadline, then invokes nooseOnEvent as a notification to configured listeners with no arguments. Selecting this value alone does not create the joint or initialize its deadline.

remarks.para: This value is 2. When PageView.Render builds the visible page, it assigns the item to buttons[2], the third entry in the view's configured button array. member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RoundProfileGroup.ArenaGameMode.CHALLENGE
member.summary: Selects the challenge category that can apply the chosen medium or hard difficulty to a non-stacked profile on entry.

remarks.para: This value is 1. When the player enters with MEDIUM or HARD selected and the group is not stacked, the controller requests its challenge-difficulty adjustment. That routine copies the group, increases the copied profile’s difficulty, and makes the copy the assigned group. EASY leaves the profile unchanged in that adjustment routine.

A stacked group, meaning a group participating in a sequence of profile groups, skips that entry adjustment. Unlike CUSTOM, this category is eligible for the inspected score-submission path when the score is positive. The category does not set the round count or wave-completion rules; those come from the profile data.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RoundProfileGroup.ArenaGameMode.CUSTOM
member.summary: Selects custom-profile entry setup and excludes the group from the inspected arena score-submission path.

remarks.para: This value is 2. On player entry, the controller starts the friendly-character spawning routine using the number of entries in the current wave’s friendly list. A coroutine is a routine Unity pauses and resumes across later updates; starting it requests that work rather than reporting that every character has already appeared.

This category skips the entry-time challenge-difficulty adjustment performed for ordinary non-stacked challenges. ARENA_SubmitScoreByType also declines submission for CUSTOM even when the score is positive.

Assign this category explicitly. CreateCustomRound constructs round and wave data without setting the group’s arenaGameMode to CUSTOM, and ARENA_CustomChallengeSelect assigns the supplied group without changing its category. A helper’s custom name therefore does not guarantee that these category-specific rules are selected.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RoundProfileGroup.ArenaGameMode.INSTA_DEATH
member.summary: Selects the player-health instant-death path when the player enters the arena.

remarks.para: This value is 5. The entry routine calls ToggleInstantDeathMode(true) on the player’s health component before any challenge-profile difficulty adjustment. That call saves the previous health mode and selects its instant-death mode; it does not set current health to 1, alter each hit’s damage, or immediately kill the player.

In the inspected damage path, damage is subtracted from health points, and health at or below 0 enters dying. Instant-death handling then starts its death-effect routine using instaDeathTimeAmount, a separately configured duration in seconds, instead of the ordinary dying path. The category therefore does not promise that any small hit is fatal or that the death effects finish in the same frame.

MEDIUM and HARD can adjust a non-stacked group on entry as in the challenge category. The inspected end-of-mode cleanup switches instant-death health back off when that health mode is active. The controller’s HARDEST difficulty can also enable instant-death health independently of this arena category.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RoundProfileGroup.ArenaGameMode.KING_OF_THE_HILL
member.summary: Selects the king-of-the-hill category and its ordinary challenge-profile difficulty adjustment on entry.

remarks.para: This value is 6. With MEDIUM or HARD selected and a non-stacked group, player entry requests the same copied-profile difficulty adjustment as CHALLENGE. EASY leaves that adjustment inactive. Round and wave progression still comes from the group’s profile data.

The complete inspected ARENA_PlayerEnter and ARENA_StartMatch routines do not create a hill, track who occupies it, or add an ownership timer for this category. Configure the scene and profile’s objective behavior for those effects; the tag alone does not build them in these entry and start paths. This is a statement about those inspected routines, not every other script that might read the category.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RoundProfileGroup.ArenaGameMode.PROTECT
member.summary: Selects protected-king setup and the failure rule for a registered friendly king’s death.

remarks.para: This value is 3. During ordinary player entry, the controller clears its bell state, starts friendly spawning from the current wave’s friendly list, and starts a king-entrance coroutine. A coroutine is a routine Unity pauses and resumes later. The king routine requests a 5-second real-time wait, unaffected by game slow motion, then requests the king spawn and rings the bell; frame scheduling and asynchronous spawning mean this is not a guarantee of a completed spawn exactly 5 seconds later.

At match start, if the assigned WeaponSpawner exists, the controller asks it to disable new weapon spawning and clear its weapons. In the non-objective death path, a registered friendly character marked as king causes the controller to enter FAILED and begin its failure effects and reset routine, unless the arena has already reached WIN.

MEDIUM and HARD can also adjust a non-stacked profile on entry as in the challenge category. Separate objective-mode configuration changes which death-handling path runs, so the category alone does not override all objective rules.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RoundProfileGroup.ArenaGameMode.SURVIVAL
member.summary: Selects the category that adjusts arena difficulty according to the current round number.

remarks.para: This value is 0, also the default category of a fresh group. When an active wave starts, the controller sets EASY for rounds 1 through 4, MEDIUM for rounds 5 through 9, and HARD from round 10 onward, then refreshes the difficulty display before starting enemy spawning. Round numbers are whole-number counts, not seconds.

For example, starting a wave in round 5 selects MEDIUM even if a different difficulty was stored earlier. This category does not by itself guarantee endlessly generated waves. A RoundProfileGroup holds a roundProfileList of RoundProfiles, and each RoundProfile holds its own waveGroupList. When the current profile’s wave list is exhausted, the inspected CheckProfileForNextWave routine follows the later-profile path if another profile remains. Only when no later profile remains does it read the first RoundProfile’s separate RoundMode: LIMITED sets the arena state to WIN; UNLIMITED creates another wave when the group has fewer than two profiles, otherwise it creates another round.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RoundProfileGroup.ArenaGameMode.WEAPON
member.summary: Selects the category that disables the assigned weapon spawner and requests weapon cleanup at match start.

remarks.para: This value is 4. ARENA_StartMatch checks for an assigned WeaponSpawner, then calls it to disable new spawning and clear weapons it manages. The setting does not itself choose a gun, give the player a weapon, or guarantee that cleanup finishes when required references or event handlers are missing.

On player entry, this category takes the ordinary challenge-difficulty path: MEDIUM or HARD can adjust a copied profile when the group is not stacked. In the inspected entry setup switch, it does not start the CUSTOM friendly setup or the PROTECT king-entrance routine. The profile and scene still supply the actual weapons, enemies, and objectives.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SaveData.GraphicsManager.FoveatedRadii.RDMInnerRatio
member.summary: Selects the inner-to-outer angle percentage for the fallback foveated method, moving the inner region boundary.

remarks.para: Foveated rendering keeps more image detail near the view center and reduces shading work toward the edges. RDM is its fallback method; VRS means variable rate shading, which uses supported graphics hardware to vary shading detail across the image. Projection converts viewing angles into positions on the image. Its tangent calculation, a trigonometry conversion from angle to image radius, means scaling an angle does not directly scale its pixel radius.

The outer angle is the stored outer-radius percentage multiplied by a reference angle of about 88.2 degrees from the view center. The inner ratio says what percentage of that angle the inner boundary uses. For example, outer = 40 and inner ratio = 50 mean outer 35.28 degrees and inner 17.64 degrees before projection.

VRS applies this ratio on both ellipse axes; its separate anisotropy percentage also scales one axis. RDM and VRS inner-ratio selectors edit the same stored percentage. The ratio is dimensionless and is applied to the angle before a tangent projection, so 50 does not promise half the projected pixel radius.

These values choose which setting a radius-control method edits; they do not select the rendering mode. For manual radii, use the Custom foveated preset: an enabled built-in preset replaces the stored percentages with its own values, while Disabled leaves the edit unapplied. The increase/decrease controls choose Custom first; SetFoveatedCustomRadii does not.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SaveData.GraphicsManager.FoveatedRadii.RDMOuterRadius
member.summary: Selects the outer-region angle percentage for the fallback foveated method, changing how far the central detail region extends.

remarks.para: Foveated rendering keeps more image detail near the view center and reduces shading work toward the edges. RDM is its fallback method; VRS means variable rate shading, which uses supported graphics hardware to vary shading detail across the image. Projection converts viewing angles into positions on the image. Its tangent calculation, a trigonometry conversion from angle to image radius, means scaling an angle does not directly scale its pixel radius.

A radius-control value of 40 means 40 percent of a reference angle of about 88.2 degrees from the view center, or about 35.28 degrees before projection. These are angular settings, not meters or percentages of image pixels. Within the normal 0-to-100 percent settings, with the other valid settings held fixed, a larger percentage expands that boundary. The direct radius setter does not clamp out-of-range values.

The RDM and VRS outer-radius selectors edit the same stored percentage. The renderer applies it to the currently selected mode, so choosing this selector does not switch modes. Projection uses a tangent calculation rather than copying this percentage directly into a screen-space radius.

These values choose which setting a radius-control method edits; they do not select the rendering mode. For manual radii, use the Custom foveated preset: an enabled built-in preset replaces the stored percentages with its own values, while Disabled leaves the edit unapplied. The increase/decrease controls choose Custom first; SetFoveatedCustomRadii does not.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SaveData.GraphicsManager.FoveatedRadii.VRSAnisotropy
member.summary: Selects the percentage scale of one axis of the VRS region, changing its ellipse shape.

remarks.para: Foveated rendering keeps more image detail near the view center and reduces shading work toward the edges. RDM is its fallback method; VRS means variable rate shading, which uses supported graphics hardware to vary shading detail across the image. Projection converts viewing angles into positions on the image. Its tangent calculation, a trigonometry conversion from angle to image radius, means scaling an angle does not directly scale its pixel radius.

The outer-angle setting is the outer-radius percentage multiplied by about 88.2 degrees from the view center. The anisotropy percentage multiplies that angle on one VRS axis: 100 gives equal angle scales, while 60 uses 60 percent of the angle on the scaled axis.

For example, outer = 40 gives a base angle of 35.28 degrees; anisotropy = 60 gives 21.168 degrees on the other axis before projection. The inner boundary uses its inner-ratio percentage on both of these outer angles. This is a unitless angle scale, not texture filtering or a distance.

This stored setting changes VRS radii; the RDM circular radii do not use it. Hardware support can still make the renderer use its fallback method. These values choose which setting a radius-control method edits; they do not select the rendering mode. For manual radii, use the Custom foveated preset: an enabled built-in preset replaces the stored percentages with its own values, while Disabled leaves the edit unapplied. The increase/decrease controls choose Custom first; SetFoveatedCustomRadii does not.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScreenOptions.GUIType.BOX
member.summary: Selects an item that the current ScreenOptions renderer skips.

remarks.para: EndGUI has no per-item drawing or layout action for BOX. The item does not draw its label, invoke either callback or reserve an option row’s height. A callback is a routine called to perform an action or report a result.

The surrounding options-panel box is drawn separately by EndGUI, regardless of whether a BOX item is present. Selecting this enum value therefore does not create another background or border. Use one of the implemented item types when adding visible rows; this description is specific to the current ScreenOptions.EndGUI implementation.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScreenOptions.GUIType.BUTTON
member.summary: Draws a labelled button and reports whether it was clicked.

remarks.para: GUIButton adds this type with the item’s label and optional callbackBool. EndGUI draws a Unity GUI button, then calls that callback with the button’s result whenever the callback exists: true means a click was reported in that drawing pass, and false means none was reported. A callback is a routine called to perform an action or report a result.

The callback is not called only on successful clicks. Put an if(isClicked) check inside it when the action should happen only when the button is pressed. Without a callback, the button is still drawn but its result is ignored by this renderer. The item’s numeric value, range and callbackFloat do not control this type.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScreenOptions.GUIType.LABEL
member.summary: Draws the item’s text as a noninteractive information row.

remarks.para: GUILabel creates this type from the supplied label string. EndGUI draws that string with Unity GUI.Label and advances the vertical layout by the configured label height and margin. It is useful for a heading or explanation alongside controls.

This branch does not draw a button, slider or editable number and does not call the item’s callbacks. A callback is a routine called to perform an action or report a result. Setting numeric fields or supplying a callback does not turn a LABEL into an interactive control; choose BUTTON or SLIDER for that behavior.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScreenOptions.GUIType.LINE
member.summary: Draws a thin horizontal divider and adds spacing before the next row.

remarks.para: GUILine adds this type. EndGUI stretches its line texture across the configured option width with a height of one GUI layout unit, meaning one screen-layout coordinate; it is normally one pixel before the program applies any scaling or translation to the GUI. The texture is created as a solid black pixel when first needed.

The layout advances by that one-unit line height plus guiMargin, the spacing between rows in the same GUI units. This is a visual separator: the item’s label, numeric fields and callbacks are not used to draw text or respond to a click. A callback is a routine called to perform an action or report a result.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScreenOptions.GUIType.SLIDER
member.summary: Draws a horizontal slider with an editable number and reports the resulting value.

remarks.para: GUISlider adds this type with value, start, stop and an optional callbackFloat. value is the current number; start and stop are the supplied range endpoints. EndGUI draws the slider, optionally draws the nonempty label above it, and draws a numeric text field beside it so the number can also be typed. The text field accepts at most five characters.

After reading the controls, the renderer parses the text using a culture-independent number format and limits the result to the supplied range. With an ordinary increasing range of 0 to 10, for example, a value of 3 represents 3 in that range; it is not automatically 30 percent or a distance in metres. Units and the gameplay effect belong to the setting supplied by the caller.

If callbackFloat exists, it receives the resulting number each time this item is processed, including passes with no value change. A callback is a routine called to perform an action or report a result. The renderer does not save that result back into the GUIItem; the caller must retain any setting change and supply the updated value when rebuilding the controls. callbackBool is not used for this type.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScrollButton.ScrollButtonDirection.DOWN
member.summary: Chooses a negative scrollbar-value step toward 0 when stepSize is positive.

remarks.para: This enum value is 1. Start, Unity’s initialization call, saves the negative of stepSize. Scrollbar values are unitless fractions from 0 to 1, rather than pixel or metre distances. Configure a positive step size when you want this named direction; a negative step reverses the movement.

In incremental mode, the target is current value - stepSize. For a current value of 0.6 and stepSize of 0.1, the target is 0.5. In repeating scroll mode, the change is also multiplied by the scrollbar handle’s size, a unitless 0–1 fraction rounded to two decimal places, and the target is limited to 0–1.

Later endpoint checks disable the button and stop its scrolling when the current value, rounded to two decimal places, is approximately 0. These checks read direction again, while the movement step keeps the sign saved at initialization. Set direction before Start; changing it afterward does not refresh that cached step. The connected scroll view determines the visible direction of content movement.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScrollButton.ScrollButtonDirection.UP
member.summary: Chooses a positive scrollbar-value step toward 1 when stepSize is positive.

remarks.para: This enum value is 0. Start, Unity’s initialization call, saves stepSize unchanged. Scrollbar values are unitless fractions from 0 to 1, rather than pixel or metre distances. Configure a positive step size when you want this named direction; a negative step reverses the movement.

In incremental mode, the target is current value + stepSize. For a current value of 0.6 and stepSize of 0.1, the target is 0.7. In repeating scroll mode, the change is also multiplied by the scrollbar handle’s size, a unitless 0–1 fraction rounded to two decimal places, and the target is limited to 0–1.

Later endpoint checks disable the button and stop its scrolling when the current value, rounded to two decimal places, is approximately 1. These checks read direction again, while the movement step keeps the sign saved at initialization. Set direction before Start; changing it afterward does not refresh that cached step. The connected scroll view determines the visible direction of content movement.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SplineEntity.ContactCount.FOUR
member.summary: Uses four physics connections at the corners of the entity’s configured contact rectangle.

remarks.para: A spline is the curved path the body follows. A contact is an attachment location for a ConfigurableJoint, a physics connection that restricts or drives motion; four contacts does not mean four collider collision points.

The rectangle is centered on anchor, an offset in Unity distance units from the object’s origin along its local axes. Its full length is _size.y Unity distance units along the contact frame’s X direction, and its full width is _size.x Unity distance units along that frame’s Z direction. These values correspond to metres only when 1 Unity unit equals 1 metre in the scene. axis and secondaryAxis orient this body-relative frame; its directions need not match the scene’s X and Z axes.

Each corner adds one of the combinations of plus or minus half the length and plus or minus half the width to the anchor. For example, _size = (2, 4) gives a width of 2 Unity units and a length of 4 Unity units, with corners at X = plus or minus 2 Unity units and Z = plus or minus 1 Unity unit relative to the anchor in that contact frame. If 1 Unity unit equals 1 metre in the scene, those values correspond to a 2-metre width, a 4-metre length, and offsets of 2 and 1 metres.

The solver locates the two ends along the spline and applies the width offsets to create the four connection targets around those ends. The individual joints’ angular axes are free; the four separated attachments still affect how the body turns. Choose this before SplineBody.Awake, Unity’s initialization callback—a routine called when setting up that body—which creates four contact joints. Changing contactCount later does not itself resize the created contactJoints array.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SplineEntity.ContactCount.ONE
member.summary: Uses one physics connection at the entity’s anchor to follow the spline.

remarks.para: A spline is the curved path the body follows. A contact here is an attachment location used by a ConfigurableJoint, a physics connection that restricts or drives motion; it is separate from a collision point reported by a collider.

The single connection uses anchor itself, without the extra endpoint or corner offsets from _size. anchor is an offset in Unity distance units from the object’s origin along its local axes; it corresponds to metres only when 1 Unity unit equals 1 metre in the scene. The solver obtains a path position at the entity’s contact origin, then updates that connection to follow it. The contact origin is the entity’s scene position plus its anchor offset rotated into scene coordinates.

This mode applies angularXMotion to turning around the joint’s primary axis and locks the other two turning axes. The primary direction is configured by axis. TWO and FOUR instead use several separated attachment locations and free the individual joints’ angular axes.

Choose this mode before SplineBody.Awake, Unity’s initialization callback—a routine called when setting up that body. It creates one contact joint. Changing contactCount later does not itself rebuild the already created contactJoints array.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SplineEntity.ContactCount.TWO
member.summary: Uses two physics connections at opposite ends of the entity’s configured contact length.

remarks.para: A spline is the curved path the body follows. Each contact is an attachment location for a ConfigurableJoint, a physics connection that restricts or drives motion; this choice does not count collider collision points.

The two locations are anchor plus and minus half of _size.y along the contact frame’s X direction. anchor is an offset in Unity distance units from the object’s origin along its local axes, and _size.y is the full contact length in Unity distance units. These values correspond to metres only when 1 Unity unit equals 1 metre in the scene. The contact frame is oriented by axis and secondaryAxis, so these are configured body-relative directions, not the scene’s fixed X axis. _size.x, the contact width, adds no sideways offsets in this mode.

For example, a contact length of 4 Unity units places the endpoints 2 Unity units in each direction from the anchor; these values correspond to metres only when 1 Unity unit equals 1 metre in the scene. The solver uses a path position for one end and finds a second position along the path with that full end-to-end separation, instead of attaching only at the middle.

The individual joints’ three angular axes are free in this mode; the separated attachment locations still affect how the body turns along the path. Choose this before SplineBody.Awake, Unity’s initialization callback—a routine called when setting up that body—which creates two contact joints. Changing contactCount later does not itself resize the created contactJoints array.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TimeTrial_GameController.TTDifficulty.EASY
member.summary: Selects the easy spawner preset and the first configured enemy kill target when the time trial applies difficulty.

remarks.para: This value is 0. UpdateDifficulty uses it as an array index, so it reads diffReqKillCount[0]: a whole number of enemy deaths required to finish an active kill-all trial. Array indices count from zero. For example, targets of 3, 5 and 8 select 3 deaths for EASY. These numbers are an example, not built-in targets.

Each assigned SpawnerDifficulties component applies its easy data: the asset to spawn, its enemy configuration, its home-post setting, and an optional spawn-point position and direction. A spawn point moves the spawner in world space, the scene-wide coordinate system, where position is measured in metres. Changing difficulty configures these spawners; SpawnDifficultyCrates is the separate call that requests new objects.

Assigning ttDifficulty alone stores the choice. Call UpdateDifficulty with this integer to apply the kill target and spawner settings. The target must be positive and no greater than the number of configured profile spawners; an invalid target falls back to that spawner count. The selected array entry and all required spawner components must exist.
At startup, a kill-all trial with at least one assigned difficulty spawner resets the choice to EASY and applies these settings, even if ttDifficulty previously held another value.

SetLeaderboardByDifficulty separately chooses leaderboard entry 0 using the stored choice. Applying difficulty does not call that method. How challenging this preset is depends on the level author's configured data.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TimeTrial_GameController.TimeTrialMode.KILLS
member.summary: Ends an active time trial when its recorded enemy-kill total reaches the required count.

remarks.para: This mode has integer value 0. On a registered character’s death notification, the controller compares totalEnemiesKilled, its recorded number of enemy deaths, with reqKillCount, the required number. Both are whole-number counts. It finishes only if the trial is active and the total is at least the requirement.

For example, with a requirement of 10 and a total of 9, another counted enemy death raises the total to 10 and allows this finish branch. It calls the routines registered for OnKilledAll, requests the finish sound, optionally despawns the remaining characters when despawnAllOnKillComplete is true, then calls EndSession to stop the trial. Despawning removes those characters from play.

This completion check does not wait for the exit trigger; the end-trigger routine’s finish branch is for SPEED_RUN. Selecting KILLS alone does not begin a session. A separate timeTrialStartMode decides whether startup or a start-trigger call begins it.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TimeTrial_GameController.TimeTrialMode.SPEED_RUN
member.summary: Ends an active timed run when the controller receives its player end-trigger call.

remarks.para: This mode has integer value 1. TIMETRIAL_PlayerEndTrigger checks that this mode is selected and the session is active, requests the finish sound if one is assigned, then calls EndSession to stop the trial. That finish branch does not test the required kill count.

For example, if the level calls the end-trigger routine at its finish line, arriving there can finish the active run even below the configured kill requirement. Death notifications can still update the recorded enemy counts, but the kill-check routine’s quota-finish branch runs only in KILLS mode.

Selecting SPEED_RUN does not itself begin or end a session. A separate timeTrialStartMode chooses automatic startup or a start-trigger call. The controller reads the selected trial mode when a later death or end-trigger call reaches its completion check.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TimeTrial_GameController.TimeTrialStartMode.ON_START
member.summary: Begins the trial session automatically from the controller’s Unity Start callback after its setup work.

remarks.para: Start is a callback, a routine Unity calls before this enabled component’s first regular Update. The controller first runs its base startup work and any applicable difficulty/spawner setup, then calls BeginSession when this mode is selected. This is that component’s startup point, rather than a guarantee about the exact instant the whole level finishes loading.

BeginSession fires sessionBegin before marking isSessionOngoing true and starting the configured timer. A listener therefore sees the previous ongoing flag while that event runs. The timer is a coroutine, a sequence that continues over several frames; the separate timerMode decides which timer routine is used.
Changing to this value after Start has already run does not rerun Start or immediately begin a session.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TimeTrial_GameController.TimeTrialStartMode.ON_TRIGGER
member.summary: Waits for TIMETRIAL_PlayerStartTrigger to be called before beginning the trial session.

remarks.para: The start-trigger method acts only while this mode is selected and isSessionOngoing is false. It optionally plays timeTrialBeginClip, then calls BeginSession. Calls made during an ongoing session are ignored; after the session ends, another eligible call can begin a new one.

For a physical starting area, connect the start trigger’s OnPlayerEnter event to TIMETRIAL_PlayerStartTrigger. The inspected controller setup does not automatically connect those events merely because timeTrialStartTrigger is assigned. Selecting this enum value alone therefore does not make every trigger crossing begin the trial.

BeginSession invokes sessionBegin before setting isSessionOngoing true and starting the configured timer. Event listeners observe the previous flag value. The timer is a coroutine, a sequence continuing over several frames, selected separately by timerMode.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.UtilityModes.REMOVER
member.summary: Selects the spawn gun’s object-removal firing action.

remarks.para: This mode has integer value 1. Selecting it stores the gun’s mode and updates its interface; selection alone does not remove an object.

When the gun fires in this mode, it uses the collider from its saved aiming hit. A collider is the shape physics uses to detect contact. The hit must lead through an attached Rigidbody, the component that lets an object move under physics forces, to a tracked game body and its spawned entity. The gun skips entities with the configured player tag, which marks the player as protected.

For an eligible target it requests the disappearance effect, flashes the gun screen, and calls the entity’s Despawn routine. Despawning removes that active entity from the scene; it does not delete the object’s reusable content record. For example, use this mode to remove a spawned prop rather than placing another copy. This action depends on a valid target and the gun’s configured references.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.UtilityModes.SPAWNER
member.summary: Selects the spawn gun’s action for creating its selected object or requesting an avatar change.

remarks.para: This mode has integer value 0. Selecting it stores the gun’s mode and updates its interface for the selected content record; selection alone does not create an object.

Firing starts the gun’s selected-crate operation. A crate is the catalog record for a reusable object or player body. For an ordinary spawnable crate, that operation asks the object-spawning system to place it at the gun’s cached placement position and orientation. For an avatar crate, it can instead request a change of the held player’s avatar, meaning the player body.

The operation can continue asynchronously, meaning after the firing call returns. A firing request does not prove that an object has successfully appeared or an avatar change has completed. For example, select a prop in the gun’s menu, choose SPAWNER, then fire to request placing that prop.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.WeaponPack.WeaponType.MELEE
member.summary: Marks a pack as holding a close-contact weapon and enables its melee grip lookup during spawn setup.

remarks.para: Melee means a weapon used by striking or cutting nearby targets, such as a bat or sword. Choose the matching weapon asset in weaponSpawnable, which determines the object the spawner requests. This enum value supplies the pack's classification.

When the spawned weapon is returned, a callback, a function called with that result, looks for a Grip on the weapon or its child objects and stores it in weaponGrip. A Grip is a component describing where a hand can hold an object. This lookup is part of spawn setup; choosing MELEE by itself does not fill that stored reference. The WeaponPack constructor selects MELEE initially.

member.name: F:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.WeaponPack.WeaponType.RANGED
member.summary: Marks a pack as holding a distance weapon, so its spawn setup skips the melee-only grip lookup.

remarks.para: Ranged means a weapon intended to hit from a distance, such as a gun. Choose a matching weapon asset in weaponSpawnable, which determines the object the spawner requests. The enum classifies that setup rather than checking whether the returned object can shoot.

In the inspected spawn callback, the function called when the requested weapon is returned, common setup still collects the weapon's hand grips and other interaction references. RANGED skips the extra lookup that stores a single Grip in weaponGrip for MELEE. A Grip is a component describing where a hand can hold the object. For example, choose RANGED when configuring a gun pack; the gun's own components provide its firing behavior.
