remarks.para: A category tree has parent and child categories, like folders and subfolders. FilterTagTree shows this control and its highlight when the current category has a parent, and hides it at the root.

TreeBackButton moves to that parent, resets both page indexes to 0, clears the item highlight, and refreshes the browser. The previously selected crate can remain selected after going back. Other standard tabs hide this control.

member.name: P:Il2CppSLZ.UI.SpawnablesPanelView.treeButtons
member.summary: Provides the navigation button slots that determine how many category, package, or author rows fit on a page.

remarks.para: UpdateTagPageItems writes names from _activeTags into these buttons, hides slots without entries, and displays fallback category names such as Gun Other as Other. The list can contain different kinds of rows depending on the selected tab.

The array length is the page size. With 5 buttons, category page 0 displays list indexes 0–4 and page 1 displays indexes 5–9. When SelectCategory(idx) is called, idx is the slot number on the current page; the method combines it with the current page and array length to look up a row in the full list. The highlight routine marks that row only while its index is on the displayed page.
Configure a nonzero number of slots and their holder references before populating the menu. Assigning a different array does not itself redraw the browser.

member.name: P:Il2CppSLZ.UI.SpawnablesPanelView.treePageText
member.summary: Shows the category-page number and total when at least two category pages are available.

remarks.para: The stored page index starts at 0, but the displayed number starts at 1. With index 1 and three pages it reads "2 of 3". UpdateTagPageText clears this label and hides both category arrows when fewer than two pages are needed.

member.name: P:Il2CppSLZ.UI.SpawnablesPanelView.treePathText
member.summary: Displays the current category path, or the NEW/ABC sort label on the Pallets tab.

remarks.para: In the category tree, FilterTagTree joins the current category and its ancestors with " / ". This shows which branch the browser is in. Fallback category tags such as Gun Other are displayed as Other at the path end.

SelectTab reuses this text on the Pallets tab. NEW sorts by cached package dates, newest first: an existing package folder contributes its last-write time, a missing folder receives a very early placeholder date, and the built-in BONELAB Content pallet is assigned the current time. ABC sorts package titles alphabetically. Developer Tools, Favorites, and Authors hide this text.

member.name: P:Il2CppSLZ.UI.SpawnablesPanelView.treeScrollDownButton
member.summary: Next category-page control whose visibility follows the available page range.

remarks.para: UpdateTagPageText hides both category arrows when fewer than two pages are needed. This arrow is shown only before the last category page.
NextTagPage changes one whole page, refreshes button labels and highlights, and stops at the boundary without wrapping. It does not scroll the list continuously or choose another spawnable crate.

member.name: P:Il2CppSLZ.UI.SpawnablesPanelView.treeScrollUpButton
member.summary: Previous category-page control whose visibility follows the available page range.

remarks.para: UpdateTagPageText hides both category arrows when fewer than two pages are needed. This arrow is shown only after the first category page.
PrevTagPage changes one whole page, refreshes button labels and highlights, and stops at the boundary without wrapping. It does not scroll the list continuously or choose another spawnable crate.

member.name: T:Il2CppPuppetMasta.SubBehaviourHandPose.HandPose
member.summary: Chooses a finger-curl target for PuppetMasta’s hand-pose behavior, using preset gestures or five custom curl amounts.

remarks.para: SetHandPose uses the chosen value to blend fingers between this behavior’s configured OpenHand and Fist pose assets. A curl of 0 means the open endpoint, 1 means the closed endpoint, and 0.5 is halfway between them; these are unitless pose blends, not joint angles.

The named presets replace the supplied curl arguments. Custom keeps those arguments so each finger can be chosen separately. SetHandPose records a desired pose for the selected hand, and later OnUpdate calls apply blended local rotations to its configured hand and finger transforms. This choice does not itself apply a grip force or attach an object.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Achievements
member.summary: Requests known BONELAB Steam achievements through code attached to a scene object or a direct call from another script.

remarks.para: A component is a piece of code attached to a Unity scene object. A Unity event, a signal that tells selected routines to run, can call AWARDACHIEVEMENT on that object. Unlock is a static method: code can call Achievements.Unlock("ACH_DESCENT") directly without an attached Achievements object. Both validate against AchievementsDict and request the supplied key from Steam. The dictionary values are readable log names, not platform-key translations.

Unknown keys log an error. A known-key award log still does not prove the Steam update succeeded, because both methods discard its success result. note stores descriptive text and does not select the achievement.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArenaLootItem
member.summary: Configuration entry that tells the arena which loot object to spawn and how some loot-selection paths treat it.

remarks.para: Set spawnable to the object’s crate, which identifies the packaged object asset to create, and its pool policy, the rules for creating new instances or reusing old ones. In ordinary wave loot, every valid configured entry is requested. In weapon mode, percentage is a threshold compared with one shared roll for the list, so multiple entries can be included together.

lootType is used when CopyWaveProfile replaces entries with randomized weapons: light chooses pistol or SMG, medium rifle, melee blade or blunt, and heavy shotgun. title is a configuration label; these audited selection and spawning routines do not display it.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArenaLootItem.LootType
member.summary: Selects the replacement weapon list used when arena wave loot is randomized.

remarks.para: CopyWaveProfile with randLoot enabled reads each original entry’s lootType: light chooses pistol or SMG, medium chooses rifle, melee chooses blade or blunt, and heavy chooses shotgun. If randomization is disabled, the copy keeps the original entry reference.

This enum does not itself spawn a weapon, set its ammo type or measure its physical mass. Ordinary arena loot spawning reads spawnable directly. The six random weapon-list selectors choose an index from the selected list, without using candidate percentage settings as weights.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArenaMenuController
member.summary: Connects the arena menu to challenge selection, custom-wave building, match preparation and saved survival records.

remarks.para: TrialSelect and ChallengeSelect select a configured group and update description labels. StartMatch prepares the selected challenge; SurvivalSelect and CreateCustomGameAndStart also prepare their selection, refresh active labels and invoke OnChallengeSelected. Preparation marks the player ready and requests arena geometry; enemy spawning follows the controller's later arena flow.

Custom controls choose enemy profiles, repetitions per profile, allies, ammo and an enemy-at-once limit. Creating the game rebuilds customProfileGroup's round list from those settings. Changing a menu setting afterward does not automatically rebuild the generated waves.

OnLoadSaveFile displays already loaded survival records and controls resume visibility. ResumeSurvivalFromRound selects the cached round, generating a projected profile when needed. Assign arenaGameController and the UI references before use, and keep the enemy-profile arrays aligned by index.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Arena_GameController
member.summary: Runs BONELAB arena ready-up, rounds, enemy waves, objectives, scoring, loot and end-of-mode cleanup.

remarks.para: A RoundProfileGroup supplies the rounds, each round supplies waves, and each wave supplies enemy choices, spawn limits and rewards. Select or resume a prepared group before starting its wave. round and wave are one-based stored numbers: 1 selects the first list entry. currentRound and currentWave are cached profiles refreshed during entry and StartNextWave; editing a number does not immediately refresh those caches.

Awake is Unity’s initialization callback, a routine Unity calls to initialize the component. It initializes the base controller and marks this controller as the arena game type. NPC means a non-player character controlled by the game. OnEnable connects session, player, NPC-registration/death, damage, headshot and projectile notifications, plus optional NPC-entrance and king-spawner connections. In the normal paired lifecycle, OnDisable removes the matching connections. Repeated manual enable calls can add duplicate delegate registrations, connections that tell a routine to run when a notification fires; one matching removal is not a promise to remove every duplicate.

Starting a match marks isPlayerReady true before playerReady fires; entry requires that flag. Trigger-start and bell-start modes schedule their opening countdown through different paths. An accepted bell action marks isRung true before ringBell fires. Ready and bell notifications come before their later geometry or countdown work, so a callback, a routine called to perform or report an action, can observe a flag change before setup finishes.

StartNextWave requires ACTIVE, looks up the selected profiles, invokes roundBegin on wave 1, refreshes the display and sets isWaveOngoing true before waveBegin. The new timer and enemy producers start afterward. A frame is one game-display update. Normal enemies use a cancellable sequence that can wait across frames; the objective initial batch and other timed work use coroutines, sequences that continue over frames. Changing a stored flag or handle is not equivalent to cancelling or stopping those sequences.

The checked routines invoke the UltEvent fields such as playerEnter, roundBegin, waveEnd and modeEnd. An UltEvent stores configurable function calls. The similarly named on... UnityEvent fields are separate stored action lists and are not also invoked by the complete checked Arena methods and their continuations. Attach actions to the event actually used by the relevant flow rather than assuming both lists run together.

The wave-reset sequence fires waveEnd before clearing its spawning and ongoing-wave flags, then cleans NPC records and counters over later frames. EndOfRound advances the round number and resets the wave number before roundEnd. EndOfMode resets both numbers to 1 before modeEnd, then clears readiness and changes state to WAITING afterward. These events report stages of a sequence, not proof that every cleanup action has already completed.

Scoring combines eligible enemy-death points with later movement, shot, difficulty, ammunition and damage arithmetic. Movement adds dx² + dy² + dz² for each sample, where dx, dy and dz are changes along the scene’s world X, Y and Z axes in Unity distance units. The accumulated value is in squared Unity units, rather than walked distance: one sample with a 2-unit change on one axis adds 4, while two separate 1-unit samples add 1 + 1 = 2. Headshot and projectile counters receive global notifications without player-attribution checks. Repeated CalculatePlayerScore calls can apply bonuses again, and not every counter is automatically reset for a new run.

modeWin is conditional end-of-mode handling rather than a WIN-only signal: EndOfMode reaches it when the state is not FAILED and either the group is SURVIVAL or the state is not QUIT. A SURVIVAL quit can therefore run it. The event follows score and completion handling but precedes the round/wave reset and modeEnd. Read the stored state and assigned mode when a listener needs to distinguish outcomes.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Arena_SpawnCapsule
member.summary: Arena enemy capsule whose timed trail, beep and collider-growth sequence can request an enemy at its current position or fall back to a normal spawner.

remarks.para: A firing impulse is a brief push that changes motion. The arena launcher supplies that impulse separately and calls OnLaunchedArena to enable the trail and start a coroutine, a sequence that continues over frames. The capsule uses timed waits rather than waiting for a landing collision. Game time follows the game clock and slows during slow motion. These numbers are requested waits; the coroutine resumes on later frames, so actual elapsed time can be longer. Its beeps begin after 0.25 game-time seconds and repeat 10 times with gradually shorter game-time delays.

During one bounds-check stage, the sequence tests world Y from 0 through 4 and distance from the world origin, reading the world position separately for those two tests. It then enables its spherical collider, the sphere used for physics contacts, waits 0.1 game-time seconds, interpolates its radius over a 0.5-game-time-second interval, and disables/resets the collider. The radius values use collider-local units, measured before object scaling; the positional bounds use world units.

If the saved bounds result is acceptable and the arena is ACTIVE at the post-growth test, it plays a positional explosion sound, waits 0.1 game-time seconds and requests the enemy profile’s spawnable at the then-current capsule position. Its callback, a routine called to report the spawned object, passes optional AI configuration only when the profile has it and the object has an AIBrain, the component managing enemy behavior. It then activates the object even without that component. A found AIBrain must also have its behaviour component, the code controlling its actions, for death/reactivation wiring and registration; a missing behaviour causes an error at that step. If an AIBrain with that component is found, it uses the arena’s first normal ProfileSpawner to connect death/reactivation handling and register the enemy character; without an AIBrain it skips that wiring and registration.

OnSpawn fires after the success spawn request, while the collider is already disabled/reset and before the final wait/trail cleanup. It does not wait for the spawned object’s callback. An invalid earlier location or non-ACTIVE success test calls SpawnFailedHoiPoi instead; that helper can request the same profile through a random normal spawner while ACTIVE.

Provide the trail, collider, OnSpawn event, controller/profile and a nonempty normal-spawner list before using the sequence. Capsule despawn depends on finding its Poolee component, which manages spawned objects kept for reuse. Despawning removes the capsule from active play through that component; outside a pool it deactivates the object rather than guaranteeing a return to a pool. Changing the radius or bounds settings does not itself launch it, and another OnLaunchedArena call starts an additional sequence without cancelling the previous one.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArmFinale
member.summary: Controls the giant mechanical arm’s finale stages, ceiling tile connections, player grip/seat handling and windmill alignment drive.

remarks.para: Awake, Unity’s initialization callback, is a routine Unity calls to set up the component and selects Preshow. A joint is a physics connection controlling how bodies move relative to each other or the world. OnEnable, the routine Unity calls when this component becomes enabled, subscribes to hostManager’s hand callbacks, routines called to report attachment or detachment. Start, which Unity calls once before the first Update after the component is enabled, builds the ceiling tile connections from _ceilingTiles and _jointInfo and caches them in _tileJoints. Supply the scene references and valid, active tile bodies before those setup steps; deferred joint creation can leave null cached slots.

Update is Unity’s routine called once each rendered frame. A timeline director is the component that plays prepared animation and other scene actions. The angular drive is the joint’s physics motor, whose target angular velocity requests a rotation rate. GongHit enables offscreen arm-mesh updates, sets Decent and plays the descent director. ReadyForAscent selects Hold. A positive reported hand count on Update selects Ascent before stopping the descent timeline, playing the ascent timeline and setting the windmill angular drive. Releasing every reported grip for more than half a game-time second since the last positive-count Ascent Update selects Dropped, which repeatedly offers _lastRmToDetatch to palmSeat.

ReadyForVoid sets Void, activates holeStopper and then records Time.time, the scaled game clock in seconds that follows the game’s current speed. Void Update disables offscreen arm-mesh updates, forces remaining reported grips off after more than one game-time second and requests immediate palm-seat exit after more than 0.75 game-time seconds while the seat has a Rigidbody, Unity’s component for physics motion. Seat itself only exits a registered rig. When both timing checks pass in one Update, the force-detach request comes first.

WindmillProjectRotation is a separate caller-driven operation: it predicts blade orientation, assigns a joint rotation target and starts a coroutine, a sequence continuing over frames, that changes the angular drive over the supplied game-time duration. It has no stage guard or cancellation of an earlier projection. JointDestroyEvent locks all six movement and rotation settings of a selected ceiling joint, then sets its break-force threshold to zero; it does not test a collision or directly destroy the component.

OnDisable is Unity’s disable-cleanup callback. It removes one matching attach and detach subscription from the current hostManager but does not reset the stage, hand count, timestamp or detached-player cache, and it does not call a coroutine-stop routine. Repeated manual OnEnable calls can leave duplicate connections after one disable. Direct edits to cached fields or the stage do not reproduce the scene methods’ timeline, physics or entry actions.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ArmFinale.ArmStage
member.summary: Selects which grip, timeline-entry, seating or release rule the story-finale arm controller runs.

remarks.para: The values are Preshow (0), Decent (1), Hold (2), Ascent (3), Dropped (4) and Void (5). Awake is Unity’s initialization callback, a routine Unity calls to set up the component, and selects Preshow. Update is Unity’s routine called each frame while the component is active. A timeline is a prepared sequence of animation and scene actions, played by a PlayableDirector. The windmill physics drive is a control requesting its turning. A rig is the group of objects representing the player’s body and tracked controls. GongHit selects Decent and plays descent. ReadyForAscent selects Hold; a positive reported hand count on Update enters Ascent before the director and windmill-drive changes.

Ascent uses the stored _timer timestamp, refreshing it on positive-count Updates. Game time follows changes to game speed. Hold-to-Ascent does not seed _timer, so release before the first positive-count Ascent Update can use older data. Ascent measures game-time seconds since that stored timestamp, switching to Dropped after more than 0.5 seconds with a nonpositive count. Dropped repeatedly offers the last detached rig to the palm seat. ReadyForVoid selects Void, activates the stopper and records a new timestamp; Void requests seat exit after more than 0.75 seconds and remaining grip release after more than one second, subject to their separate conditions.

These values select controller branches. Assigning one to _armStage does not reproduce the methods’ entry actions, initialize timing, stop timelines or cancel a windmill coroutine, a sequence continuing over frames. Use the stage-changing methods when their playback, activation and timestamp actions are needed. The upstream "Decent" spelling represents descent.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BalloonGun
member.summary: Requests color-queued balloon projectiles and a muzzle effect when a held trigger is pressed, with drifting preview balloons on the gun.

remarks.para: The preview renderers draw the meshes. Their Transforms hold position, rotation and scale; this drift changes each preview object's position relative to its parent, rather than directly from the level origin. Parent rotation and scale therefore affect how that local movement appears in the world.

The grip calls a routine while held to animate the previews and process trigger input; a callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. The successfully obtained ProjectileBalloon later performs a raycast, a straight-line collision search, using its own settings. The balloon and flare are independent requests; requesting either does not guarantee a successful spawn.
The gun shifts four preview colors before each shot. Its preview renderer transforms drift in local space while the held callback runs; they are separate from the spawned balloon physics.

ProjectileBalloon performs the delayed aim raycast and surface/object attachment using its own range and layer mask. BalloonGun only supplies its spawn definition, color and muzzle reference in the checked firing path.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BehaviourCrablet
member.summary: Controls the Crablet enemy’s navigation, jumping attacks, face-grappling behavior, animation, and death cleanup.

remarks.para: The AI tracks a target, chooses when to charge a leap, and launches the simulated body toward that target. A face-mount attempt can create a physical connection to the head, then use the Engaged mode for its face-hug presentation and scheduled damage messages.

Attack permission and cooldown are inputs to the automatic decision code. They do not guarantee a hit or block every direct method call. The separate crumble setting enables a body-part loosening effect and delayed return to the object pool, where inactive enemies can be reused.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Blip
member.summary: Retains the old Blip spawn/despawn-effect interface; its two effect calls now only log deprecation warnings.

remarks.para: CallSpawnEffect does not create or reveal an object, and CallDespawnEffect does not hide or remove one. Both return after logging their respective warnings. The saved effect assets, renderer references, preview preference, velocity, and flags do not change what these methods do.

Other components can take action after requesting the old effect. A Poolee is the component that manages an object’s return to a reusable pool. If Poolee.Cache exists, ItemDropper’s TryGet lookup checks a table of previously registered Poolee references; it does not search the object for that component. When this lookup fails, ItemDropper searches the object for a Blip. If it finds one, it calls CallDespawnEffect and then disables the object itself. A failed lookup does not prove the object lacks a Poolee component. AvatarPedestal calls it before a later step hides the dome. Those changes belong to the caller, so calling the Blip method alone does not reproduce them.

Blip inherits SpawnEvents. Its inherited Awake, Unity’s initialization callback (a routine called to perform an action, here initializing the component), registers it with the assigned Poolee, the component that manages an object’s return to a reusable pool. That base registration needs an assigned Poolee. The inherited pool-initialization, spawn, and deinitialization notification routines have empty implementations here; they do not start the Blip visual effects.

Cache creates and returns a shared ComponentCache when needed. A ComponentCache is a lookup table associating a GameObject, one scene object, with Blip references previously registered for it. A lookup returns the first stored Blip, or no result when that object has no entry or its stored list is empty; it does not discover an unregistered component. Its getter does not collect all active scene instances, and the effect methods do not use the cache.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BoardGenerator
member.summary: The Board Gun placement tool: hold the primary button to aim from a first anchor, then release to request a board between the saved points.

remarks.para: A surface normal is the direction pointing straight out from the hit surface. ammoDistance is the remaining board-length budget in meters.

Grip callbacks supply input. The first shot saves a world-space hit point and surface normal, and a coroutine, a sequence continuing over several frames, updates the other endpoint while the button flag remains true. A miss leaves older anchor data in place.

Release hides the line and starts an asynchronous spawn that can continue after the asset is ready. The board is positioned at the midpoint, oriented along the gap, scaled from its measured length and connected at both ends by joints, physics connections to the hit bodies or to the world.

When isUsingAmmo is enabled, placement needs more remaining ammoDistance than the gap length and spends that length before spawning. Suitable destructible boards get a refund callback, a routine called to report their destruction. The native refund retains set membership, so repeated calls can repeat the credit.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BodyVitals
member.summary: Stores the player’s real-world measurements and applies selected body, layout, movement, and controller preferences.

remarks.para: Measurements such as height and torso circumferences are in meters. They describe the real player; the active avatar can have different dimensions. The player template is the body description used to relate tracked real movement to the avatar. CalibratePlayerBodyScale changes the scale of the object that maps tracked headset and controller motion to that avatar, and shapes the player template’s torso. The built-in wingspan and inseam setters are empty in this build.

PROPEGATE applies calibration and then PROPEGATE_SOFT. The soft pass updates layout, inventory-side choices, the Body Log pull-cord device, movement curves and direction, turning settings, handedness, quick-menu permission, and controller vibration. These are stored preferences until the appropriate application method copies them to the live systems. uiScaling, turnEnabled, and slowTimeEnabled are not forwarded by these methods.

Startup applies settings immediately when the current streaming session is not in its loading state; this includes its NONE and DONE states. While it is loading, the component registers PROPEGATE as a callback for level loading. A callback is a function called later when that event occurs. Calls need the live player and related UI/controller references. The settings loader can overwrite these fields from saved player settings and unlock progress; calling the application methods does not itself save changes to disk.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BodyVitals.MeasurementState
member.summary: Chooses a body-measurement size category for , with preset calculations performed by the measurement menu.

remarks.para: CUSTOM is 0; the seven named sizes run from XSMALL = 1 through XXXLARGE = 7. The values are unitless choices. The menu uses a named size's number as a row in its configured shirt-size multiplier list, then multiplies the medium chest, underbust, waist and hip circumferences by that multiplier. A circumference is the distance around the body, measured here in meters; underbust is around the torso below the chest.

These presets estimate the four torso circumferences. Height is a separate saved measurement, and the menu estimates wingspan, the distance between the hands with arms spread, and inseam, the inside-leg measurement, from height using separate multipliers. There is no fixed set of meter values encoded in this enum. For example, a torso multiplier of 1.1 means 110% of the configured medium circumferences, regardless of which named row contains it.

The menu recalculates and saves numerical measurements before sending them to BodyVitals for calibration. BodyVitals' calibration reads those numerical fields rather than this enum to choose measurements. Changing only measurementPresets therefore changes the stored category; a menu calculation and the normal application step are needed to update the measured body from a size choice.

Manual measurement buttons mark the set CUSTOM. An explicit CalculateMeasurements call still uses the configured row 0 when CUSTOM is selected, so that label is not a guarantee that later recalculation will leave manual torso values untouched.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BodyVitals.RescaleUI
member.summary: Defines a callback with no arguments for , so listeners can refresh after the UI layout routine attempts its updates.

remarks.para: A delegate stores one or more methods to call; a callback is that method being called at a particular point in the game's work. A RescaleUI handler takes no arguments and returns nothing. It receives neither the old scale nor the new scale, so a listener that needs current values must read the objects it cares about.

UI means user interface: displays such as menus and labels. The avatar is the player's body, and the UI and tutorial rigs are groups of objects holding those displays. BodyVitals calls its subscribed handlers during ApplyUILayoutSettings, after attempting the UI-rig resize, updating the popup-menu starting position, and requesting tutorial scaling. A nonpositive avatar arm length makes the routine skip the UI-rig resize but still continue to this notification; tutorial scaling can also skip its resize for a nonpositive eye height. The notification therefore does not guarantee that a resize happened or that every body setting has finished updating.

Inventory slots are places that hold equipped items. A child is an object nested under another object, its parent. Local position and rotation describe where the child sits and faces relative to that parent. Each slot saves its child’s return position and rotation during initial setup. If the inventory is open before the notification, the routine first returns the slot children to their ordinary parents and saved local positions and rotations. After the handlers return, it checks again whether the inventory is open; if so, it moves those children to the UI panel's target parents and positions. The notification comes before the later Inventory.FlipSlot call. These moves do not hide and restore the panel.

The layout routine reaches this notification only when the player avatar, UI rig, and tutorial rig are available. It does not compare old and new scale values before notifying. PROPEGATE_SOFT calls the layout routine twice on its normal path, so one settings propagation can call the same handler twice.
For example, a listener can reread the current UI layout and reposition its own label when notified. Make that refresh safe to repeat instead of treating each notification as one new scale change.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BonelabGameControl
member.summary: Connects a BONELAB level to saved checkpoints, inventory, completion records, and level changes.

remarks.para: Set up a nonblank LevelKey, the text identifier for this level in the save, and a ProgressionPoint list whose entries match your checkpoint numbers. A checkpoint number is a list index: 0 selects the first entry, 1 the second, and so on. It is not a completion percentage.

Unity calls Awake to initialize the component, then Start for its startup work. Awake decides whether saved progress should be resumed and registers the player-placement and checkpoint work with the scene loader. Start registers the inventory and completion work. A callback is a function saved to run when another operation reaches the right stage; the loader may run one immediately if that stage has already happened.

SaveFeatures selects completion, partial progress, and inventory behavior; inventory includes ammunition. Marking completion or preparing inventory changes the active save data in memory. JustSave asks the data manager to write the active save. A level jump requests a fade effect first and loads the selected level when that effect signals it is ready.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.BonelabProgressionHelper.Level
member.summary: Selects which campaign level is spared by .

remarks.para: This cleanup helper considers four saved level keys: Descent, LongRun, Ascent and Outro. Selecting one keeps that level's partial progress and cleans the other three. For example, selecting LongRun keeps LongRun while cleaning Descent, Ascent and Outro. Selecting None cleans all four.

For each cleaned level, it removes saved in-progress inventory, saved in-progress ammunition, the saved progress record named SLZ.Marrow.progress, and saved level-object records whose names do not start with SLZ. Other saved records whose names start with SLZ. are kept, except those three explicitly removed records. This is a partial-progress cleanup, not a request to load a level or erase the whole save.

The helper changes the supplied progression data and then requests that the active save be saved. The enum value itself does neither operation. Its default value is Descent; None must be selected explicitly when no named level should be spared.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ButtonHoverClick
member.summary: Adds sound and controller-vibration feedback to UI pointer entry, clicks, and explicit denied-action calls.

remarks.para: Attach this component to a UI button object. Its pointer-enter callback checks the feedback references, then calls HIGHLIGHT when the pointer event has an entered target. Its pointer-click callback calls CLICK when the event has a pressed target. A callback is a method the UI event system runs when an interaction occurs.

HIGHLIGHT requests subtle vibration and hover audio. CLICK requests press-click vibration and either ordinary click or confirmation audio. LOCKED requests subtle vibration and denial audio, and must be called by the code deciding that an action was denied.

These methods supply feedback; they do not implement the button's action, change its highlight appearance, or lock it. Missing individual providers skip their channel. Default sound lists still need an entry even when a sound override is supplied.

During Awake, Unity's early setup method, it registers a level-load callback that fills missing providers from the main UI rig. That callback runs immediately if the load session is already done, otherwise it waits for the level-load event. Pointer entry also refreshes missing references; direct feedback calls do not. Assigned references are preserved.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ChallengeSelectMenu
member.summary: Connects arena challenge and loadout choices to menu labels, configurable enemy-count goals, and scene actions.

remarks.para: A profile holds stored challenge settings, including rounds that group waves; a wave is a planned batch of enemies. The menu stores a challenge index and asks an assigned arena controller to choose that profile. A text component is a piece attached to a scene object that draws a label. For a valid nonnegative challenge index, the controller's difficulty-label list must be assigned and its entries valid; the controller enables those label components before assigning the profile so Unity can display them. A successful controller selection also resets its stored score to zero points and sets the score label to zero if that label exists. When the controller's cached player targeting proxy (the object enemies can target) is valid, it clears the friendly targeting pool, the list of possible targets for enemies, and puts only that saved player proxy back in the list. The controller saved that reference during level-load setup, so the reset reuses it instead of searching for the player again; with an invalid cached proxy, the reset leaves the existing list alone. It stores arenaState = ACTIVE, the controller's status value for an active arena. This state write alone does not begin a session, start its timer, or spawn waves. Its description labels show the selected profile, while separate confirmation methods update the active title and invoke events. A UnityEvent is a list of actions connected by a scene author in Unity's Inspector.

Loadout selection stores a number; a separate callback notification sends that number to listeners. A callback is a method called to react to a notification. Likewise, ChallengeStarted and CancelCurrentChallenge only invoke their configured events, so scene actions supply the actual start or cancellation behavior.

The count adjuster edits a goal for enemies present at the same time, measured in whole enemies. It does not count live enemies or spawn them directly. Difficulty text reflects the controller's existing difficulty; this menu's text-refresh method does not change that difficulty.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Control_UI_BodyMeasurements
member.summary: Lets the player adjust or estimate body dimensions, save them and apply them to the tracked player body.

remarks.para: This is the controller for BONELAB’s player body measurement calibration screen. The screen edits the active PlayerSettings: height is in centimetres, while wingspan (fingertip-to-fingertip reach with arms spread), inseam (inside-leg length), and chest, underbust, waist and hip circumferences (distances all the way around those body parts; underbust is just below the chest) are in metres. The interface displays those six dimensions in centimetres and height in both centimetres and feet/inches.

Height and shirt-preset buttons recalculate estimates. Individual measurement buttons choose Custom and change one dimension by 1 cm. A tracking rig is the group of scene objects representing the tracked player. Guess derives height from the current tracking rig, then estimates dimensions. For example, a player can use a shirt preset as a starting point and fine-tune a chest circumference with the individual buttons.

Vitals are the body measurements and player preferences copied into the current player body data. Adjustment buttons attempt saves and apply those vitals through the player controller before showing the reminder. Confirm and Guess hide that reminder and invoke the completion event after player application. Assign the interface labels, preset arrays, posture icons, player reference and completion event needed by these paths.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.DrawBezierCurve
member.summary: Draws a sampled cubic Bézier curve shaped by four point objects and a .

remarks.para: A LineRenderer is Unity’s component for drawing connected line segments through supplied positions. A cubic Bézier curve is a smooth curve with two endpoints and two shaping handles. Point1 starts it, Point4 ends the mathematical curve, Point2 bends its departure from the start, and Point3 bends its approach to the end. The point objects supply their world positions, normally meters.

Awake, Unity’s setup call when the component is loaded, caches the LineRenderer on the same object. With OnlySetOnStart true it then disables the component, without drawing or saving point positions. Otherwise the rendering callback calls UpdateLines before a camera draws the visible object.

Let N be lineSteps, the requested vertex count; i be a vertex’s zero-based index, from 0 through N - 1; and F be linePercentageFill, a unitless curve-parameter multiplier. Each vertex samples t = (i / N) * F. Here t = 0 is Point1 and t = 1 is Point4. Mathematically the last sample is F * (N - 1) / N. For ordinary vertex counts, F = 1 therefore stops short of Point4; native floating-point rounding can affect the result with very large counts.

For example, the default six vertices with fill 1 join samples from t = 0 through t = 5/6. Increasing the vertex count makes that sampled line finer, while moving the handle objects changes its bend on the next redraw. Configure the LineRenderer for world-space positions because the component does not convert its samples into local space.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.EnemyCollisonRelay.BodyPart
member.summary: Body-region labels an passes along with a collision report.

remarks.para: Set the relay's bodyPart field to describe the enemy region it represents. ReceiveCollison forwards that value with the collision to its assigned Enemy_Health component. This is configured labeling, not an automatic check of where the contact landed. A new relay starts with Pelvis.

These are flags, each using a separate bit in a number. You can combine labels with the | operator; for example, Chest | LeftArm carries both labels in one report. It does not send a second collision or add a second hit. Left and right describe the enemy's own sides.

Enemy_Health.OnReceivedCollison does not use this body-part argument when calculating impact damage. Selecting Head, another region, or several flags does not itself grant a critical-hit bonus in that handler. That handler has separate settings for collision damage and for colliders marked for critical hits. A collider is a physics shape that detects contact between objects.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.EnemyDamageReceiver.BodyPart
member.summary: Provides combinable body-region labels for an ; the current attack-damage routines do not scale damage by these labels.

remarks.para: This is a flags enum: each named value represents a separate on/off choice inside one integer. Combine values with the | operator. For example, LeftArm | RightArm stores both arm labels and has the numeric value 40. The numbers are unitless identifiers, not damage amounts.

The values are Head = 1, Chest = 2, Pelvis = 4, LeftArm = 8, LeftLeg = 16, RightArm = 32, and RightLeg = 64. Chest means the upper torso, and pelvis means the hips. Left and right refer to the enemy’s own sides. A new receiver starts with Pelvis.

The receiver stores this label as bodyPart, but its ReceiveAttack routine and Enemy_Health.OnReceivedDamage do not use it when calculating damage. They use the attack’s collider, the collision shape Unity uses to detect a hit, and its attack category, the kind of attack such as slicing, with the health component’s configured multipliers. The critical-hit setting is a list of these collision shapes; a matching attack collider can use the configured critical damage multiplier. For example, labeling a receiver Head does not by itself make it a critical-hit area; configure the actual critical-hit collider setting for that behavior.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio
member.summary: Requests UI feedback sounds for activation, deactivation, clicks, confirmation, denial and hover, with separate clip-selection settings.

remarks.para: This is a Unity component that other code calls when it wants an audio cue. Its six AUDIO methods choose a clip from the matching array, then ask the audio manager to play it. Configuring the component alone does not detect a click, hover or other action.

Each category has random, order and single modes. Random may repeat a sound; single uses the requested array index, starting at 0. Order advances a saved counter before selecting, and with three clips and an initial counter of 0 produces indices 1, 2, 0, 0, 1, 2. Provide a non-null array; an empty array skips the request. The click, confirmation, denial and hover calls can replace the chosen clip with clipOverride after a valid array selection.

A supplied location takes priority over audioPlacementOverride. Start, Unity's setup call before the first regular update, stores this component's own object as the fallback if needed. The AUDIO methods request sound at the chosen Transform's world position in Unity world coordinates, and the sound does not follow later object movement. Unity scenes commonly use a scale where 1 world unit represents 1 meter; this code does not convert the coordinates.

Volume is a unitless source level, initially 0.25. The minimum-distance radius is initially 1 Unity world unit, meaning distance alone does not reduce 3D sound volume within that radius. In a scene using the common 1 world unit = 1 meter scale, that is typically 1 meter. spatialBlend is initially 1 for fully positional 3D sound; 0 gives 2D sound. These settings are read for each request. For example, a button can use a short click asset, volume 0.5 and spatialBlend 0 to request a non-positional UI cue.

The audio manager obtains a reusable player before starting playback, which may finish after the AUDIO call returns. The component exposes no completion result from that request; a changed selection counter does not prove that a sound was successfully played.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Activate
member.summary: Selects how AUDIOACTIVATE chooses a sound from the activation-clip array.

remarks.para: Set Feedback_Audio.activateMode to one of these choices. clips_Activate holds the sound recordings available for activation feedback. Choosing a mode configures the next request; it does not play a sound by itself.

Random chooses afresh, order advances its saved counter with a repeated first entry at each wrap, and single uses the clip argument, a zero-based array position where zero means the first recording. The mode is read on each AUDIOACTIVATE call. An empty clip array returns without a playback request.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Click
member.summary: Controls how AUDIOCLICK chooses a sound from Feedback_Audio.clips_Click.

remarks.para: Set clickMode to one of these mutually exclusive choices. They are mode labels with no seconds, distance or volume units: random chooses an array entry, order advances the stored counter, and single uses the caller's clip index. Changing the mode does not itself request sound or reset the stored counter.

The clip array must be assigned. An empty array makes AUDIOCLICK return without requesting sound, including when clipOverride is supplied. With clips present, selection and array lookup happen before a valid override replaces the selected clip. The caller's index matters for single; random and order replace it.

order resets its counter only after it exceeds the list length. With three clips and a counter initially 0, its indices are 1, 2, 0, 0, 1 and so on. random can repeat a choice. single defaults to array index 0 when the clip argument is omitted.

Playback uses the supplied location's current world position. World position means the position measured in the whole scene's coordinates, rather than coordinates relative to the sound object. Position uses Unity distance units, normally meters. If location is missing, it uses audioPlacementOverride, the scene object saved as the fallback sound location. Unity's Start setup method fills a missing fallback with this component's own scene object; Start is called before the component's first regular update. The sound request stays at that sampled position rather than following the object.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Confirm
member.summary: Chooses how selects one confirmation sound from clips_Confirm per AUDIOCONFIRM call.

remarks.para: Set confirmMode to random for a random array entry, order for its advancing counter stored on this component, or single for the clip index passed by the caller. An array is a numbered list; index 0 refers to its first clip. The method reads the mode on each call, so changing it changes later selections without automatically requesting a sound.

The order counter advances before selection and resets only after exceeding the clip count. With three clips and starting counter 0, its calls select indices 1, 2, 0, 0 and then repeat. Random selections can repeat too.

A valid clipOverride replaces the selected asset after the array lookup. A missing array fails, an empty array plays nothing, and a bad caller index in single mode can fail even with an override. No mode plays an entire sequence automatically or proves that a UI confirmation occurred; AUDIOCONFIRM must be called to request the sound.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Deactivate
member.summary: Chooses how selects one sound from the deactivation clip array on .

remarks.para: Assign a mode to the Feedback_Audio component's deactivateMode setting. Each AUDIODEACTIVATE call selects at most one clip from clips_Deactivate and requests playback; selecting this mode does not itself detect deactivation or start a sequence of sounds.

The array positions are zero-based: position 0 is the first clip, position 1 the second, and so on. Random and order modes replace the call's clip index; single mode uses it. An empty array produces no playback request, while a missing array is not handled as an empty one.

The location argument supplies the sound's position in metres in world coordinates, the shared scene coordinate system, at the time of the request. If no location is supplied, the component uses audioPlacementOverride; its Start routine, which Unity calls when the component begins running, fills a missing override with this component's GameObject. The GameObject is the scene object holding this component. This call requests a sound at that position rather than making it follow the location as it moves.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Audio.Hover
member.summary: Chooses how selects an entry from clips_Hover.

remarks.para: Set Feedback_Audio.hoverMode to random for a fresh random choice, order for the saved counter sequence, or single for the index passed by the caller. A clip is one recorded sound. The mode is a selection setting; it does not detect a hovering hand, begin a sound on assignment, or wait for an earlier sound to finish.

Order advances the counter before selecting and resets only after it grows past the clip count. With a fresh counter of 0 and [A, B, C], the requests select B, C, A, A, then repeat that pattern. Random can repeat a clip immediately. Single uses zero-based positions, with index 0 as the default.

AUDIOHOVER first requires a nonnull, nonempty clip array and selects an entry, then applies a provided clipOverride whose clip still exists; a missing or destroyed override leaves the selected clip in place. It next requests playback at the supplied location or the configured placement object. An empty array produces no playback, even with an override. Start, a method Unity calls before the first frame update, sets the default placement object if needed but does not reset the saved hover counter.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Feedback_Tactile
member.summary: Provides calls that request controller vibration for hovering over, pressing and releasing UI items.

remarks.para: This is a Unity component: a script attached to a scene object. Haptic feedback means vibration you feel in a handheld controller. HOVER requests the selected controller's subtle vibration, while CLICK selects its press or release vibration according to the down argument. The UI code calls these methods when the interaction happens.

Both methods use the supplied controller, or the active controller stored by Control_UI_InGameData if the supplied one is missing or destroyed. They return without sending feedback if no usable controller or Haptor exists. A Haptor is the controller's vibration helper and must be set up with a device to receive its requests.

The vibration helper supplies the current duration in seconds, frequency in hertz (cycles per second), and strength with no physical unit. Both methods request zero delay. Duration and strength are settings for the request, and the controller's hardware determines the feedback actually felt. For example, one button can call HOVER as the pointer enters, CLICK with true on press, and CLICK with false on release.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GachaPlacer
member.summary: Controls loading-time placement of a collectible capsule using the active save, and assigns the item represented by each spawned capsule.

remarks.para: A crate is a stored item definition. Use it with an assigned CrateSpawner in Manual Mode. Set that spawner’s spawnableCrateReference to the capsule object, and this placer’s unlockCrate to the item the capsule should represent. Its inherited enable/disable handling registers and removes the spawn listener that performs capsule configuration. A spawn listener is a routine notified when the spawner reports a spawned object.

Awake is Unity’s initialization callback, a routine called to prepare the component. It registers OnPersistentLoad with the current streaming session. That loading check requires a resolved, non-redacted crate and an unlock count below one. Non-redacted means the crate’s Redacted visibility flag is false; onlyPlaceIfBeatGame additionally requires the save’s BeatGame flag. It does not continuously watch for later progress changes.

When a spawn notification supplies an object containing GachaCapsule, the placer writes selectedCrate first and then requests the preview mesh. Placement starts the spawner’s request rather than waiting for a completed capsule or granting the item immediately. A spawner outside Manual Mode has a separate loading-time spawn path that can bypass this placer’s eligibility check.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GameControl_Descent
member.summary: Runs Descent's height reveal, avatar-selection mirror, gallows milestones, timed lightning effects and the dagger stage.

remarks.para: On a fresh run, it starts a coroutine after level loading. A coroutine is a sequence that pauses and continues over several frames. It changes scene objects and effects, then waits for the mirror, avatar-die stage, noose, drop and cut milestone flags. SEQUENCE(1) through SEQUENCE(6) set the height, mirror, avatar-die, noose, drop and cut flags respectively. The inspected intro sequence waits on the last five of these; it does not check the height flag. A true flag lets its wait pass when reached; setting a flag does not skip earlier effects or start a new sequence. After the first lightning appearance animation finishes, it requests showing daggerEntity, the dagger’s scene object, then continues the remaining effects before waiting for the cut milestone.

An animation curve is a graph that turns animation progress into a value controlling the effect. The height and mirror curves change local size multipliers along parent-relative axes: the object’s X, Y and Z directions follow the object and its parent, the containing object in Unity’s object hierarchy. Timed animations and milestone waits continue on later frames. The optional force-grab tutorial is a delayed hint, not a switch for the player's grabbing ability.

After the noose milestone it requests field echo and ambience, stores the selected avatar identifiers and requests saving, then releases the player. On a resumed save it follows a separate startup path that suppresses the avatar override, requests the pit spawner and releases the player instead of running the full intro.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GameControl_Holodeck
member.summary: Controls Holodeck panel appearances, reflection and ambient lighting, preset audio, and a door-cover display.

remarks.para: CYCLEMATERIAL advances the selection and uses the fast routine: one initial frame pause, then all panel changes and lighting. SELECTMATERIAL uses the timed routine: audio and light-object setup first, random waits before individual panels, and environment lighting last. A coroutine is a routine Unity can pause and resume across later frames. A frame is one game-update step.
The two routines also handle the cover object differently. TOGGLEDOOR only switches the cover and its check image for nonzero selections; it does not directly animate a physical entrance door.

A reflection probe is a Unity component supplying an environment image for reflective surfaces. Here, the controller assigns already stored images. The lighting data is a pair of cubemaps plus saved spherical-harmonic numbers. A cubemap is a six-sided image of the surroundings, used here for reflections. Spherical harmonics are a small set of numbers describing the color and brightness of light arriving from different directions.

Startup hides the UI root, meaning the root object for the onscreen user interface of controls and displays, and registers a level-load callback that applies lighting preset 0 without changing wall materials or the saved selection. A callback is a method another system runs when an event occurs.

Configure aligned wallMaterials and cubemaps lists, valid panel references, and at least two reflection probes. The fixed timed audio presets also need both ambience-zone references and the configured audio manager. Scene and audio changes happen at different stages; the saved selection is not a completion flag.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GameControl_Holodeck.ProbePair
member.summary: Stores two reflection images and cached ambient lighting that the holodeck applies when it finishes changing to an environment.

remarks.para: A cubemap is six square pictures showing the surroundings in every direction. A reflection probe is a Unity component that supplies those pictures to reflective surfaces, such as shiny metal. This record holds the pictures: cubemap0 becomes the custom image for the controller's first probe, and cubemap1 becomes the custom image for its second probe. cubemap0 also becomes the scene's custom reflection image. Applying the record assigns these images directly.

harmonics stores spherical harmonics: a small set of numbers describing the color and strength of smooth light arriving from different directions. The controller copies these numbers into the scene's ambient-light settings. GenerateSHs rebuilds this stored lighting from cubemap0 for every record; cubemap1 is not included in that calculation. After changing cubemap0, regenerate the harmonics if the stored ambient lighting should match the new image. Applying the record uses the stored numbers rather than calculating them again.

Put one record in the controller's cubemaps array for each matching wall-material choice, in the same order. SELECTMATERIAL starts a coroutine, meaning work that can pause and continue on later frames. It changes the wall panels before applying the selected record's reflection and lighting settings. The controller needs two assigned reflection probes and a valid record at the selected array index.

For example, if the desert wall material is choice 2, put the desert cubemaps and their generated ambient-light numbers in cubemaps[2]. Array indices start at 0, so this is the third entry. Selecting choice 2 applies those images and lighting after the wall-panel changes finish; merely editing the record does not immediately apply it to the scene.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GameControl_Hub
member.summary: Coordinates the campaign Hub’s recorded key and battery progress, visible displays, airlock paths and level-transition requests.

remarks.para: The Hub restores shared key, battery, power and spawn-selection data, then rebuilds displays and requests saved seated-battery copies. On level load it restores the player’s position from the saved spawn-point selection. Recorded progress is separate from physical state: a true insertion flag does not prove an object finished spawning, and a successful door-release request is recorded before its timed sequence finishes.

Airlock entry and exit tasks stream separately loaded level areas and command the appropriate physics doors. Those tasks continue across later frames and can end on cancellation as well as a measured position threshold. A canceled wait does not necessarily stop the last applied door drive. A physics joint restricts movement, and its drive applies forces toward configured targets.

Level transitions carry inventory and ammunition toward LongRun or Ascent, request a fade-effect spawn and only start the destination load through the later fade-completion action. Setup caches lock-bar joints and bodies before the release sequence uses them.

For example, reporting KEYINSERTED(1) records the Arena module key, saves progress and refreshes its display and the inserted-key count. It does not itself open every door: the airlock and Big Walk paths apply their own power, key-count and request checks.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GameControl_KartRace
member.summary: Controls Monogon Motorway kart-race timing, checkpoint-gated lap progress, best records and race celebrations.

remarks.para: The normal scene sequence is FinishLineTrigger to start, TRACKCHECKPOINT calls for the course checklist, then FinishLineTrigger again to try a lap. NEWLAP records a split only when every configured checkpoint flag is true. After the configured number of accepted laps, ENDRACE stops timing, records bests and requests objective rewards and celebrations. DoLevelComplete is a separate inherited level-completion and transition action.

The clock adds unscaled frame seconds: the real elapsed time between Unity frames, without multiplying by the game’s slow-motion setting. It skips the addition when Time.timeScale, the game’s speed setting, is exactly zero. For example, a frame lasting 0.02 second adds 0.02 to both lap and race clocks at a time scale of 1 or 0.5, but adds nothing at a time scale of 0. The clock is updated frame by frame, so a line crossing records the latest stored frame value, not a separately measured instant of crossing.

lapTimes includes a live slot for the current lap, while the race-total clock includes all elapsed driving time and is accumulated separately. ENDRACE copies that running total into a final-result snapshot; it does not recalculate it from the array. Best records are seconds, with smaller totals being better. Saving a new personal best and deleting a best are requests whose result this controller does not check.

Call RESETRACE before a full retry. Ending keeps raceStarted true and sets finishedRace true, while STARTRACE does not reset the lap index, race-total clock or finished flag. The scene crossing events are configured separately; the stored trigger object references do not connect themselves to the race methods.

The final-lap hint appears before the last lap, not after finishing. The start action uses lap confetti; ending requests all three celebration effects. Awake, Unity’s early setup call, caches each effect’s sound component from the same object. Changing a particle reference after that does not refresh its cached sound player.

Provide non-null arrays and non-null required objects before starting. Empty display arrays are allowed if that display is not needed. lapTimes must have a slot for every driven lap, and each enabled txt_lapTimes entry needs a matching slot at the same index. The controller does not create those arrays or scene objects for you.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GameControl_MagmaGate
member.summary: Controls Magma Gate's requested loss sequence and adds the arena-key progress flag to inherited level completion.

remarks.para: LoseSequence sets each assigned laser GameObject active, then asks Unity to run DoorDissolve after a configured delay of 1.25 seconds. A GameObject is a scene object with attached components. DoorDissolve invokes loseEvent, a list of configured methods, with no arguments; listeners provide effects such as a door animation.

DoLevelComplete runs inherited campaign completion and starts its transition request, including the inherited parkour-key progress flag. It then records the arena-key hub flag as unlocked and requests a progression save. Starting a transition or requesting a save does not establish that either has completed successfully.

Set up the laser array, event listeners, active save, and inherited campaign references before using these methods. The methods implemented by this class do not decide when the player has failed: a caller or scene event must start LoseSequence. For example, a configured challenge can call LoseSequence on failure and DoLevelComplete on success.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GenGameControl_Display
member.summary: Stores game-statistic text references and provides a command to recolor text in its object hierarchy.

remarks.para: Each named field points to a TMP_Text component, a TextMeshPro object that draws a string. Code can write those components’ text values for titles, counters and arena readouts. The inspected class itself does not calculate statistics, run a timer or choose the displayed strings.

ChangeAllTextColor searches for matching text components on this object and active children, and requests textColor as their default letter color. It does not use the named fields to choose its targets, so an unrelated referenced label needs a separate color update.

For example, after assigning an aliveText component, another script can set its text to "3" for an enemy-alive readout, then call ChangeAllTextColor if that label belongs to the searched hierarchy. Changing a reference or color field alone does not perform either operation.
The hierarchy is Unity’s tree of scene objects. A child is an object nested under another object; the search includes active descendants at any depth.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GenGameControl_Spawner
member.summary: Supplies arena waves with weapons and ammo, records completed spawn callbacks, and cleans up tracked loot.

remarks.para: Initialize connects the arena controller and prepares fixed ammo and player-relative drop locations. SpawnWaveLoot then starts a coroutine, a routine that can pause until a later Unity frame, chosen from the controller's assigned arena mode.

The ordinary path can top up an existing active ammo pickup and requests weapons at this spawner. Weapon mode shows a player-relative marker, filters the weapon loot entries, and requests fresh ammo and weapons at that drop point. A spawn request and its completion are separate: callbacks, code run with the returned objects, update the tracking records afterward.

Cleanup works from those records. Weapon cleanup can spare attached objects or detach them first; automatic ammo collection visits its recorded pickup list. The lists and round counters have different purposes and are not a complete live snapshot of everything in the arena.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GeoManager
member.summary: Coordinates preset deployment, pit-cover movement and cleanup for dynamic arena geometry.

remarks.para: A GeoMover is a component that moves a geometry object between configured positions relative to its parent. Awake, Unity's initialization callback, is a routine Unity calls while setting up the component. It builds name lookups from the manager's existing mover list. The arena controller uses this manager when starting matches, selecting custom challenges and clearing a cancelled challenge.

SelectGeo and IncrementAndToggleGeo clear the old setup before requesting a preset. ToggleGeo by itself starts or schedules the chosen mover without clearing the old one. Movement uses coroutines, sequences that pause and continue across frames, and a pit-cover delay can postpone deployment.

The recorded active mover changes on a completed raise, while the saved selection counter and moverIndex have separate lifetimes. Shared move-up callbacks, routines called to report completion, run after activeGeoMover and UP are recorded, but before a death-pit floor starts lowering or dynamic props are requested. A notification is therefore not a guarantee that every part of the arena transition has finished.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.GeoManager.GeoState
member.summary: Stored markers for the geometry manager’s deployment progress.

remarks.para: The values are CLEARED = 0, MOVING = 1, UP = 2, and MOVING_TO_CLEAR = 3. They are discrete choices rather than distances, percentages, or live physics measurements.

The inspected start paths set MOVING after activating the selected mover and before starting its move-up sequence. Completion sets UP before the manager callback. The complete inspected manager routines and main mover sequence do not automatically set CLEARED or MOVING_TO_CLEAR during clearing or lowering, so the enum alone is not a reliable four-stage animation tracker.

Geometry means the movable arena objects, such as the floor or obstacles. An enum is a fixed set of named choices. A callback is a routine called to report an event. For example, hiding an object can leave UP stored, so reading this enum does not tell you whether that object is visible.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.HighlightUI
member.summary: Controls one renderer’s visibility and two shader color settings, with an optional timed color fade.

remarks.para: A Renderer is the Unity component that draws a visible surface. A GameObject is the Unity scene object holding components. A shader is the surface’s drawing program; a material stores drawing settings used with a shader for a surface. A MaterialPropertyBlock holds setting overrides supplied for one Renderer. Awake, Unity’s initialization callback (a routine called to perform or report an action), prepares a shared MaterialPropertyBlock and its shader-property IDs if the block is missing. Start applies the current color1 and color2 through SetColors, which caches the Renderer on this same GameObject when needed. The material must use the properties _Color0 and _Color1 for these settings to affect its appearance.

SetColors immediately applies a color pair and saves both values back to the fields. FadeToColors with an explicit duration starts a coroutine, a sequence that continues over several frames, when this component is active and enabled; it first stops the previous stored fade. The sequence uses real frame intervals unaffected by game time scale, the game-speed factor, blends HSV color values and alpha, and repeatedly applies the pair. HSV describes hue (the color family), saturation (how colorful it is) and value (brightness); alpha is the unitless opacity channel. With the component inactive or disabled, the same overload applies its target immediately. The overload without a duration also applies immediately and does not stop a fade already running.

EnableMesh and DisableMesh show or hide the cached renderer without changing its colors, changing GameObject activity or canceling the timed sequence. For example, a fade can keep updating its stored colors while its renderer is hidden, ready for a later EnableMesh call.

The two color values and renderer reference belong to each component. The property block and integer property IDs are shared working data. Shader behavior determines the visual arrangement and transparency; HighlightUI does not establish which color is spatially nearer or farther.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LaserCursor
member.summary: Draws a controller-directed menu laser over configured UI regions and reports queued presses to the UI input module. See and .

remarks.para: Assign the UI regions, marker views, rendered line, Bezier curve and sound references. Awake is Unity’s initialization callback, a routine called to prepare the component; it arranges Initialize through the level-load callback. Initialize maps scene controllers to the UI rig’s cursorTarget references and releases the startup pause.

The controller’s primary-interaction or B-button down action chooses which controller directs it. A region’s plane, rotating bounds, distance and direction tests determine the cached target. Valid active-region updates place the markers, show or hide the regular visuals, and can animate a pulse. Hiding visuals alone does not deactivate pointer calculations.

Trigger queues a press and the next successful ray dispatch clears it after passing it to the module. UpdateCursor accepts a world origin and direction for direct dispatch while active; its isPressed argument is not used by this implementation, which instead sends the queued flag. External dispatch does not by itself build the visual-region caches or initialize controller focus.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.LevelsPanelView
member.summary: Displays pages of eligible level records and starts loading requests for selected rows.

remarks.para: AssetWarehouse is the catalog of installed content. A level crate is a catalog record for a level, a barcode uniquely identifies that record, and a pallet is the content package containing it. The panel removes records hidden from menus, sorts candidates by their titles, and builds a cached selectable list.

Ammo deltas are saved changes in ammunition counts. The gathered final-ammo-delta map is a lookup table indexed by saved level keys. Normally a candidate must match a configured story-level save key that appears in that map, and it must pass the source flags. A valid ammo-delta record counts even with a false completion flag; an absent ammo-delta key plus a saved boolean true completion flag also counts. Only one source flag true restricts to that source; both flags true or both false allow both. BeatGame and DeveloperMode both true bypass those eligibility checks while still excluding hidden records.

Configure the story-level mapping, at least one row GameObject (a scene object), matching row title labels, two navigation objects, and a page label in the Inspector, Unity’s component-settings panel. Awake, the routine Unity calls when initializing this component, copies the configured barcode-to-save-key mapping into a runtime dictionary, a lookup table created while the game is running. Later changes to the source array do not update that dictionary automatically.

A full refresh recalculates page count and redraws the stored zero-based current page without resetting it. Enabling or activating the panel refreshes it synchronously, meaning the refresh work is performed during that call; successful pallet-added notifications also refresh an active panel after the catalog is initially loaded. PopulateMenuAsync starts a wait for that initial catalog load before refreshing.

SelectItem uses a row index within the current page. LoadFirstLevel activates and refreshes the panel, then selects row zero on that same page. Both start SceneStreamer requests; returning does not mean the selected level is ready. The loading-scene choice modLoadScreen is passed only when the selected level’s pallet is neither marked Internal nor recognized as belonging to the current game. A pallet marked Internal uses the barcode request even when current-game membership is false; source filtering uses that membership alone.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.MineCartControl
member.summary: Selects presets and sends their drive settings to a spline-guided mine cart through .

remarks.para: Each contact joint’s drive acts like a motor. Damping sets the motor force requested for each m/s of difference between target and actual speed, measured in newton-seconds per meter (N·s/m). The maximum-force setting caps each contact motor separately in newtons. The director is a playback controller for Timeline. Timeline is Unity’s timed sequence of animation, sound or other game events.

A spline is the curved path used as the track. Each preset stores a target velocity in meters per second, a velocity-response damper in newton-seconds per meter and a maximum motor force in newtons. The spline’s contact joints, physics connections guiding the cart, use these settings to try to reach the requested speed.

The control copies one preset into its current caches before storing the values on splineBody and marking its settings changed. An eligible SplineJoint physics update applies them to the joint drives. Changing a preset or the rideSpeed field directly does not perform this process; call UpdateSpeed to apply it.

Two one-shot entry points have independent flags that become true only after UpdateSpeed returns. Clear the appropriate flag to reuse that trigger. Preset names do not enforce hardcoded ride behavior, and the stored director is not used by the inspected speed methods to control Timeline playback.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.MineCartLapBar
member.summary: Watches a mine-cart seat’s lap-bar angle and, with cj.swapBodies disabled, applies a strong motor hold at the bar’s current rotation when the seated player reaches the threshold; when enabled, the helper exchanges the target and reference rotations.

remarks.para: The seat sends registration and deregistration notifications. Registration starts the angle checker and runs OnSeat. The checker first waits until a later frame, then samples the Servo’s signed twist angle in degrees. Below lockAngle it requests another check after 0.25 game seconds. Game seconds follow the game’s slow-motion or pause setting, and a check resumes on a later frame rather than an exact wall-clock instant. At or above the threshold it calls LockBar and finishes.

A Servo measures turning around the joint’s primary axis against its cached initial orientation; this is not a raw scene rotation. A physics joint is the connection controlling how the bar can move. With cj.swapBodies disabled, LockBar uses the bar’s current local orientation as target and the startup orientation as reference; UnlockBar uses the startup orientation as target and the current orientation as reference. When cj.swapBodies is enabled, the helper exchanges the target and reference roles for both commands. LockBar applies the stronger motor drive, while UnlockBar gives the motor a much lower torque cap.

Assign seat before enabling, assign cj before Start, Unity’s setup call before the first update, and make servo measure the same bar joint. Start caches the joint object’s initial local rotation. The angle checker needs the Servo’s own initialization cache as well.

The events OnBarLocked and OnBarUnlocked run after motor settings are changed, without waiting for motion to finish. Deregistration stops the checker and runs OnUnseat, but does not unlock the bar. For example, an OnUnseat listener can call UnlockBar if leaving the cart should also release the bar.
Torque is turning force; the cap limits how much turning force the motor can apply.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.NooseBonelabIntro
member.summary: Controls the Descent gallows intro: attaches the noose to the player’s chest, releases the platform connections, applies choking damage, and handles cutting free.

remarks.para: The sequence moves through Initial, Reeling, Locked, Hanging, and Cut. A suitable noose position starts a physics joint, a connection between two simulated objects, from the chest to the knot. Reeling tightens it, Locked waits for the reveal, and Hanging releases the X-rotation limits on seven platform connections before enabling damage. NooseCut only acts in the Hanging stage.

Timing settings use game-time seconds, the clock affected by game speed and pause settings. A frame here means one eligible Update pass after the scene and player are ready. nooseOnToSceneReveal controls the Locked wait, sceneRevealToPlankDrop delays the first platform release, and plankDropTimer schedules later releases. The seven joint objects remain: each release makes its configured X rotation free, in array order 0 through 6, at most one release per pass. A release schedules the next deadline from its actual current game time, so slow frames can stretch the gaps.

While hanging, damage requires the Y component of the chest-to-knot joint’s current force, one signed vector component measured in newtons, to be strictly greater than mass × 9.81 × 0.5.
