Unity’s currentForce is the force the physics solver applies to satisfy the joint’s constraints, and Unity reports it relative to connectedBody when that body is set. Here the connected body is knotRb, the knot’s Rigidbody, so the Y component follows the knot’s axes; it does not establish upward force along the scene’s Y axis or describe the total force magnitude. Here mass is the avatar’s stored mass in kilograms, 9.81 is gravitational acceleration in metres per second squared, and 0.5 is a unitless half-weight factor. The accumulated game seconds must also be strictly greater than damageTickRate, the interval setting in seconds. damagePerTick is the number of health points requested in each hit, not points per second. At most one damage request is made per checked frame; the timer resets after a request, and a fresh reading of that same connected-body-relative Y component at or below 500 newtons also resets it. These are separate force checks. For example, an 80-kilogram avatar has a computed threshold of 392.4 newtons, and the separate 500-newton timer-reset rule still applies. Frame checks do not promise exact elapsed spacing or a guaranteed health loss.

The scene must supply at least seven platform joints and nine noose grab points in the expected order. Its UnityEvents run attached listener routines and pass no arguments. Reeling writes Locked and its new deadline before nooseOnEvent. Locked writes Hanging, resets the release step to 0 and schedules the first release before nooseOnAndHeldEvent, then starts the cutscene. That event does not test whether a hand is holding the noose. On step 7, _isHanging becomes true before daggerSpawnEvent, and the same Update can then perform its first damage test. daggerSpawnEvent is a cue rather than proof that a dagger spawned. NooseCut clears the chest-joint reference and writes Cut before its dagger helper and later nooseCutEvent notification.

When Update finds health zero or below, it sets _skipUpdate and starts the delayed death coroutine, a routine that pauses and resumes later. That routine waits Player_Health.deathTimeAmount, the health controller’s death delay in game seconds, sends nooseDeath with no arguments, then waits three more game-time seconds. Only health exactly zero at that later check requests the fade effect. If the spawned effect has a FadeVolume component and that fade later completes, its callback, a routine run when an operation reports completion, requests a reload of the current scene. SceneStreamer skips that request if a session is already loading; the operation runs asynchronously and does not guarantee completed spawning or loading. The level field does not choose another destination along this inspected reload path.

OnEnable, Unity’s call when this component is enabled, saves the first five platform world rotations and the dagger’s world position and orientation. World means relative to the whole scene; a pose means position and orientation. These are setup-time snapshots rather than values read afresh when resetting.

ResetNoose only attempts a partial reset while Hanging. It restores those first five saved platform world rotations, returns their configured X rotation to Limited, restores the saved dagger pose and clears its movement. It does not recreate or restore all seven platform connections, and leaves several sequence flags unchanged. It also calls the dagger cut helper twice, so successful removal on the first call can make the second fail on the cleared joint reference.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.PageItem
member.summary: Holds one radial-menu choice so a page can display its label in a chosen slot and run its saved action when triggered.

remarks.para: A radial menu places buttons around a circle. This item contains the data for one button: name is its displayed text, direction chooses one of the eight configured menu slots, and m_Callback is a saved function called with no arguments. Put the item in a Page's items list and render that page with PageView to connect it to the matching button.

Rendering copies the label and keeps a reference to the item for later triggers. Updating name or direction requires rendering again to update the display. A trigger reads the item's current callback immediately, so replacing that callback changes the next trigger's action. An unassigned callback does nothing.

For example, a choice labeled "Inventory" can use NORTH and save a function that opens an inventory page. Creating or displaying the choice does not run that function. Invoke runs it directly, while the menu view's trigger runs the callback for its selected button.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.PageItem.Directions
member.summary: Chooses which of eight radial-menu buttons displays a page item.

remarks.para: An enum is a named set of choices. Give each PageItem one direction when building the page. PageView.Render reads it to assign the item's label and action to a configured button. The menu's own up and right define the direction names, and the scene layout determines the actual button positions.

The choices run clockwise: NORTH is 0, NORTHEAST 1, EAST 2, SOUTHEAST 3, SOUTH 4, SOUTHWEST 5, WEST 6 and NORTHWEST 7. These numbers have no physical unit; each selects the matching entry in PageView.buttons, whose first entry has index 0. For example, EAST assigns an Inventory item to buttons[2], the third button, normally at the right of the menu.

The direction is read when the page is rendered. Render again after changing it to update the visible assignment. Pointer selection follows the configured button's orientation, and triggering the selected button runs the action supplied by that item. The direction chooses the button; the item supplies what happens when it is triggered.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.PageView
member.summary: Displays a in directional button slots and handles cursor selection, feedback and opening or closing animations.

remarks.para: A Page holds PageItem data: item names, directions and action functions. Render maps those items to configured scene buttons. The surrounding UI supplies cursor and trigger input; this component caches a selected button and can invoke its action. SetHomePage both stores the default page and renders it.

Normal opening renders the home page, sets a logical activation flag, starts a coroutine and enables text. A coroutine is work that continues over later frames. Closing clears selection and text through Deactivate, while its animation can keep running before the scene object is disabled. Clear starts the close animation without all of that logical cleanup.

Opening and closing smooth button local scale, a unitless size relative to the parent, using random smoothing times of 0.02 to 0.1 seconds and elapsed time unaffected by game-speed changes. These are smoothing settings rather than exact total animation durations. The opening routine keeps yielding until stopped.

The audio placement object must be assigned. Page sounds use Feedback_Audio's click path with a clip override, so its click array still needs to be nonempty. Sound requests can return before a reusable player starts playback. Tactile feedback means controller vibration.

onActivated receives this view before Activate changes its object or state; onDeactivated receives it after closing disables the object. Trigger's true result means a selected reference was processed, even when that button has no action. onActivated is not an opening-completion signal. onDeactivated signals that closing reached its completion step, forced all button local scales to zero and disabled the scene object; it does not prove that the logical activation flag is false. Trigger returning true does not prove that an item action ran.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.PanelView
member.summary: Provides shared activation and controller-cursor behavior for panels opened from the radial .

remarks.para: A panel is a section of a menu, such as preferences or an avatar list. The radial menu arranges its choices around a center. The base panel turns its containing Unity object on or off, records a pending trigger press while active, and forwards pointing input to a menu input module, the component that turns pointing and pressing into menu input.

Cursor input describes a ray, an imaginary line starting at an origin and pointing forward. The input module uses it to find menu objects under the pointer. The origin is a position in the game world, measured in Unity distance units, normally treated as meters; forward is a direction, not a position or a distance. The pending press is forwarded with that ray and cleared after forwarding.

For example, a preferences panel can be activated when its radial choice is selected and can use CloseMenu to close its assigned popup menu. Set up the popup-menu reference and an EventSystem, Unity’s menu-input manager, with the VR input component before expecting those operations to work.

Derived panel classes can replace the virtual opening, closing, and trigger methods. The base active flag describes whether its input methods should run; it does not guarantee that a parent Unity object is allowing the panel to appear on screen.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.PlayerAvatarDecorator
member.summary: Requests a chosen player avatar during the current level’s load-completion notification.

remarks.para: This component links a PlayerMarker, which reports whether the player scene object has spawned, with an avatar package selected by overrideAvatar. Awake, Unity’s initialization callback—a routine called when setting up the component—registers the level-load routine; OnEnable separately subscribes to the marker’s spawn/despawn reports.

When the level-loading session reports completion, the decorator requests the selected avatar only if its stored _hasSpawned flag is true and preventSwap is false. The player’s avatar manager checks the package identifier and starts a swap that can finish later. This component does not continuously force that avatar.

Receiving a spawn notification or changing overrideAvatar only updates stored data; neither starts the swap. If the load notification is skipped before readiness, a later spawn does not retry it. SwapAvatar provides a separate helper that checks preventSwap but does not require the readiness flag.

Prepare _playerMarker and a non-null avatar reference before use, with the current loading session and player references available. Disabling removes the marker listener but leaves the level-load registration and readiness flag in place; preventSwap controls whether a later notification can still request an override.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.PlayerHealthDecorator
member.summary: Applies health and death rules to a player spawned by a marker, positions the player at that marker, and runs configured actions on final death.

remarks.para: Assign a PlayerMarker and the desired settings before enabling the component. On a spawn notification it copies the health mode, reload choice, and Mortal dying duration into Player_Health, requests a teleport to the marker, and connects its PlayerDeath callback. These are spawn-time settings; editing the decorator does not continuously update the already spawned player.

In the normal paired lifecycle, disabling removes the spawn-listener registration added on enable, and destruction removes the matching death subscription added on spawn. Each cleanup removes only one registration: repeated manual OnEnable calls can leave duplicate marker listeners after disabling, and repeated spawns can leave duplicate death subscriptions after destruction. Disabling leaves an existing death callback connected; a callback is a routine called to perform or report an action, here to run the configured final-death actions. The assigned OnPlayerDeath event runs at final death, after the recoverable dying window has failed.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.PlayerRefs
member.summary: Provides a global entry point to cached player rigs, the ammo receiver, and assigned body-settings and avatar-management components.

remarks.para: A callback is a method called when player-reference setup finishes. An avatar is the player's in-game body. The separately assigned BodyVitals component stores real body measurements and comfort/control choices.

A rig is a group of objects that represents or controls the player's body. Awake, Unity's early component initialization method, stores this component in Instance and registers for the persistent-scene load stage. Persistent scenes hold shared objects across gameplay levels. If that load stage has already happened, the registration calls initialization immediately; otherwise it waits for the stage.

Initialization locates a player by the configured player tag, caches the rig manager and ammo receiver, then copies the manager's controller and physics rigs. It sets HasRefs true, invokes OnRefsComplete with no arguments, and finally sets _enableWhenReadyObjects active in array order.

These are cached references rather than player searches performed by every getter. BodyVitals and PlayerAvatarManager are supplied separately by scene assignment. HasRefs is not a guarantee that every reference is non-null or that waiting-object activation has finished.

For example, obtain Instance, check its existence, then wait for HasRefs or a completion callback and check the particular component you need. Completion callbacks do not replay when added later. Configure waiting objects inactive yourself if they should remain hidden until initialization.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.PopUpMenuView
member.summary: Displays the controller-operated popup menu for choosing inventory, preferences, spawnable, level, avatar and developer-tool actions.

remarks.para: Assign radialPageView, the view that displays the selectable menu entries, and the inventory, preferences, spawnables, levels and avatars panel references before startup. This component controls those supplied views; adding a menu entry does not create its panel component.

Awake, Unity’s initialization callback, sets up storage for controller-specific magazine-ejection actions and registers instance if no instance already exists. A callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. Start, Unity’s first active-frame setup routine, replaces any earlier menu page with a new page, adds preferences, inventory and levels, and then deactivates the menu. Its avatar entry is added only when the saved completed-game flag BeatGame and the developer-mode setting DeveloperMode are both true.

Activate opens the menu using the supplied player-head and root position/orientation references and controller input. Trigger uses the current selection to run its action or forwards input to the panels after a panel has been selected. Calling Activate while already active calls Trigger(true, true, null) again. In radial mode this may invoke the selected item’s action or deactivate the menu if nothing is selected; in panel mode it forwards the trigger flags to the relevant assigned panel views. Deactivate clears the active state before deactivating the menu views and beginning to hide the cursor.

Use the relevant Add* and Remove* methods to manage available menu entries. Preferences, inventory, spawnable, level and avatar entry actions open their assigned panel and deactivate the other views. Developer-tool and magazine-ejection entries run registered action callbacks. Spawn, developer-tool and magazine-ejection entries are not automatically added by Start, and some additions depend on saved progress or supplied actions.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.PreferencesPanelView
member.summary: Controls which settings page object is active inside the pop-up preferences menu.

remarks.para: Assign the ordered pages array and choose defaultPage as a zero-based index: 0 is the first page. Unity's Awake setup call hides every page when the component first initializes; its disable call hides them again. OnEnable, Unity's call when the component becomes enabled on an active object, hides all pages and then activates a valid defaultPage. Set defaultPage = -1 for no opening page.

Use PAGESELECT with a valid index to change pages, or ALLOFF to hide them all. For example, with three page objects and defaultPage = 0, opening the panel activates the first page; PAGESELECT(2) selects the third; PAGESELECT() leaves all pages off because its omitted argument is -1.

These page methods switch Unity scene objects on and off. They do not themselves apply or save the player's preference values. Every array entry must be assigned, and page selection needs an index below the entry count.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.PullCordForceChange
member.summary: Requests a player avatar change when a physics object enters its trigger volume.

remarks.para: This is a Unity component, a script attached to a scene object. A trigger volume detects entry without acting as a solid wall. The entering collider, the shape Unity uses for contact detection, must have an attached Rigidbody, a component that lets physics move an object. The handler then uses the global player rig to find the pull cord; it does not check the entering object's identity before choosing that player.

The player inventory must have exactly one special-item slot, with a PullCordDevice on its first child. An active cord receives an animated ForceAvatarChange request. The sequence includes an initial 0.2-second wait, a glyph cycle with a 2-second timer advanced by the time between frames, and a 0.5-second wait before starting the avatar swap. A frame is one game update. Both waits and the glyph timer use scaled game time, controlled by Unity's Time.timeScale (the game-speed multiplier): positive values below 1 (0 < Time.timeScale < 1) stretch this sequence in real seconds; at 0, the waits and timer pause; Unity ignores negative values. At 1, the listed durations use normal game-time speed. Each WaitForSeconds resumes on a later game update, so the sequence is not a wall-clock completion guarantee. A cord whose own scene object is inactive instead uses the direct asynchronous SwapAvatar path, which can finish loading later.

Leave randomize false to request avatarCrate, or enable it to sample one of six candidate references and reject the rig's recorded current crate identifier. The active animation uses optionalPullCordStopIndex for a fixed request and choice for a random request. These are unitless glyph indices, with six valid positions numbered 0 through 5.

The constructor defaults onlyTriggerOnce to true and optionalPullCordStopIndex to -1. A one-use trigger is marked used after its request call without checking success, including when a busy cord ignores the request. For example, a scene transformation zone can request a chosen avatar on its first eligible entry and then reject later entries.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RandomObject
member.summary: Chooses a random list entry from when enabled, turns that entry on and turns the others off.

remarks.para: This acts on existing GameObjects, Unity scene objects holding components. It does not create copies in the inspected selection routine. Each enable on an active object makes a fresh random pick, which may choose the same position again. The Static Pick editor command runs that pick and then disables this component.

Use an assigned list of distinct, non-null objects. The routine visits positions in order, so a repeated object at a later unchosen position can be turned off after being chosen earlier. An object’s activation setting is also separate from whether its parent is active. Flipper only reapplies the current local size multipliers; it does not mirror or swap axes.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RigScreenOptions
member.summary: Chooses how the player's view appears on the spectator screen: a headset mirror, a separate following camera, or the Void overlay.

remarks.para: The separate camera follows a generated child of the headset's Camera.main through SmoothFollower. Its eye offset and tilt are set when Fisheye is applied. Passthrough instead selects Unity's headset-eye mirror output; Center in that mode selects both eyes.

Startup creates the follow target and applies saved spectator settings, falling back to cameraMode and eyeTarget if those settings are absent. Later Control_Player settings updates call SetSpectatorCamera again. To make an immediate temporary change, call that method after setup; assigning the fallback fields alone does not apply it or save it.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RoundProfileGroup
member.summary: Describes an arena engagement through ordered rounds, spawn pacing, reward rules and menu data.

remarks.para: This is a ScriptableObject, a reusable Unity data object that can be saved as an asset. Each group holds rounds, each round holds waves, and each wave holds lists of planned enemies and loot. These profiles describe what the arena should do; they are not the spawned characters or weapons.

At runtime, the arena controller is the object that selects active rounds and waves, starts spawn requests, and tracks live characters. It reads settings at different times: round and wave selection choose list entries, spawn routines read delay settings when starting waits, and mode entry applies mode and leaderboard choices. Changing a field does not necessarily rebuild the running mode or update an already started wait.

The copy and difficulty helpers have different effects. Some allocate new containers while sharing assets or friendly lists; others edit their input directly. Saved group statistics are not automatically refreshed by those helpers. Read each helper’s remarks before treating a copy as independent or a stored total as current.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.RoundProfileGroup.ArenaGameMode
member.summary: Selects the arena controller’s mode-specific entry, difficulty, protection, and score-submission behavior for a round profile group.

remarks.para: Assign one value to RoundProfileGroup.arenaGameMode. The numeric values are category choices from 0 to 6, with no physical units; they are not flags to combine. The controller reads the selected group’s value when entering, starting, running, and ending arena play. Changing the stored category alone does not immediately perform those actions.

A RoundProfileGroup’s roundProfileList contains its RoundProfiles; each profile’s waveGroupList contains that profile’s waves. Each RoundProfile also has a separate RoundMode. When the current profile’s wave list is exhausted, the inspected CheckProfileForNextWave routine proceeds to a later profile if one remains. Only when no later profile remains does it read the first profile’s RoundMode: LIMITED sets the arena state to WIN; UNLIMITED creates another wave when the group has fewer than two profiles, or another round otherwise. isObjectiveMode separately chooses objective behavior. The arena mode category alone does not supply enemies, a goal area, a weapon loadout, or an exact match duration.

Mode names are also separate from the text shown on the arena displays: the inspected display refresh uses the group’s displayTitle string. Set arenaGameMode explicitly when building a custom group; CreateCustomRound does not assign CUSTOM, and a fresh group’s zero-valued category is SURVIVAL.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SaveData.AmmoInventory
member.summary: A JSON data object representing global light, medium, and heavy ammunition totals; use for the player’s live ammunition inventory.

remarks.para: Each total is an integer stored in this object. Assigning one changes that stored value; its setter does not update the player’s ammunition, notify displays, or write a save file. For example, setting AmmoGlobalLight to 30 stores 30 in this object without adding ammunition to the player.

The audited campaign save and restore methods store ammunition in per-level dictionaries inside PlayerProgression.LevelState. Do not assume this separate data object is automatically synchronized with those dictionaries. To change the current player’s reserve, use the live Marrow.AmmoInventory component and its AddCartridge methods.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SaveData.GraphicsManager
member.summary: Applies graphics presets and individual rendering settings for the game.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SaveData.GraphicsManager.FoveatedRadii
member.summary: Chooses which central-region size or shape setting the foveated rendering controls edit.

remarks.para: Foveated rendering keeps more image detail near the center of the view and reduces shading work farther away. The selectors choose the outer-angle percentage, inner-to-outer angle percentage, or one-axis ellipse scale. Their numbered values are selector identifiers, not the percentages themselves.

RDM is the fallback method; VRS requests hardware variable-rate shading. The outer-radius and inner-ratio settings are shared between these modes. These values choose which setting a radius-control method edits; they do not select the rendering mode. For manual radii, use the Custom foveated preset: an enabled built-in preset replaces the stored percentages with its own values, while Disabled leaves the edit unapplied. The increase/decrease controls choose Custom first; SetFoveatedCustomRadii does not.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SaveData.PlayerSettings
member.summary: Stores the player’s saved avatar choices, movement controls, body measurements, audio levels, and interface switches. The save file uses JSON, a text format for stored data, and gives each setting a key (its name in the file) chosen by the JsonProperty label in code.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScreenOptions.GUIType
member.summary: Selects how ScreenOptions draws and handles one item among the on-screen controls and text.

remarks.para: GUI means the on-screen controls and text. A GUIItem is one queued item: one entry waiting in the list until EndGUI, the method that draws and handles the list, processes it. Each GUIItem combines this choice with its label, numeric value and range, and optional callbacks. A callback is a routine called to perform an action or report a result. EndGUI uses the choice to draw a button, divider, text label or slider with numeric entry. BOX items are skipped; the panel background box is drawn independently.

This is a selector for screen GUI drawing, not a size, duration or strength. The helper methods GUIButton, GUILine, GUILabel and GUISlider add the appropriate item types. EndGUI measures their layout, draws and processes them, then clears the queued list. Rebuild the items for each drawing pass and retain changed settings in the calling code rather than expecting this enum or the queued item to store the result.

Button callbacks receive true or false for click/no-click, and slider callbacks receive the resulting number even when it has not changed. Labels and lines have no action callbacks in this renderer. Selecting an interactive type provides the control; its callback determines what changing it does in the game.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScrollButton
member.summary: Makes a UI button move a scrollbar by one animated step or by repeated animated moves while held.

remarks.para: Assign a scrollbar connected to the scrollable view and its ScrollElementsContainer before startup. A Button, Unity's clickable UI component, must be on this same scene object. Awake, Unity's first setup call, caches that Button. Start, its startup call before normal updates, copies stepSize into signedStepSize, negating it for DOWN, and registers the scrollbar and container notifications.

The scrollbar position normally ranges from 0 to 1 across its travel. With incremental true, an allowed press starts one animation toward current position plus signedStepSize. With incremental false, holding the button schedules repeated moves whose target change is signedStepSize multiplied by the handle-size fraction rounded to two decimal places. For a signed step 0.1 and rounded size 0.2, a repeated move requests a change of 0.02.

Both modes animate using coroutines, routines that pause and resume across frames. scrollFrequency is measured in seconds of game time for the animation and held-mode repeat interval. Unity's time-scale setting can make game time pass faster or slower than real time, or pause it at zero. The true path uses the refactored duration-based animation. The older animation used by the false path has a calculation bug that makes positive-duration progress follow about one accumulated second of game time; frequent repeats can cancel it before it finishes.

Press permission is disabled at the directional endpoint after value rounding, and a container-change check also disables it if the handle fills the track. Those checks stop repetition and animation. Release separately schedules stopScrolls about 0.2 seconds later, so releasing need not stop motion immediately. Cache settings such as signedStepSize and event subscriptions are established at startup and are not automatically rebuilt when you replace their source fields.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScrollButton.ScrollButtonDirection
member.summary: Selects whether a scroll button increases or decreases its scrollbar value.

remarks.para: UP is 0 and DOWN is 1. With a positive configured stepSize, UP increases the scrollbar value toward 1 and DOWN decreases it toward 0. Scrollbar values are unitless fractions of the full range, from 0 to 1; they are not pixel or metre distances. The scroll view’s wiring determines how those values move the visible content.

Start, Unity’s initialization call before the component’s first regular update, calculates and saves the signed step once. UP keeps stepSize and DOWN negates it. Choose the direction before initialization. Changing direction afterward changes the later endpoint checks but does not recompute that saved step; the button can then stop at a different end from the direction it moves.

Incremental mode aims one step away from the current value. Repeating scroll mode scales the step by the scrollbar handle’s size, rounded to two decimal places, then limits the target to 0–1. Movement routines resume across frames. Direction chooses the sign; it does not choose the step size, repetition interval or a precise travel duration.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.ScrollElementsContainer
member.summary: Forwards changes to a scroll container’s child list to its registered listener routines.

remarks.para: Unity’s hierarchy is the tree of scene objects; children are objects placed directly under a parent. When Unity reports that this container’s child list changed, this component immediately calls OnContainerChildrenChanged if assigned. A callback is a routine called for a notification; these callbacks take no arguments and return no result.

Connected ScrollButton components subscribe during startup so a child-list change can refresh whether their buttons can still scroll. The container sends the notification, and those listeners perform the refresh. It does not keep its own list of scrolling items or resize the contents in this notification routine.

For example, adding an item under the container can notify a button that previously had no further scrolling available. Keep existing listeners when adding your own; replacing the callback field replaces the registered list.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SecurityCamera
member.summary: Turns a security-camera prop toward the scene’s main-view camera and provides sound and visual feedback for save-indicator requests.

remarks.para: Tracking uses Camera.main, Unity’s enabled camera marked MainCamera, and cameraRb, the simulated physics body representing the camera prop. It requests blended world rotations toward that view camera’s position. The aim-change threshold decides when to capture a new target, and cameraMoveSpeed controls the blend rate rather than a fixed number of degrees per second.

Supply the entity and camera body references, plus the sound, cone, particle system, material and renderer array for save indication. Awake, Unity’s initialization callback, registers this camera with its entity’s culling notifications; a callback is a routine called to perform or report an action. Culling is the entity system’s temporary inactivity processing. OnEntityUncull prepares a fresh aim; this camera’s OnEntityCull does nothing.

IndicateSave and IndicateSaveAsync start the same effects without making the caller wait for the whole interval. They provide feedback rather than writing game progress. The game-time delay hides only flashCone; slow motion extends that delay in real time. The routines issue no particle Stop command or material restoration, and separate requests can overlap.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SimpleGripEvents
member.summary: Connects grab, release, index-trigger presses, and short menu taps from selected grips to configurable actions.

remarks.para: Fill Grips and configure the UnityEvents before Awake, Unity's initialization callback, runs. A UnityEvent stores the function calls you want to run, such as turning on a light or playing a sound, and these events receive no arguments identifying a hand or grip.

Enable doNotRetriggerOnMultiGirp before use to run grab actions for the first hand and release actions for the last hand. That option does not combine or suppress either hand’s trigger and menu input.

Awake connects this component's callback methods to the grips' notifications, and OnDestroy disconnects them when the component is destroyed. The audited callbacks do not check whether this component is enabled, so disabling it alone does not disconnect it from grip notifications.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SmoothFollower
member.summary: Smoothly moves and turns this object toward a target transform during the player's main-camera updates.

remarks.para: A transform holds an object's position, rotation and scale. Assign targetTransform to the object whose world position and facing should be followed. The follower moves toward that position and then turns toward that rotation, remembering movement and turning rates between steps. It does not copy scale or apply a separate offset.

When enabled, it registers MoveCameraUpdate as a callback, a saved function to call later, on the player controller's camera-update signal. Disabling removes that callback. The signal fires when the main camera begins rendering, after camera-related tracking work. The target and player references must already be ready; an active update requires an assigned target.

TranslationSmoothTime and RotationalSmoothTime are unitless multipliers here. Each is multiplied by the current frame interval in scaled game-time seconds to obtain its smoother's response interval. For example, either multiplier at 0.15 with a 0.02-second frame supplies 0.003 seconds of response time, not a fixed 0.15-second completion deadline.

For example, placing a separate target beside a moving object makes this follower catch up to that point and its facing. These changes are written directly to the transform; they are not forces applied to a Rigidbody, Unity's physics-body component. Changing the target or briefly disabling the follower preserves its remembered smoothing rates.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SplineBody
member.summary: A that uses adjustable physics joints to keep a body on a curved path and drive it toward a requested speed.

remarks.para: A spline is a curved path. A Rigidbody is Unity's physics body for an object, and a ConfigurableJoint is a physics connection with adjustable movement and rotation rules. Awake, Unity's initial component setup method, adds one, two, or four contact joints on this object according to contactCount. These joints later connect body anchor points to points along the path.

Assign a Rigidbody and a splineJoint controller. The inherited Start method, Unity's component startup step, attaches the entity to an assigned controller and registers it for updates. The controller's FixedUpdate, Unity's regularly spaced physics update, reconfigures the joints after enough contact-origin movement or a requested settings refresh.

The controller allows movement along the contacts' X direction while restricting sideways movement. Each joint's X drive receives targetVelocity in distance units per second, positionDamper as the strength of speed-error correction, and maximumForce as a force ceiling in newtons. These are motor requests and settings; they do not guarantee an exact actual speed.

Use SetTargetVelocity, SetPositionDamper and SetMaximumForce for runtime changes: they store a value, request a refresh and wake the Rigidbody. Direct property assignments only change storage. For example, with valid references and generated joints, SetTargetVelocity(2) requests a drive speed of 2 metres per second at Unity's usual one-unit-per-metre scale.

angularXMotion controls X-axis rotation for a one-contact body. With two or four contacts, the configuration sets angular motion to Free. The stored angularXLimit, angularXLimitBounciness and angularXLimitContactDistance settings are not applied by the inspected body setup or spline joint configuration and update methods.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SplineEntity.ContactCount
member.summary: Chooses the attachment layout used by to keep a spline body following its curved path.

remarks.para: A spline is the curved path. These contacts are anchor locations for ConfigurableJoints, physics connections that restrict or drive body motion. They are separate from collision points produced when collider shapes touch.

ONE uses the configured anchor, an offset from the object’s origin along its local axes, without extra size offsets. TWO uses the two ends of _size.y, the full contact length. FOUR adds _size.x, the full contact width, to use four rectangle corners. Anchor and size values use Unity distance units; their numeric values correspond to metres only when 1 Unity unit equals 1 metre in the scene. The length follows the contact frame’s X direction and the width its Z direction; axis and secondaryAxis orient that frame relative to the body.

SplineJoint updates the connection targets from the path. ONE also applies angularXMotion around the configured primary direction and locks the other angular axes; TWO and FOUR free the individual joints’ angular axes and use separated contact positions that affect body alignment.

Select one named value; these are choices, not flags to combine. Set the choice before SplineBody.Awake, Unity’s initialization callback—a routine called when setting up the component. That routine allocates one, two or four contact joints. A later contactCount assignment does not itself rebuild that array to match the new choice.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.SplineJoint
member.summary: Updates physical contact joints so registered bodies can follow a sampled rail.

remarks.para: A spline is a smooth path made from curved sections. This component approximates it with sampled points and straight links. SplineBody components supply Rigidbodies, the Unity components simulating motion and forces, and contact joints. A joint connects a simulated body to a constraint; this solver places its contact anchors against the sampled path, allowing movement along the joint’s primary axis while restricting sideways movement.

Awake, Unity’s initialization routine, caches the squared movement threshold and rebuilds the path. UpdatePath also replaces membership lists and reattaches the previous entities, which can change their positions and rotations. Generic SplineEntity entries are registered but are not processed as physical SplineBody entries in FixedUpdate.

FixedUpdate, Unity’s routine for physics steps, samples each physical body’s contact origin and sends segment-index notifications before checking the movement threshold. The threshold gates contact-joint refresh rather than rebuilding the rail or all lookup work. Set up the spline and body components, and use attachment and rebuild routines instead of changing only the internal cache lists. Segment notifications have their own index rule and are not ordinary collider collision events.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.StaticProfiles
member.summary: Stores shared game-wide lookups for NPC profiles, arena loot, ammunition, pickup assets, controller templates and alliance defaults.

remarks.para: This is a ScriptableObject, a Unity asset that stores data separately from scene objects. A newly constructed profile has empty NPC, loot, alliance and private weapon-crate lists, plus the default hub-level reference. Supply the other settings through the configured asset or your own setup code.

CreateStatProfile makes a supplied profile the shared object returned by instance. BaseGameController normally does that during Awake, Unity's setup call when a component starts, if the shared object is missing. Reading instance does not load the asset named by path.

Each setting takes effect when a controller reads it: for example, round helpers choose a saved NPC profile, while a later spawner requests its object. Assignment alone does not create NPCs, refill ammunition or rebuild an already configured controller. Some lists depend on their entry order, so read the individual list remarks before changing them.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TimeTrial_GameController
member.summary: Controls kill-quota or speed-run completion on top of the base session and timer controller.

remarks.para: Configure a kill trial with difficulty quotas and spawner profiles, or a speed run with a scene finish notification. Startup can begin automatically or wait for the start callback. The inherited timerMode selects how the timer advances; a coroutine is a routine that pauses and resumes over later frames to update it.

The controller listens for registered NPC deaths and player spawning while enabled. Enemy counts are maintained by the base controller before the trial’s death checker runs. Player spawning adds configured ammunition, and kill thresholds can request separate indicators pointing toward remaining enemies.

Completion events run before the session flag is cleared and the stored timer is stopped. Configure assigned arrays, spawner references and scene notifications before starting. Selecting a difficulty, requesting a spawn and receiving a completed spawned object are separate stages; the controller’s flags are not proof that all spawn requests succeeded.

Its leaderboard helper selects and queries the board for the current difficulty; the inspected helper does not submit a score. Required quota text and recorded kills are separate values, and ProgPointKillCount changes the quota rather than awarding kills.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TimeTrial_GameController.TTDifficulty
member.summary: Chooses which configured kill target, spawner preset and leaderboard entry a time trial uses.

remarks.para: An enum is a named integer choice. EASY is 0, MEDIUM is 1 and HARD is 2. These numbers are zero-based array positions, not damage multipliers, seconds or fixed enemy counts. UpdateDifficulty reads the matching entry in diffReqKillCount, a list of whole-number enemy death targets, then applies the matching preset to every assigned difficulty spawner.

A preset chooses the asset that the spawner will create and the enemy configuration attached to that spawn. It also copies its home-post setting and, when a spawn point is assigned, moves and turns the spawner to that point. The position is in world space, the scene-wide coordinate system measured in metres. An enabled preset aggression flag sets the spawner's aggression mode; a disabled flag leaves that mode unchanged, so switching presets can retain a previous mode.

The selected kill target must be positive and no greater than the number of configured profile spawners. Otherwise the controller uses that spawner count. For an active kill-all trial, reaching the applied death target ends the session. For example, if the level provides targets of 3, 5 and 8, applying MEDIUM selects 5 deaths; those values come from the level, not this enum.

Setting ttDifficulty only stores the choice. UpdateDifficulty applies the target and spawner configuration. SpawnDifficultyCrates separately requests the configured spawns; applying a preset does not itself create an object. SetLeaderboardByDifficulty separately focuses the corresponding configured leaderboard entry. These calls do not guarantee a spawn or a network result has already completed.

During Start, Unity's one-time startup call, a kill-all trial with a nonempty difficulty-spawner array resets and applies EASY. Later choices can be applied through UpdateDifficulty. Required arrays, entries and components must be assigned before applying a choice.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TimeTrial_GameController.TimeTrialMode
member.summary: Selects whether a time trial finishes on reaching its enemy-kill requirement or receiving its player end-trigger call.

remarks.para: KILLS is integer value 0: a registered death notification can finish an active trial when the recorded enemy-death total is at least the required whole-number count. SPEED_RUN is value 1: the player end-trigger routine finishes an active trial without testing that count.

These are completion rules. The separate timeTrialStartMode selects starting automatically or through the player start-trigger routine. Assigning a mode changes the rule read by later completion checks; the assignment alone does not start a run, reset its recorded counts or finish it.

For example, a ten-kill challenge can use KILLS to finish as soon as the death check sees a total of ten. A race can use SPEED_RUN and arrange for the level’s finish area to call the end-trigger routine.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TimeTrial_GameController.TimeTrialStartMode
member.summary: Chooses whether the trial starts during controller startup or through its configured start-trigger action.

remarks.para: ON_START makes the Unity Start callback begin the session after setup; a callback is a routine called to perform an action. ON_TRIGGER skips that automatic start and allows TIMETRIAL_PlayerStartTrigger to begin it while no session is ongoing. Configure the physical trigger’s event connection when using that route.

This selects these start paths, not the timer’s counting direction or pacing; timerMode selects the timer routine. Changing the mode does not itself start or end a session, and a direct BeginSession call is a separate way to begin one.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Treadmill
member.summary: Scrolls a material's _BaseMap texture each frame to make a conveyor or treadmill belt look as though it is moving.

remarks.para: Put this component on an object with a Renderer, the component that draws its surface. Start, Unity's one-time startup call, stores that renderer's material in materialMill. Each later Update call, which runs once per frame while the component is enabled, changes the texture offset on the stored material. The material must support a visible _BaseMap texture offset.

directionMill contains horizontal and vertical scrolling rates in texture-coordinate units per game second. Texture coordinates, also called UVs, choose which part of an image is drawn on the surface. Each frame sets the offset to (x × t, y × t), where x and y are the two current rates and t is elapsed game time in seconds. It uses time since the game's time origin, not time since this component started. An offset of 1 is one full texture-coordinate width or height.

For example, directionMill = (0.1, 0) gives an offset of (1, 0) at 10 game seconds. A repeating texture can keep showing the belt pattern as the offset grows. The inspected update changes only the material offset, so physical conveyor movement or forces on riders need separate behavior. Changing the rate during play can make the pattern jump to the newly calculated offset.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Trial_SpawnerEvents
member.summary: Tracks reported deaths from configured enemies and runs local completion actions at a calculated quota.

remarks.para: The component registers for spawn notifications while enabled. For each suitable spawned object, it connects a callback, a method called when an event happens, to that AI brain's NPC death event. Both death-handler methods record one death per call.

The quota is the configured array length multiplied by requiredPerc, then rounded upward to an integer. The array length is the number of crateSpawners entries, and requiredPerc is a unitless fraction: 0.5 means half, while 1 means all. For five entries and 0.5, the product is 2.5 and the quota becomes three deaths. Inactive entries still count toward the length; this does not count how many enemies have actually spawned.

Startup sets the optional quota text and can broadcast a count through the static OnTotalKillCalc callback, which is shared across instances. useSpawnerTotal selects that broadcast's number, not the local quota. A qualifying death invokes the completion listeners, requests sound, sets the completion flag and then refreshes the death text.

The inspected lifecycle methods do not reset the death count or completion flag on re-enable. Completion is normally handled once after the flag is set, but listeners can re-enter a death handler before that assignment. Configure the spawner references and event listeners before enabling this component.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TutorialElevator
member.summary: Runs the tutorial elevator's timed door closure, moving shaft scenery, scripted cab motion, and fall-to-level-completion sequence.

remarks.para: StartElevator requires playerInElevator to be true. It begins a coroutine, a sequence that can pause and continue on later frames: request door closure, wait doorWaitDuration seconds of game time, freeze and place the panels with SealDoors, then start the director timeline. It also sets the cached player health to Invincible. The remaining public methods provide the later ascent, slowdown, swing, fall, and impact steps.

The ascent and fall methods move TutorialShaft scenery around the cab to simulate travel. The swing and near-weightless phase also change the cab's physics joint, a connection that constrains movement between objects. During the near-weightless phase, the Y curve requests a joint target rather than directly setting the cab's measured position.

The fall changes Physics.gravity for the whole physics scene, including objects outside the elevator. StartImpact stops the shaft loops, disables the spark objects, freezes the cab's moving physics body, and starts a brief gravity pulse. The completion sequence restores the saved gravity before completing the Descent level if its game controller is found.

This expects the tutorial's scene setup: valid shaft references, door controllers, a cab joint and physics body, and at least four door panel bodies in the expected order. SealDoors writes fixed parent-relative panel X positions. The stored doorRoutine handle and isClosing flag record requests and sequence bookkeeping; they do not prove the panels are currently moving or that the ride has finished.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TutorialRig
member.summary: Shows controller models, button highlights, direction arrows, and text or pictures for one controller tutorial at a time.

remarks.para: CUSTOMTUTORIAL applies a new display immediately: it selects controller art for the detected hardware when needed, chooses the hands to show, sends text and pictures, starts following and fading, and optionally schedules display deactivation. Starting another tutorial replaces the staged contents and cancels the previous display timeout; this is not a waiting queue.

Level-load setup connects hand attachment events to tooltip holding-state updates and gives headTitles its player-manager reference. The separate head-title display has its own API. The saved tooltip-display setting can deactivate this rig's entire GameObject.

DEACTIVETUTORIAL fades controller prompts out, hides arrows, and clears active-tutorial bookkeeping. TUTORIALSCALE sizes this object for avatar eye height. Directly editing cached fields does not perform these display/setup operations.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TutorialRig.InputHighlight
member.summary: Chooses which control illustration blinks on a tutorial's controller model.

remarks.para: TutorialRig.CUSTOMTUTORIAL passes the left and right choices to ControllerTutorialArt.HIGHLIGHTACTION on the selected models. Their GameObjects must be active in the scene hierarchy for a highlight to start. The selection changes renderers on the tutorial model, not actual controller input. In the audited implementation, none and touchpad start no highlight and do not cancel one that is already blinking.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TutorialRig.LocationHighlight
member.summary: Chooses the direction arrows shown around a tutorial controller's joystick.

remarks.para: Use values ending in _l for CUSTOMTUTORIAL's left-hand location argument and values ending in _r for its right-hand argument. The switches recognize different numeric ranges for the two hands; a value for the other hand does not select the corresponding direction.

The arrows are configured art objects parented to the selected controller model's joystick, not directions in world space or targets for the player to walk toward. none_l and none_r hide that side's arrow root and all four directions. Other choices turn their arrows on without clearing every old direction, so an earlier selection can remain visible until it is explicitly cleared or the tutorial ends.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TutorialRig.SpecificHand
member.summary: Chooses which controller instructions a tutorial sends, and which hand can start it through the standard grab or trigger callbacks.

remarks.para: both sends instructions for both sides; either follows the hand that caused the interaction; left and right select a fixed side. These choices do not control which physical hands are allowed to hold an object.

CUSTOMTUTORIAL applies the choice when starting a display request. Its either choice uses isRightHand; callers must supply the side they mean. TutorialGrip and TutorialTrigger also use the choice to decide which hand notification starts or ends a tutorial, subject to their repeat and exit settings.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.Tween
member.summary: Prepares its object with disabled collision shapes and zero local scale.

remarks.para: During Start, Unity’s setup call before this component’s first normal update, this component saves the colliders on its own object and its children, including inactive children. A collider is an invisible shape Unity uses to detect contact. It disables those colliders and then sets its own object’s local scale to (0, 0, 0).

Local scale gives three size multipliers along the object’s own axes relative to its parent. The values have no distance unit: 1 keeps the original size along an axis, while 0 shrinks that axis to zero. Setting all three to zero collapses the object’s size. This does not turn off its Unity object.
The private EnableColliders helper enables the saved collision shapes, but does not restore scale or search for new colliders. DoTheTween performs no operation in this implementation.

For example, an object with this component can disappear when startup shrinks it to zero. Showing it later requires restoring its scale separately; enabling its cached colliders only changes their contact detection.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.TweenRotation
member.summary: Turns its object toward a saved target position over one game-clock second, using a curve to shape the rotation blend.

remarks.para: LookAtRotationTween reads the supplied target Transform's world position and starts a coroutine. A Transform stores an object's position, orientation, and size; world position means its position in the scene's shared coordinate system. A coroutine is a routine Unity can pause and resume on later frames.

When the routine starts, it saves this object's world orientation and calculates a target orientation from the direction to that saved position. The target points the object's forward axis, its local positive Z direction, toward that position, with the scene's positive Y direction as the usual up reference. It does not copy the target object's own orientation. Both orientations are stored as quaternions, Unity's four-number representation of orientation.

Each update advances a timer by Time.deltaTime, the game-clock time since the previous frame. It limits the curve input to the first second, reads curve for a unitless blend amount, blends the saved starting and target orientations, writes this Transform's world rotation, and pauses until the next coroutine step. Slowing or pausing the game clock also slows or pauses timer progress; frame timing determines the exact real-time duration.

The target position and both orientations are calculated once. A moving target is not followed after that snapshot, and moving this object during the turn does not recalculate its aim. For example, if a sign starts turning toward a walking player, it continues turning toward the place where the player was when the call began.

Provide a valid target Transform and curve before calling the method. The routine finishes when its timer reaches one game-clock second and keeps the last blended orientation. To reach the target orientation, the curve's output at time 1 must be 1; there is no separate final snap. The curve's output is a blend amount rather than an angle in degrees.

Calling LookAtRotationTween again starts another routine without stopping an earlier one. While both run, they can write different rotations to the same Transform on successive updates. This component writes orientation directly; its inspected methods do not apply a turning force or torque through a physics body.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.UIControllerInput
member.summary: Polls a selected VR controller to position a UI input object, operate the popup menu and request hold-to-reset scene reloads.

remarks.para: isLeft selects both the controller input and the matching virtual-skeleton hand pose. The virtual skeleton is the set of body-pose Transforms stored by the player rig. Update copies that hand's world position and rotation to this scene object. A Transform holds position, rotation and scale; world coordinates are relative to the scene. CursorTarget separately chooses a valid override Transform or the configured default for popup opening calculations.

The normal menu-button hold path uses a real-time press timestamp and a strict hold longer than 0.15 seconds, together with its controller/global-menu conditions. Menu reports are forwarded to PopUpMenuView, which performs the selected action or forwards input to its panels. The separate app-menu input starts a scaled-time reload counter; releasing it normally cancels that sequence. Exact hardware button bindings depend on BaseController.

A coroutine is a sequence continuing across several frames. When the counter reaches m_levelReloadCounter, it calls ResetLevel if still held, then disables the release-opening flag. ResetLevel requests the default fadeout effect; a callback, a routine called to perform or report an action, connects fade completion to SceneStreamer.Reload. A counter finishing is not proof that a level has loaded.

This component relies on initialized PlayerRefs, controller/player rigs, UIRig popup and HUD references, and a usable cursor Transform. Start stops its existing coroutines, clears the recorded app-menu held flag and enables release opening. Its stored flags/iterator are recorded state, not reliable live hardware/menu/loading status in every early-return or cancellation case.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.UIRig
member.summary: Connects the player's HUD, pop-up menu, settings and feedback components, and resizes selected UI roots for the avatar.

remarks.para: Awake, Unity's initialization callback, registers Instance. Startup refreshes and initializes the HUD; enabling the rig registers an early-update action that shares the menu's active state with the player controller rig. These references point to existing configured components; assigning them does not create the UI.

UI_AVATARSCALE records the arm-length ratio and applies that ratio times uiScale to scaleOffset transforms. The normal BodyVitals layout refresh additionally sends the ratio to the pop-up menu to update its placement. Menu pages and settings panels can copy the shared feedback and settings references, so changing a rig field does not automatically replace copies already held elsewhere.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.UI_HUD
member.summary: Displays the player’s reserve ammunition, positions HUD panels near the head or inventory, and animates the level-reset popup.

remarks.para: HUD means heads-up display: information shown to the player during play. Setup connects this component to ammunition changes and hand-slot insert and remove notifications, and caches a player-head Transform. A Transform stores an object’s position, rotation, and scale. A GameObject is a scene object that can hold components and be active or hidden. A Renderer draws a scene object; its material stores visual settings. An AudioSource is a component that plays sounds. Assign the panel GameObjects, their position targets, the reset AudioSource, and the reset scale curve before using these routines.

The ammo text reads the inventory’s light, medium, and heavy reserve counts, measured as whole numbers of rounds, rather than bullets currently loaded into a gun. A zero count shows emptyNote instead of the number. SHOWAMMO chooses None to hide the panel, Belt to place it at the belt target, Head to use the selected left or right head target, or Inventory to use the inventory target. While active, the ammo-follow routine copies that target’s world position and rotation each physics update; world space is the shared scene coordinate system.

HEADHUDFOLLOW enables a separate follower near the cached player head. Its requested position is the head’s world position plus its forward direction multiplied by offset_HeadDistance, a signed distance measured in Unity world units—the units used by positions in the shared scene coordinate system. This code does not convert that value to metres. The constructor sets the distance to 1 world unit; for example, a head at world position (0, 1.6, 0) facing world +Z gives a requested position of (0, 1.6, 1). Smoothing can add up to 0.2 world units of movement correction. Turning following off resets the follower’s world position to zero and its rotation to identity (no rotation), then deactivates its GameObject. With a positive HEADHUDFOLLOWTIMED countdown, the timer starts following if it is off, subtracts Time.deltaTime in scaled game-clock seconds (slow motion makes it count down more slowly in real time), and turns following off when the countdown reaches zero or less on a later physics update; a zero or negative countdown turns following off the first time the timer runs.

POPUPRELOADSCENE starts an opening or closing animation for the reset panel and enables head following when needed. Opening starts a progress routine with a 2-second timer target only when no progress routine is already stored; it requests the hold sound whether or not it starts one. Closing stops that progress routine, requests the cancel sound, and shrinks the panel before hiding it and turning head following off. The progress routine updates a material value on the bar and clears its stored routine reference when its timer finishes; that completion body does not itself request a scene reload.

The animations run as coroutines, sequences that Unity pauses and resumes over several frames. Their counters use Time.deltaTime in scaled game-clock seconds between physics updates, so slow motion makes them take longer in real time and timer limits do not guarantee completion at an exact wall-clock time or frame. The reset scale curve’s horizontal input is elapsed animation seconds divided by the reset routine’s internal duration in seconds; its vertical output is a unitless blend fraction clamped from 0 to 1, from the cached starting scale toward the open or collapsed scale. In this build, the constructor initializes the separate public timeToScale field to 1 second and the internal duration to 0.5 seconds; the curve uses the internal duration. While opening, the counter advances by Time.deltaTime; while closing, it advances by six times Time.deltaTime, so the closing scale sweep traverses the same curve six times faster.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.UtilityModes
member.summary: Chooses whether the spawn gun fires its placement action or its object-removal action.

remarks.para: SPAWNER is integer value 0 and REMOVER is integer value 1. These are choices, not distances, times, or flags to combine. The gun’s mode-selection routine stores the choice and updates its user interface, meaning its menus and labels; firing later reads that stored choice.

SPAWNER requests the selected catalog object or, for an avatar record, a player-body change. REMOVER tries to despawn the eligible entity found by the gun’s saved aiming hit and protects targets carrying its player tag. Selecting a mode by itself performs neither firing action.

For example, choose SPAWNER to request a copy of a selected prop, then choose REMOVER and fire at an eligible spawned prop to remove its active entity. The placement request can finish later; a selected mode is not a report of successful spawning or removal. The inspected firing routine performs neither action for other integer values.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.VRInputModule
member.summary: The shared base for VR menu input modules, storing pointer input and preparing Unity UI pointer records.

remarks.para: The EventSystem is Unity’s manager for menu input and selection. This abstract base supplies pointer caching, mouse-style and touch-style data collection, hover and drag helpers, and selection cleanup. Abstract means another component, such as VRStandaloneInputModule, supplies the processing loop that uses these helpers.

UpdateRaycastPosition stores a caller-supplied origin, direction and press flag. Mouse collection updates the primary record with ID -1 and asks registered raycasters for hits. The press flag becomes Pressed or Released on every collection pass, without detecting whether a physical button changed from the previous pass. A menu can supply a one-update pulse rather than a continuously held value.

The registered raycaster decides how hits are found. In the inspected VRGraphicRaycaster path, the pointer’s 2D position is used; the stored 3D origin and direction are copied to pointer data but do not by themselves prove a hit test in that direction. Hit collection, hover updates and click dispatch are separate steps, so an immediately queried hover cache can still describe an earlier target.

ClearSelection sends hover cleanup for cached pointers, clears their dictionary and deselects the EventSystem object. It retains the stored supplied input and mouse-state object. Pointer IDs, such as -1, identify cached records; button types, such as Left with value 0, identify buttons inside mouse state. Those numbers are different kinds of labels.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.VRInputModule.ButtonState
member.summary: Pairs an input-button identifier with the reusable event data consumed by the VR UI input processor.

remarks.para: MouseState.GetButtonState returns the already tracked record for the requested button, or creates one with a new MouseButtonEventData object. The button property identifies the UI button role: Left, Right or Middle. The eventData property holds the reported press/release state and the pointer record used to find the UI target and process the interaction.

MouseState.SetButtonState updates the existing event-data object. The press and release checks read its buttonState, including both checks for PressedAndReleased. The UI processor then consumes its pointer data to handle the reported button action, pointer movement and dragging. These are reports for processing during a game update, not a record of how long a physical button has been held.

For example, the VR raycast-pointer update fills the Left record, which the standalone UI processor reads. Left here is the UI mouse-button role; it does not choose a left-hand controller. Records are reused, so retaining eventData keeps a reference to changing data. Replacing that reference alone stores data and does not dispatch an interaction.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.VRInputModule.MouseState
member.summary: Caches pointer-button event records and the latest raycast-hit flag for the VR input module to process.

remarks.para: Each button record saves which mouse-style button it represents, its event label and its pointer details. GetButtonState reuses the record for that button or creates one on first request; SetButtonState updates the saved label and pointer details. The press and release checks scan all tracked records, and PressedAndReleased counts for both checks.

The base VRInputModule gathers pointer-raycast results, updates hasHitUIElement from the selected result's object validity, and refreshes the left-button event from its stored pressed-input flag. A raycast tests what the pointer's pointing line meets. This cached hit flag does not identify which object was hit; the pointer event data carries those details.

For example, a stored PressedAndReleased record makes both button checks true even when the hit flag is false. Button labels and hit status describe different pieces of saved data. Querying this object does not take a new sample or consume an event, so refresh its records before using them for another frame.

The base producer writes Pressed while its stored pressed-input flag is true and Released while it is false, without detecting a change from the previous sample here. Treat its labels according to that behavior rather than assuming every true check proves a new physical press or release. Mouse-event processing later copies the cached hit flag into VRStandaloneInputModule's public report.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.WaveProfile
member.summary: Describes one arena wave’s enemy entries, friendly target count, concurrency limit, loot and ammunition.

remarks.para: A wave is one group of enemy spawn requests inside a round. This class stores the settings; arena controllers and loot spawners act on them. Ordinary enemies follow the enemy list in order, with a limit based on the recorded active enemy count. In CUSTOM and PROTECT modes, the friendly list’s size sets a target count; the inspected friendly routine uses a predefined friendly type.

A new profile starts with empty enemy and friendly lists, maxConcurrent = 3 and hoiPoiChance = 2, meaning a 20% capsule-request chance when the ordinary enemy loop has a launcher. Its ammunition counts start at 0, and lootItems still needs a list assigned. For example, add four enemy entries, keep a limit of 3, assign an empty loot list and set lightBulletAmount to 40: the ordinary loop can request three enemies before waiting for room, and a separate loot request supplies 40 light rounds through a pickup.

The controller chooses its current wave at wave startup. Ordinary spawning repeatedly reads that wave’s enemy list, limit and capsule chance. Friendly target counts are captured at arena entry, while newly spawned ammo pickups obtain their amounts in later callbacks, meaning code called when an object has been created. Keep those different times in mind when changing settings during play.

Generated continuation waves are copies with difficulty adjustments. CopyWaveProfile creates new enemy and loot lists but shares the friendly list; profile objects inside the enemy list are also shared. The show flags are stored values and are not playback gates in the wave-start, enemy, friendly and loot routines inspected here.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.WeaponPack
member.summary: Stores a weapon pack's asset configuration and instance references, with grip notifications and return-to-spawn reset handling.

remarks.para: WeaponSpawner requests weaponSpawnable at weaponSpawn's world position and orientation. Its completion callback later saves the weapon object, discovers its pool component, host, grips, and root physics body, and performs the pack's spawn bookkeeping. A callback is a method another system runs later when a result or event is ready.

OnSpawnWeapon registers already supplied weapon and optional magazine hosts for WeaponResetVolume, sets isSpawned, and subscribes its grab notification to allGrips. It does not itself request asset creation. OnWeaponGrabbed sends this pack as the notification payload.

ResetHostObj returns a matching weapon or magazine host to its own configured spawn Transform and clears the corresponding saved physics body's motion when available. A Transform stores position, orientation, and size; a Rigidbody stores physics motion and responses to forces. Resetting changes world position and orientation directly, without rebinding components or inserting ammunition.

OnDespawnWeapon unregisters hosts and clears the spawned flag. Actual weapon pool despawn is a separate WeaponSpawner operation. Saved component references can remain after despawn bookkeeping; the flag is not a live existence test for a weapon and magazine.

The inspected spawner path also follows secondaryPack with a separate spawn request after this weapon completes. Separate magazine configuration fields are retained, but that complete request/completion path does not create or populate a companion magazine automatically. Configure required hosts, grips, and reset points before invoking their setup or reset methods.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.WeaponPack.MeleeType
member.summary: Labels a weapon pack’s melee category as bladed, such as a sword, or blunt, such as a club.

remarks.para: Store the category in WeaponPack.meleeType: use BLADE for the bladed category and BLUNT for the blunt category. This is separate from the pack’s main weaponType and its assigned weaponSpawnable object.

The checked WeaponPack spawn/despawn bookkeeping, grab notification and object-reset methods do not read this category. Choosing it does not change those operations or give a weapon new cutting or impact behavior through them. Any selection or damage rule using the category outside those methods needs its own consumer.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.WeaponPack.WeaponType
member.summary: Classifies a pack's configured weapon as ranged or melee and controls its melee grip lookup during spawn setup.

remarks.para: RANGED describes a distance weapon such as a gun. MELEE describes a close-contact weapon such as a sword or bat. The WeaponPack constructor initially chooses MELEE, while weaponSpawnable supplies the actual weapon asset requested by the spawner.

The spawner requests an object first; this classification is read later in the callback, the function called when the object is returned. With MELEE, it looks for a Grip on the weapon or its child objects and stores that result in weaponGrip. A Grip describes where a hand can hold an object. RANGED skips that extra lookup, while both choices receive the common interaction setup.

For example, configure a bat asset with MELEE or a gun asset with RANGED. Choosing the enum value describes the expected weapon and selects that setup branch; successful spawning and the weapon's damage or firing behavior depend on the requested asset and its components.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Bonelab.WeaponSpawner
member.summary: Connects weapon kiosks to preset and crate spawning, ammo replacement, tracked counts, and inventory cleanup.

remarks.para: A crate reference identifies an asset to request. A preset WeaponPack adds a weapon spawn point and optional secondary weapon; a default SpawnablePack is a list of crate selections. Spawn requests can finish later. A Poolee is the component that lets a completed object be removed from active play and reused by pooling.

Kiosk crate selections require permission and a tracked count below weaponLimit. Completed callbacks add objects to the count when a Poolee is found, rather than reserving count as each request starts. Direct preset and special-weapon methods have their own behavior and bypass that kiosk gate.

During Start, Unity’s setup call before the first normal update, the component registers assets, builds its preset lookup, and optionally schedules the default loadout. Default ammo uses three separately configured world spawn targets. World positions use Unity distance units, normally meters; orientation determines which way each object faces.

For example, configure a list of preset packs, a default crate list, the default/special points, and three ammo targets to build a kiosk. The broad DespawnAllWeapons reset can also remove items from cached or scene-wide inventory slots, while DespawnAllAmmo handles the cached ammo boxes separately.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Combat.AttackReceiver
member.summary: Turns an attack delivered to its ReceiveAttack method into a parameterless Unity event.

remarks.para: Use OnAttackReceived listeners for a configured response to a combat notification. A listener is a callback, a routine called to perform or report an action. The component implements IAttackReceiver so the attack-dispatch interface can call it; adding the component does not itself deliver an attack.

The checked ReceiveAttack implementation invokes the assigned event and does not inspect the Attack payload, apply damage, or maintain health. Its listeners receive no attack details. For example, several delivered attacks can produce several effect notifications without this component keeping a damage total.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Combat.RigidbodyProjectile
member.summary: A moving physics object that detonates on a collision or when it receives a piercing attack, sends a blast attack to eligible targets, and spawns its configured blast effect.

remarks.para: Assign the Rigidbody that carries its motion, a collider, audio arrays, and blastSpawnable. Awake, Unity’s initialization callback (a routine called to initialize the component), prepares targeting storage. OnEnable performs collision-ignore setup and, after the first two seconds of the level, zeroes the Rigidbody's velocity and clears the attacker reference. Another component must supply launch motion.

The blast searches around the incoming attack's origin or the collision contact point. Only returned colliders with an attached Rigidbody and a TriggerRefProxy on that Rigidbody object qualify; attack delivery goes to the GameObject of that proxy's targetHead. An object merely being inside BlastRadius is not enough. The temporary query buffer normally holds at most six colliders, and multiple colliders can represent the same target.

The blast disables col, applies the attack-layer and wall-blocking checks, spawns blastSpawnable at this projectile's world position and rotation, plays a hit clip there, and despawns this object if its GameObject is found in the Poolee cache. The audited blast method sends attacks but does not itself apply an explosion force to every nearby Rigidbody.

member.name: T:Il2CppSLZ.Combat.SpawnLauncher
member.summary: A component that registers a configured item crate and runs repeating waits, without requesting an item spawn.

remarks.para: Startup begins an asynchronous sequence, meaning work that can pause while the rest of the game continues.
